metadata.title: Level-Funded Health Plans Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Level-Funded Health Plans Explained.

Level-Funding is a hybrid employee health plan between a self-funded plan and a fully-insured plan.

Level-Funded plans have fixed monthly premiums to pay for claims, stop-loss insurance, administrative fees and the PBM.  That monthly premium is set for the year and goes through a 'renewal' similar to a fully-insured plan.

If the Level-Funded plan's claims come in lower than expected, then the insurance company 'may' credit back the employer or give them a refund.

If the Level-Funded plan's claims come in higher than expect, then the stop-loss insurance covers the higher claims.

There may a 'catch' where even if the employer's claims are low, the health insurance company may not give them a credit or refund, but instead just keeps the excess premium collected.

Level-Funded plans have grown in popularity.  For employers with 50-500 employees, 10 years ago, about 10% percent of covered lives were on Level-Funded plans.  Today, 45% of of covered lives for these size employers are covered by Level-Funded plans.

Lower risk employers have left the fully-insured market to become Level-Funded.  As result, the overall risk for fully-insured groups has gone up and accordingly, fully-insured premiums have risen rapidly.

Perhaps Level-Funding is creating a 'Death Spiral' in the fully-insured market.

Sources:

metadata.title: Level Funded vs. Fully Insured Health Plans: What Every Employer Needs to Know
metadata.author: Warp
metadata.shortDescription:
Health insurance rates jumped double digits in 2025, and many employers are stuck on fully insured small group plans with fixed rates and no flexibility. There's another option most brokers won't bring up: level-funded insurance.

In this video, Warp's Benefits Advisor, Dylan Munn, breaks down what level-funded plans are, how they work, and why they can deliver 60%+ cost savings compared to traditional fully insured plans. He also covers the tradeoffs you need to know, including how medical claims impact renewal rates, what an Individual Medical Questionnaire (IMQ) is, and why stop-loss policies matter.

You'll also learn why most brokers don't mention level-funded plans (hint: it's more work for them) and what to look for in a broker who actually understands how to make them work for your team.

Warp is the only AI-native HR & Payroll platform built for ambitious companies. Instead of clicking through clunky dashboards or .gov websites for taxes, Warp's AI agents open every state tax account, file every payroll form, and resolve every tax notice, automatically. Every company gets a dedicated Account Manager and Benefits Advisor included to guide them through payroll setup, multi-state expansion, and benefits selection.

Have questions? Reach out to our team at warp.co/benefits

  *  monetary advantages to level-funding

metadata.author: Tyler Dutchover
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a level-funded health plan? How does a level-funded health plan work? What are the Pros and Cons of a level-funded health plan?

This video breaks down how level-funding works for employers and businesses. With health insurance costs rising significantly for employers, level-funding is increasingly becoming a viable option to take back some control of healthcare costs. 

0:57 - Why Level-Funding Is Gaining in Popularity
2:18 - What is a Level-Funded Health Plan?
3:06 - An Example (Hypothetical)
4:02 - Pros & Cons

Other Videos 
What is an ICHRA? Pros & Cons: https://youtu.be/6Ig9Nd5MUoY
What is a Pharmacy Benefit Manager? Simple Explanation: https://youtu.be/ufeHEzWD1Cc
Why US Healthcare Is Crushing America’s Businesses: https://youtu.be/qO9tof7FxTE 
The Business of Weight Loss Drugs: https://youtu.be/8c0bNOXezMw 
Will AI Make Medical Bills Cheaper?: https://youtu.be/XIoOuDjlehU

of a work health insurance is projected
to increase 9.5% the highest increase in
17 years. This affects millions and
millions of Americans and hundreds of
thousands of American businesses. The
issue is with GLP-1s like Ozempic
exploding in popularity and big hospital
systems consolidating, this is actually
just the start of what's coming. Now,
most small and medium-sized businesses
will just accept these increases
believing that they are powerless.
They're too small to negotiate with
massive insurance carriers, so they just
accept the cost. But a growing number of
employers have discovered that they
don't have to participate in this
specific system. They can adopt
something called level funding to take
some control back. It's not as risky as
paying their employees medical bills all
themselves like big companies do, think
Tesla or Walmart, but it still legally
allows them to get their unused money
back at the end of the year if their
employees are relatively healthy. In
this video, we're going to break down
how level funding works in plain English
and look at the pros and cons of leaving
the traditional market. Let's dive in.
To understand why level funding is
gaining popularity with American
businesses, you have to understand the
fundamental problem of how most American
businesses buy insurance right now. Most
small and mid-size companies buy what's
called a fully insured plan. In this
setup, your company pays a fixed premium
to a big insurance company every single
month. In return, that insurance company
takes on all the risk. If somebody gets
sick or needs surgery, the insurance
company pays the bill. Sounds pretty
fair. It's kind of how insurance works,
but it might not actually be fair for
some of these businesses. Let's say your
business pays 300,000 in premiums over
the course of a year, but your workforce
is relatively young and healthy. They
only end up using 100K worth of actual
health care. So, what happens to that
extra 200,000? The insurance company
keeps every single penny of it, even
though you technically just helped them
pay for the health care needs of some
other company and help them pay their
shareholders. In this model, you're not
going to get a refund or even a thank
you for helping them out. Instead,
you're going to get higher rates the
next year. And this is exactly why level
funding was created. Big corporations
like Amazon and Walmart don't buy
traditional health insurance. They
self-fund, meaning they pay their
employees medical bills directly out of
their own bank accounts. But a typical
50-person company won't do that because
if they have an employee who gets a bad
cancer diagnosis or needs heart surgery,
it could literally bankrupt their entire
business. And level funding is a hybrid
model between the traditional fully
insured, the one I explained where
you're getting higher rates every single
year, and self-funding where you pay
your employees medical bills. It was
designed for small and mid-size
companies. Instead of paying a flat
amount to an insurance company, your
monthly payment is split into three
separate buckets. There's the admin fee.
This goes to a third-party administrator
to handle the paperwork, print the
insurance cards, process the claims. Or
said another way, they handle the bills
whenever your employees need to go to
the doctor. There's stop-loss insurance.
This is an insurance policy that
protects your business from a
catastrophic claim. For example, if an
employee has a million-dollar medical
emergency, the stop-loss insurance pays
anything over a set limit, say 30,000.
Your business is never on the hook for a
million-dollar claim the way some
companies who self-fund are. And third,
there's the claims fund. This is a
dedicated pool of money that belongs to
your plan and is used to pay for
everyday doctor visits, prescriptions,
and routine care. It's called level
funding because you, the company, pays a
level amount, a specific amount every
single month. It's a fixed cost. Let me
give you a concrete example of how this
looks. Let's say you run a company with
40 employees and your level-funded
payment is $30,000 a month. $6,000 will
go to admin, $8,000 goes to stop-loss
insurance to protect against disasters,
and $16,000 goes straight into your
claims fund. We'll say over the year you
put $192,000 into that claims fund. If
your employees have a rough year with
lots of medical needs, that's okay. The
claims fund pays the bills, the
stop-loss insurance covers the big
emergencies, and then you never pay more
than your fixed monthly rate. On the
other hand, if your employees have a
healthy year and only use $92,000 of
that claims fund, there is $100,000 left
over. In the traditional insurance
market, fully insured market, the
insurance company will keep all that
$100,000. Under level funding, the
insurance company actually splits that
surplus with you. Depending on your
specific contract, you get anywhere
between 50 to 80% of that money back in
a cash refund or with lower rates the
next year. The idea that you can get
some of your medical dollars back sounds
amazing, but level funding isn't right
for everybody. Let's take a look at the
main pros and cons. The pros. I already
mentioned this one, you get your money
back. If your employees use healthcare
responsibly and stay healthy, your
business actually gets rewarded with
unused claims dollars, at least a
portion. Total cost predictability.
Stop-loss insurance caps your risk so
you don't face unexpected surprise bills
the way a self-funded plan can't fully
predict. Data transparency. With
traditional insurance, you don't really
know if you're getting a good deal or if
really most of your money is actually
going to help some other company that
has a ton of sick employees. Level
funding gives you monthly reports
showing where your money is actually
being spent, so you can see if you're
overpaying for certain prescriptions or
services. Tax savings. Because level
funded plans legally operate under
self-insured regulations, they are
exempt from many state-level insurance
taxes and mandates, which naturally
lowers the baseline cost. Now, let's
look at the cons. Medical underwriting.
To get a level funded quote, insurance
carriers look closely at your group's
health history. If your employees
currently have major ongoing health
conditions, the quote might be too
expensive to even make sense. Not for
high-risk groups. If your employees
historically use a ton of healthcare,
staying in that traditional health
insurance pool might make more sense.
The volatility. If you have a great
year, your company likely gets a refund
with level funding. But if you have a
few major medical emergencies amongst
your employees in one year, the
stop-loss carrier will see that risk and
could dramatically increase your monthly
rate for year two. So, those are the
pros and cons of a level funded plan.
But I would say for most small and
mid-size businesses, level funding is
definitely an option that makes a lot of
sense to take a look at. It doesn't
magically fix the entire American
healthcare system, but it stops you from
blindly subsidizing somebody else's
medical bills if your company is
relatively healthy. And it's definitely
a way to take back some control of
healthcare costs. If you found this
video interesting and you'd like to
learn more about the business of
healthcare in the future, please
consider subscribing. This is Todd
Dachover. Thanks for watching.

segments.text: ﻿Small employers shopping for a health plan face the critical task of finding
a policy that balances cost, coverage, and the well-being of their employees.
While fully insured policies have been the traditional option, rising premium
costs have more employers turning to both level-funded and self-funded health plans.
In this video, I’ll break down the key differences between them.
What is a level-funded plan? A level-funded health plan is a
type of employer-sponsored health insurance that combines features of fully insured and
self-funded plans. It provides a balance of predictability and flexibility.
In a level-funded plan, the employer deposits a fixed monthly amount into
a claims account and pays a monthly premium toward stop-loss insurance.
The employer covers employee healthcare claims throughout the year. If the claims
exceed the amount saved in the claims account, the stop-loss policy kicks in.
According to KFF, 33% of employees who work for a small business had coverage
through a level-funded plan in 2024. A level-funded plan allows employers to
better manage their healthcare budgets while still sharing some financial risk with their stop-loss
carrier. If the actual claims are lower than expected at the end of the plan year, the employer
may receive a refund of unused funds. What is a self-funded plan?
A self-funded health plan, also known as a self-insured plan, is a type of
health insurance arrangement where an employer assumes the total financial risk for providing
health care benefits to its employees. Organizations cover medical costs instead
of purchasing a fully insured plan from an insurance company, and they forgo the
option of having a stop-loss policy. KFF found that 20% of covered workers
at small organizations were enrolled in self-insured health plans in 2024.
In this model, the employer funds the health claims out-of-pocket as they're incurred. This
approach can save money and allow more flexibility in benefit design if your employees don’t have
many medical expenses. But it also requires employers to maintain sufficient cash flow and
reserves to cover unexpected, high-cost claims. A self-funded plan without
the hassle or financial risk A stand-alone health reimbursement arrangement
(HRA) provides the benefits of a self-insured health plan without the potential risks.
You set a monthly allowance for your employees to use on individual health insurance premiums
and out-of-pocket expenses. Unused allowances roll over month-to-month until the end of the
benefit year. You’ll never pay out more than this amount, giving you cost predictability.
With an HRA, you can reimburse more than 200 employee healthcare costs, such as:
* Premiums for health, dental, and vision plans * Doctor visits
* Prescription drugs * Over-the-counter medication
Level-funded plans provide a predictable budgeting approach with potential savings,
while self-funded plans offer greater flexibility and control over healthcare spending. However,
an HRA offers the advantages of a self-funded health plan without the headache.
To learn more, you can read our article on this topic. We’ve
provided a link to it in the description. If you're an employer looking to provide
employee health benefits, PeopleKeep can help. Our HRA administration platform makes it easy
to set up and manage personalized health benefits in just minutes each month.
If you found this video helpful, be sure to give us a like and subscribe to our channel
for more employee benefits and small business tips. Thanks for watching.

A self-funded plan without the hassle or financial risk A stand-alone health reimbursement arrangement (HRA) provides the benefits of a self-insured health plan without the potential risks. You set a monthly allowance for your employees to use on individual health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket expenses. Unused allowances roll over month-to-month until the end of the benefit year. You’ll never pay out more than this amount, giving you cost predictability. With an HRA, you can reimburse more than 200 employee healthcare costs, such as: * Premiums for health, dental, and vision plans * Doctor visits * Prescription drugs * Over-the-counter medication Level-funded plans provide a predictable budgeting approach with potential savings, while self-funded plans offer greater flexibility and control over healthcare spending. However, an HRA offers the advantages of a self-funded health plan without the headache. To learn more, you can read our article on this topic. We’ve provided a link to it in the description. If you're an employer looking to provide employee health benefits, PeopleKeep can help. Our HRA administration platform makes it easy to set up and manage personalized health benefits in just minutes each month. If you found this video helpful, be sure to give us a like and subscribe to our channel for more employee benefits and small business tips. Thanks for watching.

segments.text: Employers setting up a health plan want to
know the best way to structure coverage for their employees.
Let’s explore two of the most common ways to structure a health plan:
fully insured and self-funded.
Under a fully insured health plan, employers pay a fixed premium to an
insurance carrier that in turn covers the medical claims of the employees.
This typically makes fully insured plan premiums higher because the administrative duties and
expenses fall on the insurance carrier. One of the trade-offs to those costs is
the peace of mind that the plan is prepared to compensate for a larger volume of medical claims.
Typically, fully insured plans can be more rigid than self-funded plans
because they give fewer options for customization or changes down the road.
Possible cons of fully insured plans include potential rate
hikes and having to negotiate with the insurance carrier.
If the employees are healthy and don’t use much health care,
then the employer does run the risk of paying for more coverage than they needed.
WPS Health Insurance and WPS Health Plan
offer fully insured health plans for Wisconsin and Illinois businesses.
Under a self-funded health plan, employers have more flexibility but take on more responsibility.
Self-funded plans are often more flexible because they are subject
to fewer state regulations or requirements. Self-funded puts employers in the driver’s
seat. They fund the health plan and make the benefit decisions.
As the driver, they take on more responsibility, but they also have more opportunities.
With self-funded plans, the healthier the employees are,
the less the employer will spend on health care costs.
The other side of that coin means that with high-cost claims,
the employer could then be responsible for some of those additional costs.
WPS offers flexible stop-loss insurance options to help protect organizations from unexpected claims.

plans for Wisconsin businesses. Weighing self-funded versus fully
insured depends on the needs and expectations of the individual
business. There is no one-size-fits-all health plan perfect for everyone.
WPS is here to help. Contact our
knowledgeable Sales Team today to learn more. At WPS, we strive to make getting health care
easier for the people we serve, so they can focus on what’s really important—living their best life.

If your broker walks in with donuts and a 20% fully insured renewal — and no real solutions — it’s time to ask three simple questions that could save your company thousands.

questions to ask broker, level funded questions small business, how to lower health insurance costs, level funded broker conversation

how to sell level funded plans, level funded sales process, broker referral system, level funded broker training, how to explain level funding to clients

Level-funded health plans have been around for decades, but many brokers avoid them because they require more work. In this video, Tom Stein, CEO of American Trust Administrators (ATA), explains the exact questions business owners should ask to uncover savings, protect their claims dollars, and take control of one of the largest expenses in their business.

⭐ WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

1. “Have we looked at level-funded?”
Why level-funded plans are often the smartest option for small and mid-sized employers — and why some brokers won’t bring them up.

2. The real underwriting requirements
What IHQs, wage & tax statements, and validation steps actually mean for your business.

3. Nationwide PPO vs Local PPO
How switching networks can lower access fees, improve discounts, and drive real savings.

4. “What is my surplus?”
If you’re already on a level-funded plan, you own your unused claims dollars. Learn where they should go — and why 100% surplus return keeps Main Street’s money local.

⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS FOR SMALL BUSINESSES

Health insurance is one of the largest line items for businesses with 5–200 employees. Level-funded plans allow some employers to:

Lower premiums

Keep unused claims dollars

Increase transparency

Avoid hidden fees

Choose better networks

Stop subsidizing mega-carriers

ATA has helped Main Street employers do exactly this for over 50 years.

⭐ FOR BROKERS: GET TRAINED THE RIGHT WAY

If you’re a broker who wants to sell level-funded plans with confidence — and avoid the mistakes that lose cases — join Level Funded University (LFU).

Inside LFU you’ll learn how to:

Explain level funding clearly

Use surplus and stop-loss to win more cases

Position yourself as a trusted Main Street advisor

Understand networks, contracts, and pricing

Leverage ATA’s 100% surplus return as your competitive edge

👉 Enroll in Level Funded University: https://thomas-stein.mykajabi.com/offers/4vEU34b2/checkout?preview=true

⭐ ABOUT ATA

American Trust Administrators (ATA) serves Main Street employers with transparent plan accounting, 100% surplus return, and U.S.-based service. For 50+ years, ATA has helped businesses protect their people while keeping more of their money local.

⭐ KEYWORDS (SEO)

Today we discuss the differences between an employer being fully insured vs self insured with regard to their healthcare insurance.

Mark Combs illustrates this by going through exactly what make up employer healthcare costs. 

By looking at where every dollar of insurance premium goes, it is easy to understand the differences between group medical insurance plans that are either fully insured of self funded.

Level funded health plans are also discussed in the presentation and Mark explains the differences between partially self funding and level funding as well.

By better understanding how these healthcare plans are structured employers can more intelligently plan for their employee benefit dollars.

Visit us at: SelfinsuredReporting.com

Email us at: Support@selfinsuredreporting.com

metadata.title: Fully Insured vs Level Funded: Health Insurance Explained
metadata.author: Tyler Dutchover
metadata.shortDescription:
What's the difference between a small group 'fully insured' health plan and a level funded health plan? 

This video is a basic breakdown of the similarities and differences between these two business insurance models in plain English with examples. It will also help you answer the following questions: 

-Does level funding typically save employers money? 
-What's an example of level funding?
-What are the risks of level funding? 
-What happens if we have a bad year with level funding? 

0:00 – Intro
0:35 – How many small companies level fund their health plan?
1:00 – Example of Self Insured vs Level Funded
2:34 – Where does money go in level funding?
3:27 – What happens if we have a bad year with level funding? 
4:04 – What happens if we have a good year with level funding? 
4:43 – What are the risks of level funding?
6:42 – The benefits of level funding

Other Videos 
What is Stop Loss Insurance? Explained in plain English: https://youtu.be/b2StkpG4yOY
Level Funded Health Plans Explained - in Plain English: https://youtu.be/ExcUj28jzzc
What is an ICHRA? Pros & Cons: https://youtu.be/6Ig9Nd5MUoY
What is a Pharmacy Benefit Manager? Simple Explanation: https://youtu.be/ufeHEzWD1Cc
Why US Healthcare Is Crushing America’s Businesses: https://youtu.be/qO9tof7FxTE 
The Business of Weight Loss Drugs: https://youtu.be/8c0bNOXezMw 
Will AI Make Medical Bills Cheaper?: https://youtu.be/XIoOuDjlehU 


*The information contained in this video is for informational use only, it should not be considered advice or as a recommendation. Neither legal nor financial.

mid-size businesses are in what's called
the fully insured market. Insurance
speak for tons of different companies

from these major insurance companies.
The issue with this system is if your
employees use your insurance a lot, your
rates go up. If they use your insurance
very little, your rates still go up. And
this is why up to 37% of companies with
10 to 199 employees have now switched
from this fully insured model to
something called level funding. And this

fully insured and level funded health

look out for. Let's dive in. So, I think
explaining complex insurance topics

a great way to put people to sleep. So,
I've created a hypothetical company that
will allow you to see the differences
between a level funded health plan and a
fully insured health plan. Hypothetical
numbers as well. Let's say it's a 50
person company and then we're going to
call them Mediocre Corp. They do
accounting or manufacturing or some
combination of the two. Under the fully
insured model, that means that they're
going to pay 500,000 during the year for
their employees insurance. They're going
to pay monthly, so just under $42,000 a
year. Now, if their employees have a
really healthy year and use say 280,000
in total medical care, the insurance
company will keep the difference. That
extra money goes toward their admin,
taxes, and profits. On the flip side, if
their employees have a really rough year
and rack up 650,000 in medical care
costs, the insurance company covers the
spread. In that terrible scenario,
Mediocre Corp is paying less if they had
absolutely no insurance. Under this
fully insured model, everything is
predictable. You know exactly what
you're writing a check for every single
month. But the issue is you're
essentially renting out your insurance.
That's one way to look at it. And you
have no idea how much your employees
actually go to the doctor. You don't get
that data. Now, let's look at that exact
same company, 50% company, Mediocre
Corp, but they've chosen a level funded
health plan. Let's compare the
differences here. Right off the bat, the
total maximum price tag is typically
lower depending on where this company is
based. So, instead of 500,000 fully
insured quote, a level funded plan might
cap Mediocre Corp's cost at 470,000 for
the year. And just like that fully
insured plan, they're going to pay a
fixed amount every single month. This
one is 39,000. But behind the scenes,
their money doesn't go into a general
insurance fund like it might in the
fully insured plan. It gets split into
three different buckets. Bucket one is
admin fees. This pays the company
running the plan to process medical
claims, print ID cards, handle customer
service issues for employees. Bucket two
is stop-loss insurance. This protects
Mediocre Corp's business if an employee
has a catastrophic health event. Like
let's say an employee gets a rare cancer
diagnosis or some other employee has a
major coronary bypass surgery. Stop-loss
also helps Mediocre Corp if they spend a
ton across company. Maybe they don't
have one single individual who gets a
million-dollar cancer diagnosis, but
everybody spends a lot. They're still
protected in that case as well.
Together, this admin and stop-loss
bucket might run 120,000 for the year.
Bucket three is the claims reserve. In
this case, that's roughly $350,000.
That money technically belongs to
Mediocre Corp. It sits in an account
waiting to pay for employees' regular
doctor visits, urgent care trips,
prescriptions, etc. You get it. So,
let's break down two scenarios. Let's
say Mediocre Corp has a healthy year and
then an unhealthy year. Let's see how
this would look under a level funded
health plan. Let's start with a rough
year. An employee needs a complex
surgery, somebody else has a high-risk
pregnancy, and Mediocre Corp's total
medical claims climb to 430,000.
That's how much employees have spent on
medical care in this case. And they've
gone right past that 350,000 in their
medical claims bucket. So, what happens?
That stop-loss insurance kicks in and
pays the 80,000 over that $350,000.
There is some nuance in how stop-loss
insurance works, but I'll link that
video that I've made on stop-loss
insurance in the description, so you can
watch that if you want. But, the main
point is that Mediocre Corp's total
expense was hard capped at that original
$470,000 maximum. That is a worst-case
scenario, and rates will be higher the
following year almost certainly. So,
let's look at scenario two. So, a solid
healthy year. The team mostly just gets
preventative check-ups, fills generic
prescriptions, and manages their health
well. Total claims for the entire year
come out to a very low $280,000. So, at
the end of the plan year, they look at
their claims reserve and see that there
is $70,000 sitting in it. Under a
level-funded plan, the carrier will
split a portion of that 70,000 with
Mediocre Corp in the form of a direct
credit or lower rates, depending on
their contract setup. It is possible
they just direct cut them a check of
35K. But, to recap, Mediocre Corp gets
the exact same month-to-month budgeting
safety as a fully insured plan, but they
actually capture the financial upside.
But, level funding is not a good option
for every small and mid-size business.
Let's take a look at why. There are two
major catches Mediocre Corp has to
navigate with level funding: medical
underwriting and the renewal trap. Let's
start with underwriting. Under a
standard fully insured plan, Mediocre
Corp is protected by something called
community rating. The insurance company
or carrier cannot legally ask the
employees about their specific health
history. They're going to look at
baseline demographics like age and zip
code, and just hand over that $500,000
renewal. Level-funded health plans do
not play by the same rules. Because they
technically fall under different federal
guidelines, the insurance company can
actually look under the hood before
offering a quote. This means Mediocre
Corp's employees might actually have to
fill out health questionnaires. The
underwriters review the group's medical
history to evaluate the financial risk,
and if the workforce is generally
healthy, great. They will likely get
that $470,000 quote. But, if they have
an older workforce and a few employees
that have severe ongoing chronic
conditions like, let's say, rheumatoid
arthritis or a hemophiliac, they might
decline to quote Mediocre Corp entirely.
Or, perhaps they set the claims reserve
so high that would actually cost
Mediocre Corp more money if they did the
level-funded health plan option. So,
that's issue number one. A company can
only get that upfront savings if they
can pass the initial health test. But,
let's assume Mediocre Corp passes that
test, they do well, they get the quote,

employee health. Like in our scenario
one from earlier where claims spiked and
they blew way past the reserve. In that
year, they are fine because the
stop-loss insurance kicks in and they're
basically capped on how much they'll
spend. But, the following year is when
the issues arise. The insurance carrier
just lost money. And because the data
transparency in level funded plans, they
know exactly why the medical claims were
high or why the costs were high. When
Mediocre Corp's renewal arrives, they
are likely going to see a pretty
significant rate increase. Even worse,
the stop-loss carrier might apply what's
called a laser. Let's say one specific
employee developed a severe, expensive
illness, the carrier might say, "We're
going to renew your plan, but we're
putting in a laser on that one specific
employee." The specific stop-loss safety
net won't kick in for them until they
hit 200,000 in claims. So, now Mediocre
Corp is asked to take on a larger
financial risk for that one specific
employee. And on paper, this sounds
terrifying, but there is something that
works out in Mediocre Corp's favor here.
They're never trapped. If they get hit
with a bad level funded renewal or a
terrible laser, they can simply pivot
right back to the fully insured
community pool for the next year. The
fully insured market legally has to take
them back. No health questions asked at
the standard community rate. Granted,
that community rate will definitely be
10% or more higher. So, instead of
500,000, they're probably looking at
550,000. So, that's something to take
into account, too. But, let's stop and
think about something here for just a
second. As healthy companies leave this
fully insured market to capture savings
with level funding, who's left behind in
that community pool? Typically, it's
going to be the companies with higher
medical costs. To cover those costs,
insurance companies have to increase
rates for everybody who remains. This
creates what those in the industry call
a death spiral. Higher rates push more
healthy groups to leave that market,
which makes the remaining pool even
sicker, driving rates up yet again. And
this has actually happened in
Connecticut. And ultimately, staying in
this fully insured market, rates will
continue to rise at a fairly
unsustainable rate. If you found this
video interesting, you'd like to see
more on the business of US healthcare,
please consider subscribing. This Tyler
Dutchover, thanks for watching.

metadata.title: How pharmacy benefit managers influence drug pricing
metadata.author: STAT
metadata.shortDescription:
The point of prescription drugs is to help people improve their quality of life. When a doctor writes a prescription and sends it along to the pharmacy, oftentimes they’re more focused on the drug’s effectiveness than its cost.

But when a patient picks up that drug, the price they will be asked to pay at the counter takes center stage — and it depends on a complex combination of factors. Is it a brand-name or a generic drug? Does the patient have health insurance? If so, does that insurance cover the drug?

Also, how do health insurers decide which drugs to cover, and what amount they’ll cover?

We answer all of these questions in Part 2 of this series. The video outlines what pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are; how formularies and rebates work; and how PBMs use them to mediate with drugmakers, health insurers, and pharmacies in ways that influence the cost of drugs.

segments.text: When you get sick, sometimes your doctor prescribes you a drug. This drug was developed by
researchers at drug companies, manufactured, then distributed at pharmacies to help you get better.
The process seems simple enough, but there’s a lot of money baked into each step of bringing
a new drug to market. Drugmakers want to recoup their costs, hence the high sticker price of most
new treatments. Paying out of pocket for these costs would be really financially disruptive,
if not impossible, for most people, which is where health insurance comes in.
Health insurance works by spreading risk — a lot of people pitch in money (aka,
pay a premium) every year on a bet that they will get sick and need health care and, hopefully,
most will not. Most health insurance plans provide coverage for some prescription drugs,
so if you have a plan, you’ll most likely pay less than the list price.
So you pay for your health insurance to help you out with paying for the drug,
and you pay for whatever health insurance doesn’t cover. This is technically not so
different from the way you can get prescription drugs in other countries, many of which also
use some form of cost-sharing. So what makes prescription drugs so much more expensive in
the U.S.? One big factor might be pharmacy benefit managers, which only exist in the United States.
Clip: We have excellent health insurance … the best.
PBMs are the middlemen between the drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacies. In the 1960s,
insurance companies started to offer prescription drug coverage to their members. Soon after, PBMs
arrived on the scene to help insurers manage the administration of these prescription drug claims.
And because PBMs do a lot of admin stuff for a lot of hospitals,
insurers, and drugmakers, they wield a lot of influence on the cost of drugs.
One of the ways PBMs influence drug cost is by creating formularies. A formulary is a list of
drugs an insurance company will cover. These lists are tiered, typically with cheaper drugs in tiers
1 and 2 and more expensive drugs in tiers 3 and 4. If two different drugs pretty much work the same,
insurance companies will likely put the cheaper drug on the lower tier.
Insurance covers more of the cost of lower-tier drugs, and thus consumers pay less for them.
Drugmakers want their medicines in tiers 1 or 2 — because they’re available to the most patients,
they’ll make the most sales. But how do they get their drugs in these tiers? They can offer the PBM
a rebate, or money back, on a drug, which makes the drug cheaper for the insurance plan and moves
it up on the formulary. So whenever a patient buys a drug in the top tiers, the PBM gets a
rebate. The more expensive the list price of the drug, the higher the PBM’s rebate tends to be.
There are two lines of thought here:
On one hand, because PBMs have a lot of purchasing power — they work with hospitals and insurers,
they have a lot of people they can negotiate with — they can negotiate better prices
for certain drugs for everybody. On the other hand, there’s not a
lot of transparency in the relationship between drugmakers and PBMs, so we often don’t know how
much the actual rebates are. So if a drugmaker offers a rebate to PBMs to lower the cost of a
drug (aka, raising it up on the formulary), we don’t know how much of the rebate goes towards
lowering the cost of the drug for the consumer. The PBM could be pocketing a higher amount of the
rebate. And if drugmakers have to offer rebates to PBMs to push their drugs up higher on the
formulary, sometimes they have to raise the list price of their drugs to help cover the rebates.
So let’s bring it all back. Drugs cost a lot of money to make, health insurance costs money.
Even if you have insurance, if your drug is not covered by your plan, the cost you pay goes up.
And if you don’t have insurance, your drug might be available as a low-cost generic,
but for many brand-name drugs, you might have to pay the list price.
On top of all that, there’s this complex formulary ranking system managed by PBMs
that’s pushing higher overall list prices for drugs — and it might be
one clue why the cost of prescription drugs is so high for consumers today.
But there’s yet another side of this story, and it starts back at the beginning, with the
drugmakers. In the next video, we’ll talk about the role of patents in prescription drug costs.

metadata.title: Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) Explained - Learn How the Money Flows
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) process prescription claims for health plans.

PBMs are one of the seven parts of the prescription medication ecosystem.  All the members include:
1. Plan Sponsor
2. Health Plan
3. PBM
4. Pharmaceutical Manufacturer
5. Drug Wholesaler
6. Pharmacy
7. Patient

The money flows from Plan Sponsor to Health Plan to PBM to Pharmacy to Drug Wholesaler to Pharmaceutical Manufacturer.

The prescription medications flow from the Pharmaceutical Manufacturer to the Drug Wholesaler to the Pharmacy to the Patient.

Sources:
https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/JOP.19.00606

https://www.optum.com/business/insights/pharmacy-care-services/page.hub.specialty-pharmacy-myths.html

https://dfwbgh.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/DFWBGH-Specialty-Rx-Workshop-Report-Final-7-25-22.pdf

https://www.healthcarevaluehub.org/advocate-resources/publications/pharmacy-benefit-managers-can-they-return-their-client-centered-origins

AHealthcareZ is 200+ Healthcare Finance Educational Videos.

💥 BOOK: Check out Dr. Bricker’s Book 16 Lessons in the Business of Healing here: https://www.ahealthcarez.com/healthcare-money-campfire-stories-book

AHealthcareZ Viewers Include: Employee Benefits Professionals, HR, CFOs, Insurance Brokers, Benefits Consultants, Doctors and Nurses in Leadership Roles, Hospital and Health System Administrators, Health Insurance Carrier and PBM Professionals, Pharma and Med Device Professionals, Academic Professors and Students in Healthcare Administration and Public Health.

metadata.title: The PBM Insider - What is Spread Pricing?
metadata.author: PBM Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
Everybody is talking about spread pricing, but many ask me, "what is it?" It's actually a lot more simple than many in my industry make it out to be, take a listen...

#PBM #ThePBMInsider #PrescriptionNetwork #letustakecareofyou #PBMdoneright

segments.text: Welcome to the PBM Insider. I'm Jim
Lodge, an actual PBM insider. Today
we'll be discussing spread pricing, an
all too common tactic used in the PBM
industry. What is spread pricing, you
ask? Well, let me tell you. It's
actually pretty simple. And while a lot
of PBMs will assure you that the pricing
of drugs is very complex, lots of puts
and takes involved, the reality boils
down to two basic contracts in the PBM
ecosystem. When we're talking about
spread pricing, one contract is between
the PBM and the plan sponsor and
typically includes the list of drugs on
the formulary with their price and
estimated rebates identified. and the
other contract is between the PBM and
their
dispensingarmacies. The contract between
the PBM and the pharmacies varies from
pharmacy to pharmacy as you can imagine
but generally includes two components. A
reimbursement amount that the PM PBM is
willing to pay the pharmacy for the drug
and a professional dispensing fee to
cover things like the pharmacy staff,
light bill, technology, counseling of
patients, etc.
Spread pricing is the difference between
the pricing in these two contracts. It's
really no more complicated than that. In
an earlier edition, we talked about the
Johnson and Johnson fiduciary duty case
where a set of high-cost drugs were
being marked up on average almost 500%
to J&J versus what was being reimbursed
to the
dispensingarmacies with that difference
being kept by the PBM as pure profit
because that spread is above and beyond
the administrative fees that the PBM was
already collecting for managing the
claims.
So, what can plan sponsors do about it?
Well, they can make sure that their PBM
is charging them the same ingredient
cost and dispensing fee as what they are
reimbursing the pharmacy and only
collecting the administrative fee as
their revenue source. That's just the
correct and transparent way to do
things.
This is the PBM insider keeping you
informed.

metadata.title: Pharmacy Benefit Managers: Companies In The Thick Of Prescription Drug Pricing
metadata.author: KFF Health News
metadata.shortDescription:
For the past seven months, the GOP push to replace the Affordable Care Act has consumed Washington. All the while, many consumers continue to be focused on the rising costs of prescription drugs.

Pharmacy benefit managers — companies that are often unnoticed and even less understood by most consumers — hold an important place in the prescription drug-pricing pipeline. In this video, Kaiser Health News details the emergence of these multimillion-dollar corporations and the impact they have on medication costs and patients’ access to these treatments.

segments.text: Once upon a time, in the thorny world of health insurance and prescription drug costs, someone
came up with a novel idea: The Pharmacy Benefit Manager.
A what?
A Pharmacy Benefit Manager, or PBM.
You might never have heard of them, but if you're insured, these companies help decide
the drugs you get at the pharmacy and how much you pay for them.
So, what are they and where do they come from?
Back in the late 1960s, health insurers began expanding drug coverage and they got tangled
up in the sheer volume of claims for these prescriptions.
Then came a bold business idea: Why not make money by processing those drug claims for
them?
So PBMs took the messy task out of the insurers' hands, and that's how PBMs were born.
Later, when drug spending spiraled out of control for employers and health plans, PBMs
touted their ability to use their negotiating power to secure better prices and even bulk
discounts from drugmakers.
But that's not all they do now.
PBMs also help draft lists of the drugs that are covered by an insurer.
They're called formularies.
For drugmakers, getting a preferred spot on the formulary is really attractive.
Kind of like getting on a VIP list at a popular club, it can mean a leg-up on the competition.
In the 1990s, drugmakers found this concept so appealing that companies, like Merck and
Eli Lilly, started owning PBM businesses.
But that didn't sit well with some consumer watchdogs.
What if the drug companies kept competitors off their lists?
So, the Federal Trade Commission stepped in and drug companies spun off their holdings
and, bada bing, bada boom, now three large PBMs control about 80% of the market: CVS
Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts.
They say they save employers and insurers millions a year, but they also make money.
How do they do this?
They pit one drugmaker against another for the best price in a class of drugs and for
a seat on the formulary.
Does this bring down the price?
It can, but not all the time and not often for patients.
As businesses, PBMs need profit margins; they make money by pocketing the difference between
how much they pay for the drugs and how much they charge their clients for the drugs and
other services they provide.
You know, the markup.
Another way PBMs make money is through rebates.
Yep, rebates.
Think of them like the coupons you send in when you buy a new brand of soap or an electronic
gadget.
Pop it in the mail and a few months later you get a check for $3.
That happens with PBMs, but on a much larger scale.
PBMs insist that they pass most of the rebate savings onto their clients, but they keep
the actual numbers a trade secret.
Recent studies suggest that PBMs and insurers pocket the money, leaving little direct benefit
for patients.
And some experts say rebates just encourage PBMs to favor the medications with the biggest
rebates.
That's instead of the cheaper alternatives that are just as effective.
Lawmakers in California are working on legislation that requires PBMs to provide more information.
Congress and other states might, too.
So, are PBMs a good idea?
Yes and no.
They have helped keep some drug prices and premiums lower, but consumers don't see that
savings directly and may be limited in their drug choices.
And, of course, prices for some drugs keep going up.

metadata.title: What is a Pharmacy Benefit Manager (PBM)?
metadata.author: CancerCare
metadata.shortDescription:
This patient education video from CancerCare defines and explains the practices of Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs), the companies that create and oversee your prescription drug benefits.

PBMs use several practices designed to save the health plan money, but these cost-control measures may negatively impact people with cancer. This video explains what to do in the face of PBM practices, including Formularies, Price Negotiations, Pre-Authorizations, Step Therapy, Specialty Pharmacies and Claim Denials.

** Key Takeaways **
»   PBMs control drug access and costs through formularies, prior authorizations, and claim denials.
»   These practices disproportionately impact cancer patients.
»   There are steps patients can take to improve their access to medications.

To see more animated videos from CancerCare, visit:   https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLRC9I1wusxkaFdUAesfFIAPpbIx69ZTeu&si=EFKn6Ii2xvnZpAhZ

segments.text: Navigating your prescription benefit
plan. Pharmacy benefit managers, PBMs.
A pharmacy benefit manager or PBM is the
company that designs and manages your
prescription drug benefits, but they do
much more than fill your prescriptions.
PBMs manage pharmacy benefits for
insurance companies and employer
provided plans as well as Medicare Part
D and Medicaid. You see, drugs do not go
directly from the manufacturer to your
local pharmacy. There is a complex
supply chain with several middlemen that
each play a role. PBMs handle drug price
negotiations and payments with the drug
manufacturers,
distributors, and pharmacies. In short,
PBMs work to control costs by
controlling how you access health care
services. PBMs use several practices
designed to save the health plan money.
But these cost control measures may
negatively impact people with cancer. So
let's take a look at each of these
practices and how best to navigate them.
Starting with formularies,
PBMs decide which drugs will be included
in or excluded from coverage. This
information is outlined in a list called
a formulary. The formulary includes
generics, brandame drugs, specialty
medications, and bioimilars.
The formulary is arranged in pricing
tiers that encourage the use of drugs
that are less costly to the health plan.
Get familiar with your formulary. You
can find it on your plan's website or by
calling member services. Check to make
sure any drug you're prescribed is on
the formulary. If the drug is not on the
formulary or it's on a high cost tier,
talk with your doctor about your
options.
The sheer volume of prescriptions
handled by PBMs gives them bargaining
power with drug manufacturers. PBMs may
also offer manufacturers a preferred
spot on the formulary in exchange for a
cashback rebate on a drugs list price.
Drugs with higher list prices are better
able to offer larger rebates. This could
incentivize the PBM to give a higher
price drug a preferred position in the
formulary even if a lowerric drug would
actually be cheaper for you or the
overall plan. Exactly who gets these
rebates is not always clear. There is a
growing demand for greater transparency
coming from lawmakers, patient advocacy
groups, and independent pharmacies. It's
worth noting that when you go to the
pharmacy and pay for a drug, the list
price you see is often much higher than
the price the PBM or the plan pays after
rebates. This can impact your co-pay and
if you have a high deductible, the
amount you might pay for a drug out of
pocket.
Pre-authorization, also called prior
authorization, may be required before
your insurance company will cover
certain drugs. The idea is to make sure
the drug prescribed is quote medically
necessary, especially if there are less
expensive drugs available.
[music]
Pre-authorizations are usually handled
by your doctor's office, but sometimes
the process of obtaining
pre-authorization can delay your
treatment, limit your access to certain
drugs, and cause stress. If you're faced
with a pre-authorization, talk to your
healthare team. They can help navigate
the process and can also let you know if
there is a suitable drug that might not
require prior authorization. If you need
the specific drug your doctor prescribed
and it's urgent, your doctor can request
an expedited review.
Step therapy may be required if your
doctor prescribes a higher price drug or
a non-preferred drug according to the
formulary. Step therapy is also known as

metadata.title: Modern PBM 101 with Alan Pannier, PharmD, MBA: Transparency
metadata.author: SmithRx
metadata.shortDescription:
True transparency can transform your pharmacy benefits.

Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) often lack transparency in drug pricing, leading to hidden costs and misaligned incentives. SmithRx is changing that. As a next-generation PBM, we use a transparent, pass-through model to provide clear insights into drug pricing.

Alan Pannier, SVP of Product Strategy at SmithRx, explains how our transparent approach lowers costs for patients and plan sponsors by eliminating conflicts of interest and ensuring everyone has access to the lowest-cost medications.

Connect with Us:
Website: https://www.smithrx.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/smithrx

segments.text: My name is Alan Pannier. I'm the Senior Vice President of Product Strategy at SmithRx and
we'll be talking about transparency in the PBM space. Sadly, in the ecosystem that we exist in,
Pharmacy Benefit Managers have really taken the term transparency and exacerbated it to various
levels of opaqueness to the point now that you could say that there's different shades
of transparency that exist in the marketplace. At SmithRx, we don't believe in any of that.
We truly believe that patients should have the right to know the price of their medications and
plan sponsors and industry partners should be able to understand exactly what the cost of drugs are
through their total course of the supply chain. That means the contracts that we have with our
pharmacies and the pricing that exists there, negotiation that we do with drug manufacturers
to lower costs, whether that's through low list price products or drug manufacturer rebates that
come as discounts for providing market share to preferred products. At the end of the day,
all of that should be available to our plan sponsors and they're able to see that through
our Partner Portal and our Member Portals where members and ecosystem partners are able to see
the true cost of medications. At SmithRx, we do not own any pharmacies or assets across the
supply chain. We feel like this is an important capability for Pharmacy Benefit Managers to align
their incentives with the plan sponsors and patients that they serve. By not having any
ownership structure in these areas, it allows us to partner with industry partners that are aligned
with us and providing true transparency and access to information and data—and also leverage
our platform to lower pricing for our patients and plan sponsors. By having this platform-based
structure, it allows us to operate in a world of true transparency. We're able to share insights,
provide information to not only patients but plan sponsors and ecosystem partners as well.
By aligning this level of information through transparency, we're able to align our incentives
in driving down cost and ensuring patients have access to the lowest cost source of supply.

metadata.title: PBM Spread Pricing for Generic Prescriptions Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
PBM Spread Pricing Explained:

AWP = Average Wholesale Price
AWP - 'Discount' = What Plan Pays PBM for the Prescription

MAC = Maximum Allowable Cost = What the PBM Pays the Pharmacy
What the Plan Pays PBM for Drug - MAC = 'Spread Price' Fee That PBM Keeps

NADAC = National Average Drug Acquisition Cost = What the Pharmacy Pays to Buy the Drug
MAC - NADAC = Fee that Pharmacy Keeps

Example:  Amlodipine (common generic blood pressure medication)
AWP = $2.38  AWP - 80% = $0.48
MAC = Proprietary (Unknown)
NADAC = $0.019
So the Plan Pays 48 Cents a Pill for a Drug that Costs 2 Cents a Pill!!

Sources: https://www.healthaffairs.org/do/10.1377/hblog20190426.775617/full/; https://www.46brooklyn.com/research/2018/11/7/visualizing-how-aint-whats-paid-awp-really-is
