And so, the FTC is now looking at GPOs as well as the initial, um, six PBMs. And the FTC has stated that its inquiries aimed at shedding light on several PBM practices, um, including charging fees and clawbacks to unaffiliated pharmacies, methods to steer patients to PBM-owned pharmacies, potentially unfair auditing of unaffiliated pharmacies, um, the use of complicated pharmacy reimbursement methods, and how negotiated rebates and fees with drug manufacturers impact the cost of prescription drugs. So, they're sort of looking at all all of these aspects, um, of the drug chain drug supply chain, um, and I think most recently, and one of the most interesting developments out of the investigation is that in July, the FTC, at least so far, um, is that in July, the FTC issued a statement warning the public not to rely on prior FTC advocacy statements and studies opposing mandatory PBM transparency and disclosure requirements. And one of the more interesting points in the statement was a note that in the past, the FTC was concerned that mandated disclosure requirements between PBMs and their customers, which are namely large employers and health plans, um, would encourage, um, price coordination and collusion. Um, however, the ET FTC is now of the view that that that the trends towards extensive consolidation by PBMs and extensive vertical integration by PBMs into the um, into the entire drug supply and payment chain has put employers and other payers at a disadvantage. Um, and in both the marketplace, you know, and just in terms of the information that they have to make purchasing decisions. And so it's interesting cuz now the FTC in that statement has suggested that it's appropriate for policy makers to require PBMs to provide accurate and timely information for buyers. So I feel like now Congress and you know, of course state legislatures as we're going to talk about have sort of now, you know, picked up that um, picked up that mantle, you know, and they're now sort of um, you know, pursuing those um, those um, initiatives. I I say that, you know, that that recent statement really kind of points out the FTC saying, you know, historically, you know, perhaps they've been less active in pushing back on the vertical consolidation that that basically took over 40 different companies and consolidated them into three. Um, that that, you know, have by some measures 70, 80, 90% uh, of the market and I think there's been an interest in in at the Senate a number of of of senators on a bipartisan basis have have said to FTC publicly, you need to hurry up and finish your inquiry. Um, you know, because we want to see the findings and if you, you know, don't move fast enough, we're going to step in front of you and and continue our own efforts because these issues are so um, so paramount uh, in the in the on drug pricing and cost overall and I think it's interesting that the FTC has also been looking at that these same same vertical vertically integrated entities more as platform companies in similar ways they look at the technology industry as having platform companies and are there platform company type abuses uh, that are going on on in the supply chain due to this vertical integration uh, rather than that's, you know, um, um, uh, pricing or or, you know, self-dealing, or steering, um, using certain information that the platform has because it's it's facilitating all these transactions across the industry. And so, I think everyone is equally anticipating the close of the inquiry, the report to be issued, uh, likely, you know, by the spring, um, if not sooner. Uh, and then, you know, as is often happened in happened in past FTC inquiries of this type, uh, there may be new investigations launched into one or more of the vertically integrated PBMs, or public exposure that there's already an ongoing investigation, and and here's where, uh, it currently sits. Uh, but as I, uh, Kendra mentioned, uh, the, uh, the Hill, in particular, has been active on this front. I think we've seen, you know, this past year, um, you know, close to to 30 different bills introduced in the House and and Senate, uh, taking on different aspects of of PBM reform. And while, you know, in this podcast, we don't want to walk through every single one of those bills, I think as Kendra I and I discussed, there are certain themes that come out of of these bills, and and there's about half a dozen, uh, that maybe I'll highlight, and then Kendra and I will walk through, uh, what what the policy goals are, uh, with with each of those those types of themes. And so, the half dozen or so are are transparency reporting requirements, prohibitions on spread pricing, rebate pass-through requirements, uh, restrictions on patient steering, uh, delinking of PBM fees to rebate amounts, uh, and then additional government investigation and oversight authority over the PBM industry. So, Kendra, maybe you want to take the the first handful of those first, and and give a lens on on what it is that policy makers at the federal level uh, are trying to achieve with with with some of these bills that that mention those themes. Sure. Well, measures to increase PBM transparency are a common provision um across the multiple bills aimed at PBMs and I think this is one of the um measures that has the most bipartisan support and we're likely to if if anything passes this fall, I think it definitely will get something on transparency. Um the Senate Health Committee in May passed the Pharmacy Benefit Manager Reform Act, which would require disclosure of certain information and prohibit employers and health insurers from doing business with a PBM that fails to make those disclosures and that seems to be sort of a common thing theme among many of the of of the bills. Um the Senate Commerce Committee bill, the PBM Transparency Act, um would require PBMs to disclose complete the complete aggregate amount of compensation received from prescription drug manufacturers and other payments or credits retained by the PBM. And the House has similarly passed bills requiring PBMs to provide employers and health plans with information on prescription drug spending. So I I think generally large employers support strong transparency. I I think one of um when their concern is that they just think um PBM reform needs to go further. Um so while they're supportive of transparency, I think they're looking for additional measures um to be included to address the rise of prescription drug costs um including policies that address consolidation and unbundled services that um can drive patients to you know the more high profit pharmacies. So um so I think um you know there is support for transparency and we're probably likely to see to see something on that included in one of the bills. Um the prohibition on spread pricing. So spread pricing is where um PBMs charge the plan more um more than what the PBM pays the pharmacy for a prescription drug um and then the PBM is able to sort of keep the difference, right? between what the plan pays the PBM and what the PBM paid the pharmacy. And so, um so there are at least some bills, um particularly one of the the Senate bills, the Senate PBM Reform Act, that would propose um prohibiting spread pricing. Um And then rebate pass-through, um so rebate pass-through is the concept there is that, you know, prescription drug manufacturers will pay rebate on prescription drugs that are purchased by plan participants, right? And so, the idea is, you know, how much of that rebate gets retained by the PBM and how much of it gets passed through to the plan and ultimately may makes its way, you know, back to um potentially back to the the drug consumer, right? And so, the idea is in these provisions is to sort of require PBMs to pass through 100% of the rebates and fees and other discounts that they receive from drug manufacturers back to the health plans. I I think kind of I think the key statement you made was not just rebates, but other discounts and and amounts that are based on a percentage of the drug cost because as we've seen over the years, there's been a a narrowing and narrowing of the definition of rebate in order to create other pockets of of potential revenue and profitability that even if there is a requirement for pass-through, so it's all in, you know, what how rebate gets defined if there's a pass-through requirement. But to your earlier point, I think, you know, if I think a lot of people while getting transparency will be seen as a initial win from a policy reform perspective around the PBM industry, many will view that as a very skinny win. You know, they want some of these other aspects that you've talked about, as well as things like prohibitions on patient steering, de-linking, and additional government investigations. So, you know, patient steering, there's concern around the fact that, all the large PBMs, you know, have significant specialty pharmacy operations. Some have retail pharmacies as well. But, in particular, you know, moving patients on sometimes or oftentimes on exclusive basis, mandating use of the PBM's own specialty pharmacy, you know, creates perhaps antitrust concerns around the way in which market power and platform use is happening. But, also perhaps it creates self-dealing concerns. So, if if the PBM through its own specialty pharmacy is saying to manufacturers, "Give us larger discounts at the pharmacy and lower rebates, you know, because I have to pass the rebates along, but I get to keep all the discounts myself because I'm saying those are discounts to me as a pharmacy owner." You see how that patient steering and and consolidation of that um of that activity into your own owned assets or affiliated assets to be problematic. Uh that would certainly be a much broader reform that would be more problematic uh for the profitability of the PBM industry going forward as uh potentially delinking, which is a uh uh the notion that uh PBM payments should not be tied uh in any way to a percentage of a drug price, whether that's you know, a percentage of rebate retention, whether that's administrative fees or other service fees or other activity or spread pricing. You know, there shouldn't be any any ability for a PBM uh to to link their financial uh rewards to a percentage or based on a percentage of a drug price or a margin, but instead there should just be a a flat fee or a a non-percentage based fee for the activity that they're doing in terms of processing a claim or negotiating a contract uh or the like. And and so, that would be certainly a much more transformative reform that I'm sure uh you know, PBMs are advocating strongly on the hill against and I think is probably uh uh higher reach in terms of actually getting that type of reform into a bill at the end of this year, but I know particular Senator Schumer and others are strongly advocating for that as is the life science industry because of of the amount significant amount of profitability that is captured in the middle if you allow linking to to occur. And also just from a overall investigation and oversight perspective, you know, if you think about the size of this industry and and perhaps not having the same type of regulator that other industries of similar size and scale have at a federal level to oversee, you know, their activity, conduct audits, you know, provide regular guidance, there's maybe a call for that activity that maybe this fractured approach across FTC or DOJ or others just leaves too many gaps in the system and there needs to be strengthened oversight of those entities as well as potential new entities or regulators that would oversee the vast amount of financial transactions that are going through the PBM industry. And so with that, I know one thing thing that, you know, may or may not make it is is this notion of some form of fiduciary obligation. Tender I know, you know, employers in particular have been voicing the need for some form of fiduciary standard. Do you want to talk about that a little bit and why that's so important? Sure. Some employers would like to see PBMs be subject to a fiduciary standard that would require PBMs to conduct their business in a manner that puts the best interests of plans in their enrollees first, right? And the goal is to impose a standard of conduct on PBMs to discourage practices that are perceived as increasing drug costs and spending. I mean, I feel like we're sort of right now in a little bit of a whack-a-mole situation, right? Where you know, every time some bad behavior pops up or behavior that people think is bad, you know, they feel like they have to go run to the legislature to get a law passed to prohibit it, right? And so, I think the theory here is, well, if they're subject to the same standard of conduct, you know, um as employers are when they're plan fiduciaries to their plan participants, um then for then, you know, then there'd be more alignment in the interests and maybe, you know, it would prevent like some behaviors from arising that would later have to be addressed, you know, in some sort of statutory initiative. Um so, I do think that, you know, employers had hoped that the proposed PBM legislation that's, you know, um circulating on the hill right now would include fiduciary requirements for PBMs. So far, the only provision touching on this um is in the Senate Health Committee's PBM Reform Act, which merely instructs the Department of Labor to study PBMs fiduciary responsibilities. And I think one of the possible reasons that we haven't yet seen a fiduciary provision included in legislation that is that it's potentially difficult to reach consensus on some aspects of it. You know, for example, if a PBM has an exclusive obligation to act in the best interests of participants and beneficiaries, which is, you know, the ERISA fiduciary standard, um then presumably the legislation has to include a carve out, right? That would allow PBMs to still receive reasonable compensation for their services. I mean, I don't think, you know, I think people want PBMs to be in business, they provide useful services, right? So, we need to find a way. But then, it's, well, how would reasonable compensation be defined? And does Congress want to be in the business of defining it, right? So, um so, I think it's just going to become a question of, you know, what what we, you know, how do we come up with a standard that, you know, can be measured and is enforceable, um and that, you know, sort of achieves the goal of maybe, you know, just kind of um, you know, sort of creating a more alignment of of the interests of some of the the consumers of the prescription drugs with PBMs. I I thought I think the the, you know, the notion of creating a ERISA fiduciary standard maybe a bridge too far, especially short term, uh, just to get consensus if they're trying to get something passed, but it doesn't mean there can't be provision basic provisions on things like self-dealing. Uh, you know, that wouldn't require uh, necessarily, you know, reaching into ERISA and the complexity of of of working through there. So, I'm still hopeful that we'll see some form of maybe light fiduciary standard, uh, at least, you know, on on self-dealing in particular as a platform company uh, could be really beneficial uh, to patients and and many other stakeholders in the system. Um, you know, I think it's important for us to to to to turn and and kind of close on this notion of of state activity in this area. And I know you mentioned this notion of of of kind of play whack-a-mole on all these different areas that that the PBMs are involved in because of their vertical integration. I'll mention uh, the chapter five of of the treatise that we talked about earlier has a really helpful chart on all the different profit levers that PBMs have across the different stakeholders uh, that they deal with. And so, that can be a really helpful level setting for those that aren't as familiar with with each aspect uh, of the of the profit stream as well as some examples of how a drug moves through the system and and who what percentage of it um, and could be really enlightening. But, I know on the state level there's one, you know, clearly you know, PBMs have been have been fighting back on whether it's the the state AG efforts and investigations, but also some of these statutes that they feel have gone too far uh, and and violated existing law. And I think in particular 10th Circuit's decision um, about the Oklahoma law could be really helpful. And so, why don't we close on you you talking about um, um about that decision and how that kind of pulled back the ability to do PBM reform in certain areas. Great. So, the the case is PCMA versus Mul- Mulready. Um and in that case, what happened is the Oklahoma passed a statute um that would have required PBMs to be subject to retail pharmacy network access standards and would have prohibited PBMs, you know, from promoting in-network pharmacies by offering cost-sharing discounts and also using their mail- mail-order pharmacies to satisfy some of the retail network standards. Um it also included a prov- included a provision that said that PBMs cannot deny a provider the opportunity to participate in a pharmacy network um at preferred status if they're willing to accept the terms and conditions of participating in the network. And it also included a provision that said that PBMs can't deny, limit, or terminate provider's contract based on the employment status of an employee who has an active license to dispense um despite pro- despite probation status. So, in other words, you know, if the pharmacy has someone's on who's on probation status, then, you know, it would have prevented um the PBM from excluding that pharmacy from the network. Um so, PCMA sued to enjoin the law from taking effect on grounds that it's preempted by ERISA and Medicare Part D. And the parties then filed dueling motions of summary judgment in the wake of the Supreme Court's decision in Rutledge. Um and Rutledge, the Supreme Court held um an Arkansas PBM regulation that governed PBM pharmacy reimbursement rate was not preempted by ERISA. And by way of background, you know, ERISA preempts state laws that relate to, you know, employee benefit plans. Um and a state law relates to an an ERISA if it has a connection with with or reference to an ERISA plan. So, in Rutledge, the court stated that this boils down to asking whether the state law governs a central matter of plan administration or interferes with nationally uniform plan administration. Um and in Rutledge, the Supreme Court upheld the Arkansas PBM regulation um because it determined that the Arkansas statute, although it might increase costs to plans by requiring PBMs to pay pharmacies at least the acquisition cost of a drug, um it didn't affect the ability of employers to structure their employee benefit plans in a certain manner, right? So, in Rutledge, the court said, "Look, this is not preempted by ERISA." So, in the wake of that, the district court, you know, held that ERISA did not preempt the Oklahoma statute. Um it did hold that that Medicare Part D preempted some of the challenged provisions, but it largely held that ERISA did not. Um and the district court reasoned that the law was not preempted because it merely alters the incentives, but doesn't force ERISA plans to make specific choices, right? And so, for example, for the network access provisions, they said, "Well, that doesn't prohibit using mail-order pharmacies. It just says that you can't they don't count towards meeting the access standards. So, that's not you know, they're saying that doesn't really affect it, you know, administration." Um and they said the any-willing-provider statute, it doesn't require the plan to accept any pharmacy into the network. It just relates to whether the pharmacy has preferred status or not. Um and then on the prohibition standard, um on the probation standard, they said, "Well, that only relates to contracts between providers and PBMs, and that has a de minimis effect on pharmacy benefit design." So, so then the of course the case gets appealed right to the 10th Circuit. And the 10th Circuit says, "Well, wait a minute here. We do think that these laws are preempted, and here's why. First of all, you know, for the any willing provider standard, you know, we've by increasing the potential providers and directly we we are directly affecting the administration of the plans because we're essentially forcing them to go to a single tier network. Um because if you can't preclude a plan from you know, you know, if if you're if you're if the plan is precluded from excluding providers from a network, then you're essentially you know, no longer allowing it to have a preferred pharmacy network and you're sort of eventually collapsing it into a single tier. Um and on the network adequacy again, it said, you know, this does affect, you know, plan administration because you know, you are dictating which pharmacies must must be included in the network. You're requiring cost sharing to be the same for all of the in-network pharmacies, which is key and fundamental to benefit designs. Um and pharmacy networks the the 10th Circuit was think you know, reasoned are a cornerstone of the benefit design and you know, and the network restrictions don't say anything about PBM costs, right? So they just felt like these clearly are a target to network design. Um And on the probation prohibition again, you know, the argument is um you know, the 10th Circuit sort of disagreed with the district court's reasoning that the state laws have only a de minimus effect plan on plan design are not preempted cuz they're like that's never been a standard. They're like, you know, de minimus effect on plan design is not the Supreme Court's test for determining whether something is preempted by ERISA. Um and so there they are just saying, look, you know, the the probation prohibition forces PBMs to capitulate to all, you know, including all pharmacies in their network, um even those employing pharmacists on probation. And they're like, look, we can't, you know, we again, that goes to sort of dictating the design of someone's network and that is not something that, you know, and that goes to the heart of administration and therefore is preempted by ERISA. I mean, I think one of the other really interesting points in the case is that one of the arguments that Oklahoma have tried to make is that, well, no, the state laws are regulating PBMs. They're not They're not regulating plans and therefore this doesn't relate to employee benefit plans. And so the 10th Circuit did spend some time discussing how because of, you know, it is almost virtually or very difficult for a plan to self-administer the functions that a PBM provides, the PBM is almost synonymous to the plan and it has to be analyzed, you know, as essentially the plan in the context of an ERISA preemption analysis. So I thought that was just a really interesting, you know, point that they focused on in the case about how and they cited some other case law and precedent for that, you know, where HMOs are often synonymous to plans. Um, and there've been other cases. So there was case precedent for it, but this think this is the first time that a court has actually talked about how PBMs are, you know, synonymous to plans in many ways. And so I thought that that was just, you know, very interesting. Um, and then, you know, not really my area focus, but the 10th Circuit also ruled that the any willing provider provision is preempted by Medicare Part D as well. So um, that was just really I'll jump in there. I mean, this speaks to a great reminder that while there's a a strong appetite for PBM reform across a lot of different levers, you're often going to run into sometimes a brick wall of ERISA preemption and having PBMs rely on that have they had as they have for decades to win a number of cases and certainly the Supreme Court opened up some aperture in Rutledge for further reform, but things need to happen in line with that decision and maybe we'll see further cases that hold a little differently and then it goes back to the Supreme Court. So, it is certainly going to be an area of contentious debate in terms of what the what the um how far you can go on PBM reform and not run into a risk of preemption issues that that that that that pull it back. I also think you're going to see more activity at the state AG level, you know, where the insurance commissioners haven't perhaps been as active. The state AGs will say, you know, we we think we've got authority to look here and do more such as Ohio in particular has led the way. And in some ways the platform PBMs is particular ones that have really integrated one can make the argument that the PBM is really engaged in the practice of insurance and the state insurance commissioners should be more active because they've got state authority to to regulate them as an insurer and and part of a consolidated PBM insurer enterprise. And I think if the state commissioners the insurance commissioners don't do that, I think the state AGs will do more of that. And so, you know, it's going to play out across all these different landscapes of the states, the federal level, agencies such as FTC and DOJ, and it's just an area that that that the folks really need to to pay careful attention to and really see and predict what's coming around the corner to advise clients appropriately as to what's in the near term, what are the implications of that, what's more medium term long term, and and when do we think that'll happen, and what's the likelihood of that? And then how are different PBMs coming up to solve for some of these issues and creating more innovative models, maybe ones where they don't take a percent they don't keep the rebate or or don't tie their compensation as a percentage of drug pricing. So, that's another area to advise and be mindful of. But, this has been a fantastic discussion. I think it's been a great um springboard off of that that chapter five that you and I worked on closely in the AHLA treatise on market access and drug pricing. And I think we're just thankful for you and I to be able to connect again in a different venue and you know, appreciate the partnership and look forward to future events like this with you. Great. Thanks so much Viraj. Likewise. Hey, thanks everyone for joining us.

metadata.title: What is a PBM? (Long)
metadata.author: SmithRx
metadata.shortDescription:
Ever wondered what a Pharmacy Benefit Manager (PBM) does and how they really impact your prescription drug costs and access to medication? This video breaks down everything you need to know!

PBMs were originally created with a clear goal: to make drug costs manageable for health plans and employers through price negotiations and creating approved medication lists (formularies). The idea was to reduce overall healthcare expenses.

However, over time, the PBM industry has become incredibly complex. Many traditional "legacy" PBMs, with their outdated and often opaque structures, have introduced significant challenges for employers and patients alike, including:

❌ Lack of Transparency: Employers often can't see how drug prices are set or where their money truly goes, making it hard to assess fair dealing.
❌ Complex & Unpredictable Pricing: Layered fees and complicated models mean unpredictable costs for employers and surprise expenses for employees at the pharmacy counter.
❌ Limited Choice: Restricted drug formularies and pharmacy networks can limit patient options, making it harder to get needed medications conveniently and affordably.

These issues make it difficult for employers to control costs and can lead to significant frustration for employees.

The good news? Modern PBMs like SmithRx are leading a change! We focus on a fresh approach built on:

✅ Radical Transparency: Clear, straightforward pricing so you always understand the costs.
✅ Consumer Choice: Wider access to medications and pharmacy options.
✅ Alignment with Client Interests: Our goal is to help employers manage healthcare costs effectively while ensuring employees get the medications they need without unnecessary hurdles.

Watch this video to understand the PBM landscape better and see how SmithRx is delivering radically transparent pharmacy benefits to provide a simpler, fairer, and more cost-effective solution.

➡️ Learn more about SmithRx and our transparent approach: www.smithrx.com

metadata.title: How Prescription Drug Coverage Works: Formulary Tiers, PBM, Rebates, Spread-Pricing Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn How Prescription Drug Coverage Works with Health Insurance:

1) Formulary:  There are Formulary and Non-Formulary Medications.  Formulary Medications are Covered by Insurance.  Non-Formulary Medications are Not.

2) Formulary Tiers:  Typically Formularies Have Tiers 1-4 for Generics, Preferred Brand, Non-Preferred Brand and Specialty Medications.

3) Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs): Negotiate the Formulary Tiers for Health Insurance Coverage in Exchange for 'Discounts' from Pharmaceutical Manufacturers.  Also, PBMs Process the Pharmacy Claims for a Health Insurance Plan.

4) How PBMs Make Money: 
A) Rebates - Commissions Paid by Pharmaceutical Manufacturers to PBMs, Which the PBMs in Turn Pay Out--in part--to Their Employer Customers.

B) Spread Pricing - The Markup PBMs Place on Generic Medications, Which is Then Paid by Their Employer Client.

AHealthcareZ is 200+ Healthcare Finance Educational Videos.

💥 BOOK: Check out Dr. Bricker’s Book 16 Lessons in the Business of Healing here: https://www.ahealthcarez.com/healthcare-money-campfire-stories-book

AHealthcareZ Viewers Include: Employee Benefits Professionals, HR, CFOs, Insurance Brokers, Benefits Consultants, Doctors and Nurses in Leadership Roles, Hospital and Health System Administrators, Health Insurance Carrier and PBM Professionals, Pharma and Med Device Professionals, Academic Professors and Students in Healthcare Administration and Public Health.

metadata.title: I'm a Benefits Advisor. Here's Who Gets Paid When Your Health Insurance Goes Up
metadata.author: rodneymattos
metadata.shortDescription:
When your company's health insurance renewal goes up, who gets paid? A benefits advisor walks through the fully insured chain: the insurer, the advisor and the pharmacy middlemen, and what an employer can ask for before signing.

Mercer's survey of employers expects health benefit costs per employee to rise 8.2% in 2027, the biggest jump since 2003, and that's after the cuts employers already plan to make. In a fully insured plan, almost everyone between the employer and the doctor is paid on the size of the bill, and almost nobody in that chain earns more when it gets smaller. This video explains how that works, what part of the increase is real, and which numbers you're allowed to see.

What you'll learn:
- What a fully insured health plan actually buys: one premium, the carrier's risk for the year, and no split of the cost
- How the ACA's medical loss ratio rule works (85% of premium on care for large groups, 80% for small) and why it caps a percentage, not dollars: on a $1M plan up to $150K can go to everything else; at $1.1M, up to $165K
- How benefits advisors get paid: carrier commissions built into the premium (typically 3-6%, per ProPublica's 2019 reporting), flat per-employee fees, and carrier bonuses of up to $150,000 for a single group, some tied to keeping the employer at renewal
- Why most of the increase is still real (more care, specialty drugs, the new weight loss drugs, hospital prices), and what the premium buys you in a bad year
- Where pharmacy benefit managers sit in your plan, and why you never see them in a fully insured plan
- Three things to ask before you sign a renewal: the advisor compensation disclosure you're owed (since December 27, 2021), your own cost and claims information, and how your advisor's pay changes if you stay, cut or switch
- Self-funding's catches first (stop-loss, no MLR floor or rebate, the vendors you still pay), then what changes when the layers come apart, including the new law that has PBMs pass along 100% of drug rebates to employer plans, starting in 2029 for plans that renew in January

Chapters:
0:00 The renewal letter
0:36 Why 2027 matters more
0:58 What a fully insured plan buys
1:22 The 85% rule caps a percentage, not dollars
2:37 How advisors get paid
3:24 The fair part: most of the increase is real
4:00 The pharmacy layer you never see
4:43 One lever
5:39 Three things to ask before you sign
6:33 Changing the structure: the catches first
7:49 Every layer you can see

This video is general education, not legal, tax or plan advice; talk to your counsel or plan advisor about your own plan.

Has anyone ever shown you how your benefits advisor gets paid? Tell me yes or no, and what your 2027 renewal came in at, in the comments.

#HealthInsurance #EmployeeBenefits #EmployerHealthPlan #BenefitsAdvisor #PBM

Free checklist, what to read and ask before you sign your health plan renewal: https://rodneymattos.explorelibrary.com/paid

Rodney Mattos is the founder and CEO of Triforta: https://triforta.com

metadata.title: Direct Primary Care & Employee Benefits: Cutting Costs, Boosting Value, and Enhancing Care
metadata.author: Hint Health
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Beth Holmes, Head of Hint Connect, Fritz Busch, Principal and Consulting Actuary at Milliman, and Dr. Clint Flanagan, Founder and CMO at Nextera Healthcare, for a discussion around the value of direct primary care for employers. We’ll dive deep into:
- Primary care’s impact on overall plan cost
- Cost savings expectation from implementing a whole-person solution like DPC
- The mechanisms that create cost savings
- Impact of improved health outcomes for employees
Be sure to bring your questions for our speakers to answer as this will be an interactive webinar. We hope to see you there!

University of California.

we go through today's presentation since
we will be referencing the materials

california.edu/form/pdf/welcomekit.pdf.

metadata.title: The CAA 101 - Comply or Die?

metadata.shortDescription:
The Consolidated Appropriations Act 101 - Comply or Die?

The Consolidated Appropriations Act, otherwise known as the CAA, established protections for consumers related to surprise billing and transparency in health care.

The price transparency component is where the opportunity lies for employee benefits brokers and their employers to uncover the source of their high cost claims, and then take appropriate fiduciary responsibility in order to pay more appropriate unit costs for healthcare.  While there is a cost associated with ensuring you are compliant, the opportunity to retain and win new business for consultants is massive.

Right now, opaque network contracts make it difficult for healthcare consumers to know the cost of care prior to receiving it, and it is nearly impossible to make an informed decision as a patient.  The CAA will have a dramatic impact on Americans' ability to price shop on where to go for care, as well as their ability to plan for their out of pocket expense(s).  

Upcoming fines can and will be heavy, amounting to $100/day PER EMPLOYEE, which is substantially greater than the fines hospitals receiving for being non-compliant, which was only $300 total day.  The goal for employers immediately is not to be perfect by 12/27/22, but to at least show that they made a good faith effort to be compliant.

The goal of the CAA is simple: People should be able to know the price ahead of time, shop using that price as well as quality of care metrics, and then they shouldn't be slapped with a giant, surprise balance bill afterward. At the end of the day, the goal is to allow people to have the tools to shop for healthcare the way that they do so for any other product or service.

The CAA has 4 Pillars:
1. Gag clauses in admin agreements that prevent employers from getting their own data
2. Broker Compensation Disclosure
3. More Info about Prescription Drugs
4. Mental Health Parity

Here is a recent article covering the CAA in greater detail, and outlining the employer obligation to be compliant.  Hat's off to Dave Chase, co-founder and CEO of Health Rosetta for bringing it to my attention!

metadata.title: Consolidated Appropriations Act
metadata.author: Ameriflex
metadata.shortDescription:
What is the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA)?

CAA legislation impacts all employers offering group health benefits. Passed in December 2021, it outlines employers’ responsibilities in overseeing employee benefit contributions and expands on ERISA fiduciary duties already in place.

The Consolidated Appropriations Act is here to stay. It’s not a continuation of COVID or emergency legislation. 

How will it affect employers?

Employers have a list of legal requirements, including pre-existing ERISA requirements and new CAA-outlined responsibilities, to fulfill and need to have processes in place to protect and oversee plan assets and employee contributions.

The video includes expert perspectives, non-compliance penalties, and possible solutions for employers.

metadata.title: Fiduciary Compliance and Key Provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act
metadata.author: Walsh Insurance
metadata.shortDescription: In this session we will discuss the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA) and the numerous requirements that impact employer-sponsored group health plans. Additionally, we will review actions employers can take to reduce their fiduciary risk as it relates to the CAA.

metadata.title: Cracking the Code: What Employers MUST Know about the CAA  (Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021)
metadata.author: Mel 😊 DeWeese
metadata.shortDescription:
As an expert in employee benefits, I wanted to share my insights on the latest developments in the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA) and what it means for employers. In this video, I break down the key points of the CAA and how it impacts your business, including changes to health plans, gag clauses and flexible spending accounts. Also review P Forms and D Forms such as D-1 forms and information required within those forms.

With over 20 years of experience in the industry, I provide practical advice and actionable steps to help you navigate these complex regulations and stay compliant. Don't miss out on this essential information that can save your company time and money. Watch now to learn what you need to know about the CAA as an employer.

metadata.title: A High-Level Review of the Transparency Provisions Under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021
metadata.author: Miller Johnson
metadata.shortDescription: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (the CAA)—which was signed on December 27, 2020—contained several provisions intended to increase the transparency of health insurance, including employer-sponsored group health plans. Previous Benefits Lunch Break Webinars have covered several of these provisions in significant detail (e.g., mental health parity comparative analysis, No Surprises Act, etc.). In this webinar, Tripp VanderWal gives a high-level overview of the remaining transparency provisions in the CAA.

metadata.title: What is the Workers Comp Experience Mod?
metadata.author: The Coyle Group - Business Insurance
metadata.shortDescription:
The worker's compensation experience mod goes by many names, including the experience rating factor, the x-mod, the rating mod, or just the mod.  In this video, we take a deep dive into what the mod is, how it's calculated, and how and why it's frequently wrong, and what to do about it.

As specialists in workers compensation insurance, we've helped hundreds of employers correct their mod, improve their mod through proactive claims management and risk management, and reduce not only their cost of workers compensation but their Total Cost of Risk, an important cost factor not discussed by many insurance brokers.

0:00 Intro
0:40 What does the mod  do?
0:58 How is the mod calculated?
1:26 How is the mod used in my policy?
2:46 So, you may be asking— How can I reduce my mod?
3:41 Can my mod be wrong?
4:26 How can you verify the mod?

To find out more on how we can help you and your firm control costs over the long term, please contact me.  My information is below.

👦 Gordon Coyle is the CEO and Senior Risk Architect of The Coyle Group, a New York based insurance brokerage and risk consulting firm, focused exclusively on the business insurance market.

🎬 Be sure to subscribe to this YouTube Channel to get more insurance and risk management information!  https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC5shjbmMsDV0C8GBA993m5Q

TRANSCRIPT (for reference)

The Workers’ Comp Experience Rating Mod (also called the experience mod, E-Mod, or experience modifier) can quietly raise your workers’ comp costs for years if you don’t understand it.

Hi, I’m Gordon Coyle. In this video I’ll explain what the experience mod is, how it works, why it matters, and the biggest mistakes decision makers make—so you can avoid getting hammered by your workers’ comp premium.

What is an experience mod?
It’s a rating factor on your workers’ comp policy. If your claim experience is worse than expected, it increases (debits) your premium. If your claim experience is better than expected, it decreases (credits) your premium—based on your payroll size and class codes.

Who calculates it?
Your experience mod is calculated by either your state workers’ compensation rating bureau or NCCI (the National Council on Compensation Insurance). Your mod is unique to your business and is driven by your payroll, industry/class codes, and claim history—typically using three of the last four years.

Why does experience rating exist?
It adds fairness to the system by charging more to employers with more claims than expected and giving credits to employers with fewer claims. It also creates a strong incentive to improve workplace safety and build a safety culture.

How does the mod affect your premium?
Your payroll is multiplied by the rate for each class code to create a standard premium. Then the experience mod multiplies that standard premium.
Example: $100,000 standard premium × 0.75 mod = $75,000.
$100,000 standard premium × 1.25 mod = $125,000.

How is the mod calculated (and why audit it)?
The calculation is complex and handled by software today. Errors can still happen, so it’s smart to audit your mod every couple of years to make sure you’re not overpaying.

How can you improve your mod?
Fix past errors with an audit, then focus forward: reduce claim frequency and severity. Build stronger safety processes and culture, monitor claims closely, and consider tools like nurse triage to manage injuries and outcomes. In some cases, preventing lost-time claims can significantly reduce the mod impact.

Bottom line
The experience mod has a major impact on workers’ comp costs, but it’s never too late to improve it—starting with a mod audit, claim review, and safety improvements.

Common mistakes to avoid
Mistake #1: Nobody monitors claims—no one reviews loss runs, reserves, payouts, or trends. Fix: request 5 years of loss runs and review them with your broker to plan prevention steps.

metadata.title: How Your EMR Actually Works | The Formula Behind Your Workers' Comp Mod
metadata.author: JJ Doorhy & Associates
metadata.shortDescription:
Your experience modification rate is one of the most important numbers in your business — it drives your workers' comp premium, affects your ability to bid on contracts, and follows you for three years. But the formula behind it isn't something most brokers take the time to walk through.
In this video I open up the NCCI experience rating formula and show you exactly how it works — the split point, the W factor, how every claim is weighted, and where the real leverage is.
We get into:
→ How your mod is calculated and what a 0.90 vs 1.10 actually costs you
→ The contractors credit multiplier — how a good mod can save $94K/year on the same $200K premium
→ Why claim frequency hits the formula harder than severity
→ The medical-only 70% reduction and how to use it
→ How reporting speed directly affects claim costs
→ Six strategies to take control of your number
This is your data and your money. You should understand how the formula works.

📧 ryanhanigan@jjdoorhy.com
🌐 www.jjdoorhy.com

metadata.title: Workers Comp Class Codes, What Are They For? 2026
metadata.author: The Coyle Group - Business Insurance
metadata.shortDescription:
Workers’ Compensation Class Codes Explained | Avoid Overcharges in 2026
Are you confident your workers’ compensation policy is using the correct class codes? Misclassified codes can lead to overpaying thousands in premiums. In this video, Gordon Coyle breaks down Workers’ Compensation Class Codes—what they are, how they work, how they're assigned, and how to avoid common mistakes that cost business owners money.

👉 For expert business insurance guidance, contact us here: https://thecoylegroup.com/contact/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=workers-comp-class-codes-what-are-they-for-2026

👉 Visit our page: https://thecoylegroup.com/workers-compensation-class-codes/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=workers-comp-class-codes-what-are-they-for-2026

From understanding the difference between governing and supplemental class codes, to avoiding audit nightmares and costly reclassifications, Gordon helps you navigate the complex world of workers comp class codes in a clear and actionable way. Perfect for business owners with employees in one or multiple states, especially those buying insurance online or managing subcontractors.

⏱️ Timestamps:
00:00 – What Are Workers’ Comp Class Codes?
00:54 – How Class Codes Affect Your Premium
01:38 – Are Class Codes the Same in Every State?
02:25 – How Class Codes Are Assigned
04:31 – Can You Split Payrolls by Class Code?
06:01 – How to Find Rates by Class Code
07:13 – Class Code Impact on Cost
07:46 – Biggest Mistakes Business Owners Make
09:25 – Why Work With a Skilled Broker?

#WorkersCompensationClassCodes #WorkersComp2026 #BusinessInsurance #WorkersCompAudit #ClassCodeMistakes

↪︎Clean Transcript (For Reference)↩︎
Curious what workers comp class codes are all about—how they’re used, how to be sure your policy is using the right codes, and how to avoid being overcharged? In this video I’m going to break down workers compensation classification codes: what they are, how they work, and the biggest mistakes business owners make.

Hi, I’m Gordon Coyle. Welcome to my channel where I discuss insurance and risk issues on the minds of business owners.

Workers comp class codes sound simple, but they’re not. Most states have hundreds of codes, and the wrong one can mean the wrong premium. A workers comp class code is a four-digit identifier found in your state’s workers comp manual or the NCCI rating manual. It describes the type of work predominantly done at an employer’s location, or where permitted, the work performed by a group of employees. For example, code 8810 is commonly used for clerical office employees. Each class code has a rate attached to it, and that rate is a major part of how your premium is calculated. If your policy uses the wrong code, you may be overpaying.

Are class codes the same in all states? Not necessarily. Many are similar, but they can vary by state due to filings and different rating systems. NCCI standardizes codes in many states, while some states run their own systems or have unique rules. If you have employees in multiple states, the home state rules for those employees can affect what applies.

How are class codes assigned? When a new policy is written, the agent or broker assigns codes based on what they believe matches your operations. Then, at the end of the policy term, the insurer audits payroll and classifications. During that audit, the carrier may add, remove, or reclassify employees—sometimes because the original coding was incorrect, and sometimes because the auditor sees it differently.

Here’s the most important rule: the employer’s business operations usually determine the governing class code, not the individual job tasks. That’s where many people get it wrong. For example, if you run a landscaping company, the governing class applies to the landscaping operations. You generally can’t split lawn mowing, hedge trimming, and planting into separate codes just to lower cost. One common exception is clerical office employees, who may be assigned a clerical code if they meet the rules. There are other permitted splits in certain industries, but it requires getting the rules exactly right.

So how do you know if your codes are correct? In many cases, you need someone who can research the state rules, NCCI guidance where applicable, and how carriers apply them—then confirm the approach with underwriting and audit so you’re not surprised later.

Finally, the three biggest mistakes I see: buying workers comp online and misclassifying to chase a lower premium (audits can trigger large back bills), assuming subcontractors’ workers comp is properly set up (audit rules can push costs back to you), and accepting an online portal’s “suggested” class code without knowing better options may apply.

Bottom line: class codes directly affect your workers comp cost. If you’re unsure, get the classifications reviewed so you can pay the right premium—and avoid surprises at audit time.

metadata.title: How Workers Compensation Class Codes Impact Premium
metadata.author: Insurance for Entrepreneurs
metadata.shortDescription:
Most business owners think workers’ compensation insurance is about shopping quotes or negotiating better rates.

It’s not.

In this video, I break down the real driver behind your workers’ comp premium—your class codes—and how one simple mistake can cause you to overpay by thousands (or even tens of thousands) every year.

I’ve personally taken over accounts where nothing changed except classification… and reduced costs by up to 80%.

Here’s what you’ll learn:
• How workers’ comp class codes actually work 
• Why businesses doing the same work pay completely different premiums 
• The biggest mistake that silently increases your costs 
• How misclassification happens (even with good brokers) 
• What you should do right now to fix it 

If your payroll is being classified incorrectly, it doesn’t matter how many quotes you get—you’ll be overpaying on every single one.
________________________________________
👉 NEXT STEP:
Watch this next: 1099 vs W-2: The Workers’ Comp Cost Trap
(This is the second biggest way businesses overpay)
________________________________________
💼 If you’re a business owner and want help reviewing your workers’ comp setup, reach out here:

https://bitnerhenry.com/daryl-henry/


00:00 Why Workers’ Comp Costs Can Be 5X Higher
00:28 What Actually Drives Your Workers’ Comp Premium
01:45 How Class Codes Work (Simple Breakdown)
03:10 The Multi-Role Employee Problem
04:56 Real Example: 80% Cost Reduction
06:38 How to Check If You’re Overpaying
08:10 What To Do Next (Action Steps)
09:15 1099 vs W-2 Cost Trap (Next Video)

metadata.title: What is STOP-LOSS INSURANCE? | In less than 3 Minutes
metadata.author: Self Insured Reporting
metadata.shortDescription:
Selfinsuredreporting.com

Many businesses across the country are finding themselves with the same problem, rapidly rising health plan costs. Every year employers loath having to price new health plans for their employees. The employer gets a ton of quotes from carriers, they end up going with the least expensive which usually isn’t very good for the employee, and then next year that rate jumps up even more.

Because of this never-ending cycle of rising health insurance costs, more and more employers are moving to Self-insured healthcare plans (Otherwise known as Self-funded). Under this type of plan style, employers themselves are the ones who pay for the health benefits being provided to the employees. The employer assumes the risk of paying the claims rather than using the more traditional model of letting the insurance company take on that risk.

This type of Healthcare plan option became popular back in 1974, after a new law exempted Self-Funded plans from State regulation. Ever since then the model has moved down market to smaller and smaller companies.
Due to Healthcare Reform among other things, companies are wanting to take more control over their Healthcare spend. By setting up these types of plans, employers are now able to control more readily the costs associated with offering group health insurance.

How Can a Self-Funded Employer Protect Themselves Against Large Medical Claims?

In order to protect themselves against large unforeseen and unpredictable claims, Self-Funded employers purchase what is known as Re-insurance. This is also referred to as Stop-Loss insurance and is designed to reimburse employers for large claims that go above a pre-determined dollar level. This is not a health insurance policy but rather a legal contract between the stop loss carrier and the employer.

metadata.title: What is Stop Loss Insurance? Explained in plain English
metadata.author: Tyler Dutchover
metadata.shortDescription:
What is stop loss insurance? This video is a basic breakdown of stop loss insurance in plain English with examples. It will also help you answer the following questions: How does stop loss insurance work? What’s an example of stop loss insurance with real numbers? What happens if we self fund our health plan and an employee has a million-dollar emergency?

0:00 – Intro
0:23 – How does stop loss insurance work? 
0:53 – What is Specific Stop Loss Insurance?
1:15 – Specific Stop Loss Insurance (Example)
2:49 - What is Aggregate Stop Loss Insurance?
3:17 – Aggregate Stop Loss Insurance (Example)
4:05 – How Do These Work Together?

Other Videos

segments.text: What is stop-loss insurance? This video
is a basic breakdown of stop-loss
insurance in plain English. I've made it
because I think there's two big reasons
that many companies who should self-fund
don't, and it's risk and confusion. This
video will seek to address those issues
and then help you to answer the
following questions. How does stop-loss
insurance work? What's an example of
stop-loss insurance with real numbers?
And what happens if we self-fund and an
employee has a million dollar emergency?
So to help us understand how stop-loss
insurance really works, I think it's
helpful to have some numbers attached to
this, even if they're hypothetical. So
let's imagine there's 150 person company
that's thinking of making the jump to
self-funding. Based on their
demographics, they expect their total
medical claims or medical costs for the
upcoming year to be 1.5 million dollars.
The company can probably afford that,
but what happens if their medical costs
exceed that amount? Let's say 2 million
dollars. Maybe one single employee has a
crazy medical crisis, million dollars or
more. And this is where stop-loss
insurance comes into play. And there's
two major parts, specific stop-loss and
aggregate stop-loss. Let's start with
specific. Think of specific stop-loss as
insurance for a specific large medical
cost, typically 100,000 or more. Might
be a major heart surgery or a premature
baby who spends months in the NICU.
Specific stop-loss protects the company
from accumulating huge, catastrophic
medical costs from a single individual
over the course of an entire policy
year, so not just from one single
hospital visit. When you set up your
plan, you're going to choose something
called an attachment point. This is
basically a deductible per employee.
It's the max amount of your own money
that you're going to spend on one
person's medical bills before the
insurance takes over. For a 150 person
group, you might set that specific
attachment point at 75,000 dollars. This
means that your company and the
administrator that actually helps pay
for you pays that first 75,000 of an
individual's medical bills for the year.
The second the individual's accumulated
bills hit 75,000 and 1 dollar, the
stop-loss company steps in and pays 100%
of the rest. So let's say unfortunately
one of your employees has a baby that
has to spend a few months in the NICU.
NICU stays can be notoriously expensive,
sometimes a million or more. If you were
self-funded without any stop-loss or any
specific stop-loss, that single event
would wipe out almost your 1.5 million
dollar budget on just one single person.
That doesn't even take into account the
other 149 employees who will definitely
use some medical care throughout the
year. But if you have specific stop loss
insurance, your liability stops at
75,000. And the stop loss company
reimburses the plan for the remaining
if it's a million dollars. And this can
happen with multiple employees as well.
For example, maybe another employee gets
a coronary artery bypass that costs a
bit over 100k over the year. This
specific stop loss insurance company
again would cut you a check anything
over 75k. So that's how specific stop
loss insurance works at the basic level.
And as you can imagine, it's a little
bit difficult for an underwriter to
predict that kind of risk. How would you
know that a baby needs to spend three
months in the NICU or that somebody's
going to have a coronary artery bypass
this year? So for that reason, specific
stop loss insurance is typically more
expensive than that other form of stop
loss, aggregate. Let's get into that
one. So while specific stop loss
insurance protects you from that one
individual or multiple single
individuals who have crazy high medical
costs, aggregate is basically protecting
you from death from a million cuts.
Aggregate puts a cap on the total
healthcare spending for your entire
company over the entire year. Basically
for all of your employees' medical
costs. And we're going to say now it's
the following year and nobody hits that
specific stop loss limit. Nobody spends
over 75,000 at the doctors, but
everybody uses their medical care a lot.
This would never happen, but for the
sake of this example, there's a brutal
flu season that sweeps through the
warehouse sending 40 people to the
emergency room. Five people get knee
replacements, three get their
gallbladders removed, you have a handful
of routine maternity claims. Let's say
none of these hit over 75k, but your
employees are getting beat up. Your
aggregate attachment point or the
absolute most your company will pay for
everyone's medical bills combined for
the whole year is usually set at 125% of
your expected claims, sometimes slightly
higher. Since your expected claims were
1.5 million, your aggregate cap is 1.87
million. Meaning you pay all your
employees' medical bills up to 1.87
million. But remember, this is a brutal
year and everybody got all those knee
replacements, so you hit 2.5 million
dollars for the year. Now the aggregate
policy jumps in. The stop loss company
would then cover that final 630,000
dollars ensuring your company doesn't go
in the red for that year. And the
important thing to know is had all these
horrible procedures happened in the
exact same year, these two policies
worked together. So that 75k you paid
out of pocket for the NICU baby earlier
counts toward this 1.87 million
aggregate limit, but the 925,000 the
stop loss company paid does not. This
was just a very basic breakdown of stop
loss insurance specific and aggregate
stop loss insurance. I'll be going into
more detail and nuance in the future. If
you'd like to see videos like that,
please consider subscribing. This is
Tyler Thanks for watching.

Your stop-loss renewal just came in with a single-digit increase. Great news, right?

Not so fast. One word buried in your contract could expose your company to hundreds of thousands of dollars in additional claims.

That word is LASER.

In this episode of Healthcare Genius, Ralph Weber explains how a stop-loss laser works and why employers, CFOs, and HR leaders need to understand it BEFORE signing their renewal.

Consider this example:

✅ Your normal specific stop-loss deductible: $150,000

⚠️ One employee is assigned a $600,000 laser.

💰 Your additional financial exposure: Up to $450,000.

That seemingly attractive renewal could come with a financial surprise you never anticipated.

In this video, you'll learn:

What a stop-loss laser actually means

How lasers shift financial risk back to employers

Why a small premium increase doesn't necessarily mean a good renewal

What to look for before signing your next stop-loss contract

Don't just review your premium. Review your contract.

https://whatsinyourcontract.com

Upload your stop-loss contract, administrative services agreement, or PBM agreement for review.

metadata.title: Fully Insured and Non ERISA Plans  Advanced Topics in Preemption and Anti Subrogation Exceptions
metadata.author: Matthiesen, Wickert & Lehrer, S.C.
metadata.shortDescription:
Not all employee welfare benefit plans are ERISA-covered, and many ERISA-covered health plans are not self-funded. What if your plan is self-funded but doesn’t qualify for preemption? What if it’s fully-funded, and qualifies for preemption, just not as often as a private, self-funded plan? What if state law applies, but the Plan, the participant, and the accident aren’t all within the same state? It is just as important for subrogation professionals to know and understand how to effectively and efficiently pursue subrogation and/or reimbursement rights of a non-ERISA or fully-insured ERISA plan, as it is to be familiar with the mechanics of ERISA itself. This course addresses preemption, choice of law, and both well-known and little-known exceptions to anti-subrogation laws involving health plans. It also delves into the nuances of ERISA’s preemption, saving and deemer clauses; looking at what they mean, which state laws are preempted, and why. These concepts are often oversimplified, and when they are, they can lead to lost recoveries. This course will teach you how to make sure you aren’t missing out on recoveries for plans in the most problematic states like Arizona, California, Georgia, Kansas, Missouri, Montana, New York, North Carolina, or Pennsylvania.

You can catch up on past webinars at https://www.mwl-law.com/. Is a specific question you’d like answered during this webinar? E-mail Ryan Woody at rwoody@mwl-law.com.

 If you should have any questions on this webinar or subrogation in general, email Ryan Woody at rwoody@mwl-law.com.

metadata.title: What is stop-loss insurance?
metadata.author: PeopleKeep
metadata.shortDescription:
In some cases, self-funded group plans are more affordable than fully-insured group health insurance, especially if you have employees who rarely use their health benefit. But with self-funding comes the risk of costly medical claims which could leave your company financially strapped.

That’s where stop-loss insurance can help. It protects you from paying high-cost claims under your self-funded plan, helping you avoid surprise medical expenses. 

Read more in our article: https://www.peoplekeep.com/blog/what-is-stop-loss-insurance

CHAPTERS:
0:00 - Introduction
0:38 - What is stop-loss insurance?
1:00- How does stop-loss insurance work?
2:00 - Do I need stop-loss insurance with an HRA?
2:40 - How to determine if stop-loss insurance is the right choice for your organization
3:27 - Conclusion

Stop-loss insurance can be a good option if you have a self-funded health benefit plan at your organization. It helps you fight rising medical costs and lower your company’s financial liability for expensive medical claims.

Since starting in 2006 as Zane Benefits, we've helped thousands of organizations offer affordable benefits to their employees.

#healthinsurance #healthcare #healthinsuranceplans #healthbenefits #employeebenefits #smallbusinessowner #smallbusinesstips #smallbusiness

Pros and cons of stop-loss insurance

segments.text: ﻿In some cases, self-funded group plans are more affordable than fully-insured
group health insurance, especially if you have employees who rarely use their health
benefit. But with self-funding comes the risk of costly medical claims which could
leave your company financially strapped. That’s where stop-loss insurance can help.
It protects you from paying high-cost claims under your self-funded plan,
helping you avoid surprise medical expenses. In this video, I’ll cover how stop-loss insurance
works and how to know if it’s the right choice for your company.
What is stop-loss insurance? Stop-loss insurance, or excess insurance,
is coverage an employer buys to lessen the risk of a self-funded health plan. It shields
employers against catastrophic expenses. That way, they don’t have to assume 100% liability
for any “losses” under the plan. How does stop-loss insurance work?
Stop-loss insurance payouts use a reimbursement model. You’re responsible for paying all your
employees' claim costs upfront while they’re on your plan.
Afterward, you’ll submit any eligible claims to your insurer to receive reimbursements for
the amount that exceeds the plan’s deductible or attachment point.
Expenses must meet the following criteria to be eligible for
reimbursement by your insurance carrier: * It must be an eligible expense as defined
in your benefit plan document. * The loss must meet the definition
of a loss outlined in your policy. Reviewing your plan document is critical
to understanding your financial liability. For example, a stop-loss carrier may have policies
that don’t allow reimbursement for certain claims. A misunderstanding can result in significant
liability. So, examine it carefully with your insurer or broker before the plan period begins.
Do I need stop-loss insurance with an HRA? If you have a stand-alone health reimbursement
arrangement like an ICHRA or QSEHRA, your employees can receive tax-free reimbursements
for their individual health insurance premiums and other out-of-pocket medical expenses.
The federal government considers HRAs self-funded employee benefit plans. But they offer employers
greater cost-predictability than other self-funded insurance options. Since you
set a fixed allowance for your employees, there’s no risk of unpredicted claims. Therefore, you’re
unlikely to need stop-loss insurance with an HRA. How to determine if stop-loss insurance is the
right choice for your organization Before getting a self-funded insurance
plan and stop-loss policy at your organization, you should consider your
employees’ health and potential financial risk. If your workforce is generally young and healthy,
your financial risk for costly claims with a self-funded plan is lower. If an employee
has a health emergency, your stop-loss coverage can bridge the gap without breaking the bank.
However, if your workforce is mostly older individuals or those with families,
you may experience a higher frequency of claims. In this case, you might decide that waiting for
reimbursements isn’t worth the initial, expensive claim payouts. In this case, you
may look for alternatives to self-insured plans. Stop-loss insurance can be a good option if you
have a self-funded health benefit plan at your organization. It helps you fight rising medical
costs and lower your company’s financial liability for expensive medical claims.
To learn more about stop-loss insurance, you can read our article on this topic.
We’ve provided a link to it in the description. If you're an employer looking to provide employee
health benefits, PeopleKeep can help. Our HRA administration platform makes it
easy to set up and manage your personalized health benefit in just minutes each month.
If you found this video helpful, be sure to give us a like and subscribe to our channel
for more employee benefits and small business tips. Thanks for watching.

metadata.title: Is Reference-Based Pricing (RBP) Really That Controversial?
metadata.author: Dysrupt Healthcare Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Reference-Based Pricing (RBP) often gets a bad rap, but is it really the healthcare villain many believe it to be? In this Impact Healthcare Podcast recap episode, host Lester Morales dives into the reality of RBP, debunking common myths and clarifying misconceptions about this innovative healthcare pricing strategy.

Discover how reference-based pricing, when implemented effectively, can benefit employers, employees, and even healthcare providers. Lester shares insights and real-world stories, illustrating why understanding this approach is crucial for employers looking to lower healthcare costs responsibly.

📌 Key Takeaways:

How RBP differs fundamentally from traditional PPO programs.

Why traditional healthcare pricing methods may incentivize higher costs.

The surprising parallels between RBP and existing healthcare payment models.

Real-life examples of successful implementations of reference-based pricing.

If you're an employer, healthcare professional, or simply someone interested in learning effective ways to reduce healthcare costs, this episode provides essential insights.

👉 Subscribe to the Impact Healthcare Podcast for more powerful insights and actionable tips to revolutionize your healthcare strategies.

2:42 - Why Insurance Companies May Not Want Lower Costs
5:06 - How Reference-Based Pricing Works
6:40 - Debunking Myths about RBP & Hospital Acceptance
9:15 - The Importance of Claims Auditing

metadata.author: Holloway Benefit Concepts
metadata.shortDescription:
Reference Based Pricing explained! In this video Holloway Benefit Concepts CEO Ryan Holloway discusses how Reference Based Pricing can help transform your group benefit strategy and play outside the constraints of "Big Insurance". 

Hi everyone this is Ryan with how we Benefit Concepts. Today I’m looking for a forward-thinking business owners who are tired of increases from the health insurance companies every single year. I want to talk about Reference Based Pricing. 

Reference Based Pricing is a model where all of your claims in your insurance program are based on a percentage of Medicare. It's always a higher percentage, 150%- 200% of Medicare. What it gets away from are these negotiations that our back-door, private, no transparency negotiations between the insurance companies and the hospital -  that's where all the cost really come from. 

In the Reference Based Pricing world you're getting away from all that so your claims dollars are not nearly as high, you're not paying as much in claims and your actual cost when people go to the hospital is much lower. 

In exchange for that, your premiums are much, much lower. There’s actually a couple states in the country that have moved to this model as saving their taxpayers a ton of money. I want to make everyone understand this is also a play for small businesses, for medium-sized businesses. 

We have two clients that have been on these type models for two years in a row. Two years in a row their claim costs and overall premiums have gone down. It's a proven method it works. You do have to get to underwriting so there's some risk analysis that takes place like in true insurance. 

This is a great approach to cut costs for yourself and your employees and in most cases really improve on the benefits that you offer. 

This is a very forward-thinking approach, but for those business owners that are out there that want to get out of the system, move forward with something very different I'd love to talk to you about it more, talk to you soon!

For more tips follow us on Facebook at https://facebook.com/hollowaybenefitc... or visit us at https://hollowaybenefitconcepts.com 

Supercharge Your Group Benefits Strategy!

metadata.title: Reference-Based Pricing vs. Commercial Claims Pricing: What You NEED to Know
metadata.author: Micro-Dyn
metadata.shortDescription:
Is your organization ready for the rise of reference-based pricing (RBP)?

As more self-funded employers shift away from traditional commercial claims pricing, 
healthcare providers and payers need to understand how RBP works — and why coding 
accuracy matters MORE under this model.

In this video, we break down:

✅ What commercial claims pricing is and how it works
✅ What reference-based pricing (RBP) is and why employers are adopting it
✅ Key differences between RBP and traditional commercial health plans
✅ How coding errors compound under RBP vs. commercial pricing
✅ What providers and payers need to do to protect their revenue

💡 Whether you're a hospital billing team, a TPA, or a self-funded employer, 
this video will help you stay ahead of RBP claims.

#ReferencedBasedPricing #HealthcareClaims #MedicalBilling #RevenueCycle 
#HealthcarePayers #SelfFundedEmployers #ClaimsPricing #MedicalCoding 
#HealthcareCosts #DRG #MedicarePricing #HealthInsurance #RBP

segments.text: Did you know the way healthcare is
priced is changing and it could affect
how much patients and providers pay or
earn? Today, we're breaking down the
difference between traditional
commercial claims pricing and
reference-based pricing.
For years, health care systems relied on
commercial claims pricing, but now many
employers are switching to a new model
called reference-based pricing or RBP.
Let's explore how they work and why it
matters.
Commercial claims pricing is based on
contracts between healthcare providers
and insurance companies. Providers agree
to fixed rates to be part of a network.
When a claim is submitted, the system
checks it against these contracts and
determines the payment.
This system works well, but only when
everything is accurate. If coding or
pricing logic is wrong, it can lead to
denied claims, audits, or lost revenue.
Reference-based pricing is different.
Instead of relying on contracts,
employers set payments based on a
benchmark, often a percentage of
Medicare rates. For example, a plan
might pay 200% of the Medicare rate for
a service.
With RBP, patients can see any provider
who accepts the rate. But if providers
don't agree, patients may receive a
balance bill, meaning they have to pay
the difference.
So what's the difference? Traditional
pricing depends on contracts and
networks. RBP depends on benchmarks and
flexibility, but also introduces risks
like billing disputes.
In both systems, accuracy is critical.
But in RBP, coding errors can multiply,
leading to bigger financial losses.
As healthcare pricing evolves, providers
and payers must stay accurate,
efficient, and prepared. Whether using
traditional pricing or RBP, precision is
the key to protecting revenue.
If you found this helpful, don't forget
to like, subscribe, and share for more
simple healthcare insights.

As reference-based pricing has become an increasingly popular tool in the fight against rising health insurance costs, more self-funded employers are discovering Imagine360 — the first complete health plan solution with the cost savings of reference based pricing built in.

There are two ways self-funded employers can add Imagine360's reference based pricing solution to their health insurance strategy:
- Include reference based pricing as a standalone solution to a current self-funded health plan: https://www.imagine360.com/reference-based-pricing/
- Choose Imagine360's complete self-funded health plan with reference based pricing built in: https://www.imagine360.com/your-health-plan/

Your health plan can do better. We promise.

Imagine360 was created to empower companies to take control of rising healthcare costs. With Imagine360's solutions, employers benefit from flexibility, service and support while employees receive high-quality care at a fair price. Learn more about our reference-based pricing and self-funded health plan options at https://www.imagine360.com/.

Now is an extremely exciting time because we're seeing movement in healthcare that we've never seen before. Disrupting the marketplace entirely led by the most unlikely group that any expert predicted, and that is employers. They're demanding better; they want more value. There's more options on the market for them. Reference based pricing is becoming far more dominant in the marketplace. It has the promise of reining in surprise billing and it also ensures that claims are paid out at a fair amount. I'm always struck by how hospital services outpace inflation faster than any other industry in the United States. The less transparent the marketplace, the more you see price inflation. This is where many of us in the health policy community and academics look at reference based pricing as one of the ways to rescue us from this crazy game that nobody ever designed to be this nuts. When American hospitals were built, they were built to be a safe haven for the sick and injured, not a place where people go and get gouged. Not a place where they're taken advantage of financially. And this represents a violation of everything sacred about the public trust in the medical profession. We need more public accountability for the hospitals that are not complying with the federal regulations. We want to know what the real prices are, and we want to know what those agreements are with the different insurance companies so that we can start coming up with fair reference-based pricing for a region. Imagine that you go to look up the price of a flight when you're shopping and there's no price. The airlines have a statement that they can't give you a price; they just don't know what their true cost will be. This would be absurd, right? There would be price gouging in the marketplace. The fundamental problem in healthcare is that we have non-competitive markets. The real change is to transform those non-competitive markets into competitive markets. You guys are really setting a standard for prices that otherwise have no orbit in outer space and they need to be anchored to something — and that's exactly what reference-based pricing does in the market. That's where you guys have been great leaders, so thank you for what you're doing in healthcare. [Music]
