metadata.title: Drug Pricing Indexes: Maximum Allowable Cost (MAC)
metadata.author: TheCoyPharmer
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to The Coy Pharmer, where we break down complex pharmacy benefit concepts into clear and practical insights.

In this video, we explore Maximum Allowable Cost (MAC) — one of the most important yet misunderstood pricing mechanisms in Pharmacy Benefit Management (PBM). MAC plays a major role in determining how generic drugs are reimbursed across pharmacy networks, and it directly affects pharmacies, PBMs, and plan sponsors.

If you review pharmacy claims, negotiate PBM contracts, or analyze prescription drug spending, understanding how MAC works is essential.

In this episode, we cover:

The Basics: ( 0:25 )
• Breaking Down the Acronym ( 1:07 )
• Why MAC Exists ( 1:17 ) 

In Practice: ( 1:41 ) 
• How Mac Helps Payers ( 1:48 )
• Challenges for Pharmacies ( 4:41 )
• PBM Balancing Act ( 6:01 )

The Fine Print: ( 9:49 )
• Mac List Sprawl ( 10:29 ) 
• Take Homes for Employers ( 14:12 )
• Take Homes for Resellers ( 15:18 )

Generic drug markets move quickly as manufacturers enter and exit the market, which makes pricing strategies like MAC both powerful and controversial. Understanding this system helps explain why the same generic medication may be reimbursed differently across plans, pharmacies, and employer groups.

At The Coy Pharmer, our goal is to cultivate clarity in the complex world of pharmacy benefits so that plan sponsors, consultants, and industry professionals can make better-informed decisions.

If you want to better understand PBM pricing models, pharmacy reimbursement, and drug spending trends, this video will give you the foundation you need.

metadata.title: PBM Audits & Network Compliance in 2026 What Pharmacies Need to Know Now
metadata.author: Frier Levitt
metadata.shortDescription:
PBM audits are intensifying – and the stakes have never been higher. Recoupments, network terminations, and compliance pitfalls are threatening pharmacies that aren’t prepared for what PBMs are scrutinizing in 2026.

In this webinar, Frier Levitt Partner Harini Bupathi breaks down exactly what pharmacies need to know to protect their businesses, stay in network, and respond with confidence when audits arrive.

What You’ll Learn:
🔸The most common pressure points targeting pharmacies during PBM audits and how to proactively address them
🔸What’s changed in 2026 PBM provider manuals and agreements and which new provisions could put your pharmacy at risk
🔸How to build audit-ready operations that reduce recoupments, prevent compliance gaps, and strengthen your network standing
🔸The tools and resources available help you respond effectively to PBM audits and reduce the risk of network termination

Don’t miss this opportunity to stay informed and proactive!

For legal support or questions, contact the Frier Levitt team at www.frierlevitt.com.

👉 Subscribe to our YouTube channel for more legal webinars and updates!

#FrierLevitt #PharmacyCompliance #PBM #HealthcareLaw #PharmacyLaw #PharmacyAudit

metadata.title: PBM Deception on Rebate Pass-Through
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
PBM Deception on Rebate Pass-Through.

Professor Ge Bai moderated a panel of Mark Cuban and Dr. Patrick Conway--the CEO of Optum--at Johns Hopkins University.

During the discussion Dr. Conway said that United Healthcare's PBM--OptumRx--will pass through 100% of the rebate payments they receive from pharmaceutical manufactures on to their customers.  

The other two of the 'Big 3' PBMs--CVS/Caremark and Cigna/Express Scripts--have made similar statements as well.

However, there is a catch.  

The catch is that pharmaceutical manufactures make ADDITIONAL payments to Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) that are under that same parent company as the PBMs.  These additional payments are called 'Administrative Fees' and are not considered rebates by the PBMs... as such, these Administrative Fees are NOT passed through to customers.

A recent article by Hunterbrook Media reported that as part of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lawsuit against the 'Big 3' PBMs, it was revealed that the PBMs have DECREASED the Rebated payments that come from the pharmaceutical manufacturers (that are passed through to customers) and INCREASED the Administrative Fees (that are NOT passed through to customers).

From 2012 to 2023...
Rebates have decreased from 48% to 13%
Administrative Fees have increased from 5% to 22%

PBMs have shifted the pharmaceutical manufacturer money flow away from Rebates toward Administrative Fees so less is passed on to customers.

AHealthcareZ PBM GPO Video: https://youtu.be/dV0P-LVZWow?si=0rFsp6633now8KET

Sources:
Prof. Ge Bai, Mark Cuban, Patrick Conway Panel at Johns Hopkins: https://x.com/GeBaiDC/status/2004931798279586072?s=20
https://hntrbrk.com/pbmgpo/

https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/payers/unitedhealth-group-posts-144b-profit-4003b-revenue-2024#:~:text=UnitedHealth%20Group's%20Optum%20Rx%20unit,us%20to%20make%20it%20happen.%22

https://investors.cvshealth.com/news/news-details/2018/CVS-Health-Introduces-New-Approach-to-Pricing-of-Pharmacy-Benefit-Management-Services/default.aspx

https://www.modernhealthcare.com/insurance/mh-cigna-drug-rebates-health-plans-2027/#:~:text=Key%20Takeaways,after%20a%20medication%20is%20dispensed.

AHealthcareZ is 400+ Healthcare Finance Educational Videos.

metadata.title: Navigating PBM Audits: Ensuring Pharmacy Compliance and Mitigating Risks
metadata.author: Frier Levitt
metadata.shortDescription:
Pharmacies are facing increasing risks when it comes to Pharmacy Benefit Manager (PBM) audits. From recoupments and network terminations to governmental investigations, the stakes are higher than ever. Properly addressing audit issues and implementing preventative measures are crucial to ensuring a positive audit result.

Frier Levitt attorneys present this informative webinar where they discuss the key challenges, potential risks, and best practices to navigate PBM audits successfully.  We will share a PBM audit checklist to help you navigate a potential audit.

Webinar Agenda:
(1) Understand PBM audits and implications on network participation
(2) Learn about proactive efforts to self-audit pharmacy operations in advance of PBM audit
(3) Develop best practices for pharmacy operations

To learn more or contact us, visit https://www.frierlevitt.com

metadata.title: Best-in-Class Transparent PBMs: What the Contract Has to Say
metadata.author: Benefits Blake
metadata.shortDescription:
Every PBM calls itself transparent now. The word is free. The contract is what makes them prove it.

An OPM audit found CVS Caremark didn't pass through negotiated discounts on two of the three largest pharmacy chains. The tab? $478 million in overcharges to federal plan members. That's transparency in the pitch deck, not the contract.

So how do you tell a PBM that markets transparency from one that guarantees it? The House Oversight Committee set a four-part test in 2024. Then the CAA of 2026 went further. It made PBMs covered service providers under ERISA. Fiduciaries. Full pass-through, required. All compensation, disclosed.

The Big Three still run about 80% of claims. But 52% of employers are eyeing the exit, and the transparent challengers are winning real business: Capital Rx (now Judi Health), SmithRx, Navitus, Rightway, Mark Cuban Cost Plus, FairosRx, and RxBenefits.

When you review a contract, five clauses decide everything. 100% rebate pass-through. A spread pricing ban. Unrestricted audit rights. Data ownership. Full fee disclosure. Read those five. That's where transparency lives or dies.

For a 200-person company spending $800K on pharmacy, 20% savings is six figures back in the plan. Every year.

Don't evaluate a PBM on their pitch deck. Evaluate them on their contract.

----------------------------------------
CHAPTERS
----------------------------------------
00:00 "Transparent" means nothing without the contract
00:19 The $478M CVS Caremark overcharge (OPM audit)
01:16 What a truly pass-through PBM looks like (the 4-part test)
02:05 CAA 2026: your PBM is now an ERISA fiduciary
02:42 The Big Three run 80% of claims, and 52% want out
03:06 The transparent challengers: Capital Rx & SmithRx
04:24 Navitus, Rightway & SureSpend
05:58 Mark Cuban Cost Plus, FairosRx & RxBenefits
08:00 What the FTC found about the Big Three
09:10 The 5 contract clauses that decide everything
11:18 What transparency really saves (and the pass-through gap)
12:43 What to do before your next PBM renewal

----------------------------------------
More at benefitsblake.com
Read the full breakdown: https://benefitsblake.com/articles/best-in-class-transparent-pbms-contract-review
Subscribe for weekly Benefits Blake videos.

This is educational, not personalized financial or legal advice.

#pbm #pharmacybenefits #employerbenefits #healthcarecosts #cfo #BenefitsBlake

members.

read every pharmacy benefit manager contract.

without the appropriate contract language to
back it up.

Your job as a consultant is to know
that difference between a PBM that markets

PBM look like?
The House Committee on Oversight and Accountability

There's four tests.

The Department of Labor's proposed rule published

the pharmacy gets reimbursed with all compensation
plainly identified.

the difference. The Consolidated Appropriations

health plans are classified as covered service
providers under ERISA section 408(b)(2).
That means a hundred percent rebate pass-through
is required. All direct and indirect compensation
must be disclosed and compensation must be
reasonable to qualify for any statutory exemptions.
Plans renewing contracts after August 3,
2028 must comply.
Who's actually still doing it?
The big three still process roughly 80%

But the cracks are widening.

in September 2025.

They've more than doubled their March 2024
figure. As of January 2026, the platform has
surpassed 5 million contracted employer lives
with 54 million health plan lives total on
their platform. They signed 80 new partnerships
in both 2024 and 2025, including 13 Fortune
500 corporations and 21 hospital systems.
It's a flat administration fee,
100% pass-through, full audit access.
You also have SmithRx.
SmithRx has raised about $110 million in total
funding and serves over 5 ,000 employer clients.
They delivered about $320 million in savings
reducing client pharmacy costs by an average
of 20%. They earned URAC accreditation in March
2026. Their platform automates cost savings
at the point of adjudication, identifying the
lowest cost drug option for every fill.
Transparent fee structure, no spread pricing
once again.
Navitus Health Solutions, owned by SSM Health
serves over 18 million members across 800 clients.
They pioneered the 100% pass-through rebate
model and now offer cost plus pricing through
Costco pharmacies as of January 2026.
They also launched Navitus Key in 2025,
a streamlined pharmacy benefit manager solution
built specifically for employers with fewer
than 5 ,000 members.
No spread, no retained rebates.
Rightway combines PBM services with clinical
led navigation with about $240 million in total
funding and a billion dollar valuation.
They've grown PBM volume by over 100%
each of the last three years.
They now work with about 30 Fortune 500
companies and ranked number 42 on the 2025
Deloitte Technology Fast 500.
In January 2026, they launched SureSpend,
a pricing model with a single predictable monthly
cost and unlimited liability.

rebate pass-through.
In April 2026, ParetoHealth made Rightway available

covering about 1.3 million people.
Mark Cuban's cost plus drug company built its
reputation on radical price transparency,
manufacturer costs plus a flat 15% markup,
a dispensing fee and shipping.
No rebate games, no spread.
In April 2026, they partnered with Humana's
CenterWell to route group plan members through
cost plus pricing.
For employers shopping Humana group plans in
2026 and 2027, which I don't know that
they're in that many markets anymore,
it's a new lever to reduce prescription costs

higher copays or thinner formularies.

claims processor directly.
FairosRx, founded by Alex Fairly of Fairly

10-page contract.

About 1.2 million in savings per 500

What did the FTC find about the Big
Three? The FTC's second interim staff report
in January 2025 detailed how the six largest
PBMs process nearly 95% of all U.S.
prescriptions.
Vertical integration gives them ownership of
the pharmacies, the mail order operations,
specialty dispensing, and the health plans
that they're supposed to be negotiating against.
The Big Three's affiliated group purchasing
organizations have extracted billions in additional
fees from drug manufacturers.
Those fees doubled from $3.8 billion in
2018 to almost $7.6 billion in 2022,
according to the FTC.
In February 2026, the FTC secured a landmark
settlement with Express Scripts.
The agreement requires fundamental business
practice changes around transparency,
and it's expected to drive down patients out-of-pocket

$7 billion over the next decade.

make rebate arrangement records available for
plan audit no later than August 2028.
You also want to own your data.
Ideally your claims data belongs to you and
the contract should say so explicitly.
You may need the right to pull it
and share it with your advisor,
with a new advisor.
You may want it for benchmarking.
You can track this within your internal systems.
Lastly, fee structure disclosure.
All revenue streams, including administrative
fees, clinical fees, data fees,
and any other compensation should be itemized.
Under ERISA 408(b)(2), PBMs must now disclose
all direct and indirect compensation.
They're the same as your broker.
They've got to tell you exactly how they're
getting paid. A pharmaceutical strategies group
survey found that only 59% of employers
reported receiving 100% of rebates for traditional
drugs and 57% for specialty drugs.
Roughly 4 in 10 employers think they're getting
full pass-through and they aren't.
The contract is what you got to look
at next. How much can a transparent PBM
actually save? SmithRx clients saved an average
of 20% on pharmacy costs in 2025.
RxBenefits Clinical Management Program delivers
more than a 20% per member per
month reduction. For a 200 employee company
spending $800 ,000 a year on pharmacy costs,
that could be an easy six-figure savings
back in the plan.
Milliman found that employer sponsored plans
using rebates reduced premiums by at least
Specialty drugs now account for more than 55%

Independent clinical management not influenced

metadata.author: Vault of Profit
metadata.shortDescription:
You never make a pill, yet you sit at the centre of almost every prescription. This is the economics of owning a pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) — the middleman between health plans, drug makers, and pharmacies.

A pharmacy benefit manager does not sell medicine directly. It negotiates drug prices, manages formularies, processes prescription claims, and builds pharmacy networks, earning its place by controlling costs and access in a complex healthcare system.

In this video you will learn:

How a PBM makes money from rebates, fees, and pharmacy networks
How claims, formularies, and drug pricing work in practice
What it costs to set up the technology, contracts, and compliance behind a PBM
The regulations, risks, and hidden pressures that shape the business
Who actually wins in this model, and who pays for it
This video is for aspiring business owners, entrepreneurs, and anyone curious about how healthcare businesses really work.

Subscribe for more clear breakdowns of how real businesses make money, what they cost to run, and what owners wish they knew first.

metadata.title: Maximum Allowable Cost pricing or MAC pricing on pharmacies
metadata.author: PA Pharmacists
metadata.shortDescription:
http://papharmascists.com/

Maximum Allowable Cost pricing or MAC pricing on pharmacies and its impact. 

Pennsylvania pharmacists explain Maximum Allowable Cost (MAC) in pharmacy reimbursement and why legislation is needed to make MAC pricing fair so it works for pharmacies and patients.

Under MAC Pricing, pharmacy benefit managers or PBMs stipulate what pharmacies will be paid for generic medications. More and more, that payment is below the pharmacy’s purchase price.

PBM’s by not updating their Maximum Allowance Cost pricing  creates major financial losses for pharmacies.

When the cost of a medication goes up, updates to maximum allowable cost pricing lists can lag for several weeks or even months. This means that pharmacies are often reimbursed below what they paid to purchase the prescription medication.

The Pennsylvania Pharmacists Association is seeking legislation that would make MAC pricing work for pharmacies and their patients.

Legislation has been introduced in Pennsylvania that will establish specific requirements for what prescription medications can be placed on the MAC list. It will require PBM’s to update those MAC lists at least once every seven business days.

Please contact your elected officials and ask them to support this legislation today.

metadata.title: PBM Audits & Network Compliance 2026: Critical Strategies for New Jersey Pharmacies
metadata.author: Frier Levitt
metadata.shortDescription:
New Jersey pharmacies are facing unprecedented scrutiny from PBMs heading into 2026. In this essential webinar, Frier Levitt attorneys Harini Bupathi, Esq. and Benjamin Youssef, Pharm.D., Esq. break down what pharmacies must know to stay compliant, avoid network termination, and prepare for the next wave of PBM audits and FWA investigations.

What You’ll Learn:
✔ The most common PBM audit triggers
✔ Why inventory shortages and copay documentation are top risk areas
✔ How patient and prescriber denials lead to audit findings
✔ The growing focus on prior authorization involvement
✔ Red flags that increase the risk of PBM network termination
✔ Proactive steps every pharmacy should take before 2026
✔ Key legal tools available to New Jersey pharmacies, including AWPL protections

This presentation is especially critical for New Jersey independent pharmacies, chain pharmacies, PICs, compliance officers, and owners preparing for heightened PBM oversight.

If your pharmacy is experiencing audit pressure, increased documentation requests, network threats, or FWA investigations, this webinar provides practical, real-world strategies to protect your operation.

📌 Need help with a PBM audit or termination?
Contact the Frier Levitt Life Sciences team for experienced legal guidance:  www.frierlevitt.com/contact-us

👉 Don't forget to like, subscribe, and hit the 🔔 to stay updated on upcoming healthcare compliance insights!

About Frier Levitt:
Frier Levitt is a national boutique healthcare and life sciences law firm. Our attorneys help pharmacies, providers, life sciences companies, and payors navigate regulatory risk, PBM contracting, audits, and network access. 

#PBMAudits #PharmacyCompliance #NetworkCompliance #NewJerseyPharmacies #IndependentPharmacy #PharmacyAudit #PBMRegulation #FrierLevitt #PharmacyOwner #FraudWasteAbuse #PharmacyLaw #PharmacyLeadership #PharmacyOperations #NJPHA

metadata.title: Lower your Workers Compensation Insurance Cost
metadata.author: Jeremy Burris - Insurance Dad
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video we help introduce workers compensation savings strategies that will lower your total workers compensation insurance expense. 

Do not assume that all workers compensation polices are priced the same. 

Did you know that there are multiple ways you can save money on your workers compensation premium? In this video we discuss some of the ways we help our current worker compensation policy holders and prospects lower their workers compensation cost. 

Let our team of professionals help you explore cost savings options available to you.
We can help lower workers compensation cost via Experience Mod reduction strategies, filing for 2% safety credits, exploring 5% drug free credits, finding dividends offered by carriers, exploring deviated rates on NCCI class codes, verifying that you are in the correct workers compensation class codes and auditing your policy with our Mod Master program.

If your workers compensation policy is up for renewal, we encourage you to let us explore ways that we can save you money!

In 2026, that assumption can cost medical providers millions.


In this episode of Workers’ Comp Unwrapped, Anique and Angela break down the growing trend of retroactive denials, overpayment audits, refund demands, and recoupment threats where insurers attempt to claw back money long after payment has been issued.


We cover:

  •  Why carriers are revisiting already-paid claims
     
     
     
  •  How overpayment audits actually start
     
     
     
  •  The difference between a refund request and a legal obligation
     
     
     
  •  Common mistakes providers make when audit letters arrive
     
     
     
  •  How to protect paid claims, preserve leverage, and avoid unnecessary refunds
     
     
     

If you’ve ever received a demand letter months—or years—after payment, this episode explains what’s really happening and how to respond strategically.

☎️ Need my help with your Workers Compensation case? Call to set up a free consultation at 212-406-8989 or visit https://bit.ly/RexContact

**You Might Be Missing a 3rd Party Case in Your Workers Comp Claim!**

Most injured workers think workers comp is the only way to get paid after a job injury — but that’s not always true.

If someone other than your employer caused your accident, you might have a **3rd party lawsuit** that could be worth way more money than comp alone.

In this video, I’ll explain:

👉 What a 3rd party claim really means in a workers comp case

👉 The difference between workers comp benefits and 3rd party money

👉 The rules you need to follow so you don’t lose your comp benefits

👉 How to tell if your case might qualify — and what to do next

Don’t assume your case is “just comp.” You could be sitting on a claim that’s worth thousands — or even more — if you know what to look for.

Watch this before you settle, sign anything, or assume your lawyer already checked for a 3rd party case.

☎️ Need my help with your Workers Compensation case? Call to set up a free consultation at 212-406-8989 or visit https://bit.ly/RexContact

Workers comp settlement tips your lawyer won’t tell you! When it’s time to settle your workers compensation case, insurance companies will play a tricky game, using various methods to get you to accept less than what your case is actually worth. In this video, I share real-life stories of how and when settlements are offered, from minor injuries to complex cases requiring surgery. You’ll learn about the negotiation tactics insurance companies use, what factors impact your settlement amount, and why having a savvy lawyer can make all the difference. I also explain how to maximize your payout and settle your case at exactly the right time, so you don’t want to miss this!

It's just a bad memory or something that happened and they move on. And also some cases, they're not all winners. The facts of the case lead it to the point of whether or not it's compensable or not. And if a case is found to be not compensable, there’s not going to be a settlement. Any pro tips for injured workers settling their workers compensation claim? Having a good doctor and a good lawyer is very important. A doctor who knows workers comp, knows the forms, knows the law, knows how to do a schedule loss of use of evaluation. Very, very important. We've dealt with people who are out of state and they go and see a doctor that's an out of state doctor, and we ask them for a permanency report, and we ask them for a schedule loss of use, or we ask for a comment on a permanent disability, and we go and get a report back that reads like a different language because they don't know how to do a schedule loss of use evaluation according to the New York State rules. And it throws the whole case off. Having a doctor that knows the rules, having a good doctor that's going to get you to a point of maximum medical improvement, a high level of improvement, very, very important. Having a lawyer who knows how to apply those guidelines and the law, the facts of your case also very, very important. Another thing that's important is having reasonable expectations. Talking to your doctor about what to expect from your treatment is very important. Some people think that they're going to get surgery, and they're going to be like an 18 year old who played soccer all over again because they got their knee fixed when they're 50 years old. You need to have reasonable expectations about what is to come from your treatment and what's to come from your case. Here in New York State, workers compensation cases are not million dollar cases. By its very definition. By the nature of workers compensation, you're paid a portion of your salary. You don't even get your full salary. The goal behind the law is to get you the care, the benefits that you need to sustain you while you're getting better and get you back to work as soon as possible, not to maintain you for the rest of your life unless it's absolutely necessary. Just the other day, I had a client in here. Their medical report, their doctor's report would yield a payout of $5,400. The insurance company's permanency report would've gotten them, I believe, $500. So we're looking at $500 or $5400. The insurance company offered them somewhere in the range of $4,000, and the person's response was, “I want ten grand.” Well, we need to be realistic. We need to be reasonable. If the most I can argue for based upon your doctor's report, is $5,000. Why on earth would an insurance company give me ten? You need to be reasonable here. So that's very important. But if you have questions, and if you don't have an attorney and you're looking for some help, feel free to give me a call. 212-406-8989. Rex Zachofsky. New York workers compensation. We are here to help. Folks, thank you very much. Have a wonderful rest of your day. Enjoy the sun.

metadata.title: Reducing Workers Compensation Rates- Tactical & Practical Strategies
metadata.author: Employers Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Date: 3/5/2014

Host: Joe Stevens, President and founder of Bridge Safety Consultants

After almost a decade of containment, workers' comp rates in California have been on a sharp increase over the past three years.  The financial bottom line of every employer in California is impacted by these increases, and HR can (and should) take a proactive role in fostering a genuine safety culture within the organization.  Reduced cost is just one of the many benefits of a strong safety program!
 
Join Employers Group and safety expert Joe Stevens, the president of Bridge Safety Consultants, for a hard-hitting, insightful and interactive webinar during which we will examine:

- How and why workers' comp rates are on the rise
- The potential fiscal impact to employers
- Fundamentals of workers' comp
- Terminology
- How ex-mods are calculated
- How premiums are calculated
- Case studies
- Strategies and Best Practices

metadata.title: Compliance Overview: Group Health Plan Fiduciary Litigation on the Rise
metadata.author: Justin Burgess
metadata.shortDescription:
Enforcement of the strict standards of fiduciary conduct set forth in the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) has traditionally been reserved for retirement plan sponsors. However, a new class action lawsuit highlights the importance of employers’ adherence to their fiduciary duties when managing their group health plans.

The lawsuit, filed against Johnson & Johnson (J&J), alleges the company violated its ERISA fiduciary duties by mismanaging its prescription drug benefit, which cost the health plan and participants millions of dollars. It serves as a reminder to employers that they must prudently select and monitor plan service providers, such as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs).

Although it is the first case of its kind, more fiduciary litigation involving the management of prescription drug benefits is expected as the PBM industry faces increasing scrutiny and new transparency laws provide employees with more information regarding health care costs. This Compliance Overview includes tips to help employers understand the basic fiduciary responsibilities applicable to group health plans under ERISA to mitigate liability.

In this video, we're delving into the recent class action lawsuit against Johnson & Johnson and its implications for employers like you under ERISA (Employee Retirement Income Security Act). segments.text: I am Mike Hill, the founder of Total Control Health Plans,
and today we're here to talk about ERISA
and employers' fiduciary obligations under that law.
Let's talk about what ERISA is, stands for,
the Employee Retirement Income Security Act,
and its legislation that was passed by Congress
to make sure that employers manage their employees'
retirement plans and welfare benefit plans appropriately.
A lot of employers don't realize
that self-funded medical plans
and welfare benefits as a whole, which could be medical,
dental, or vision, are also governed by ERISA
and the same fiduciary obligations to manage those plans.
Well, exist in those plans as they do retirement plans,
although there have been examples in the past
where employees have sued employers
for the way they manage the health plans
and the fact that they did not keep the cost under control.
There was big news in the employee benefits industry a
couple of weeks ago where an employee proposed a class action
lawsuit against Johnson and Johnson,
and not just the company,
but the benefits committee
for breaching their fiduciary duties
for not managing the health plan well,
and they really focus on the pharmacy side
of the health plan and the partnership Johnson
and Johnson had with their pharmacy benefit manager
and their employee benefit consultant.
The argument goes that the pharmacy benefit manager
and Johnson and Johnson did not manage the pharmacy plan
well, resulting in employees paying thousands
of percent more for prescription drugs that they
otherwise would've paid a lot less
for had they paid cash walking into your local mom
and pop pharmacy, for example,
the employee in their argument against Johnson and Johnson
and their benefit committee laid out numerous examples of
where the inability of the benefits committee
to manage their health plan well resulted in not only
employees paying more out of pocket,
but also the cost of the plan
as a whole going up astronomically year over year,
resulting in employees paying more premium out of their
paychecks on a per pay period basis.
Let's take a look at the
arguments being made in the lawsuit.
One of the primary complaints is
that the pharmacy benefit manager was allowed
to define generic specialty drugs
how they saw fit.
And any generic specialty drugs had to go
to their particular specialty pharmacy, allowing them
to control not only what was paid,
but also what was charged for those particular drugs.
It was thousands or percent higher than they might pay if
they went to a local pharmacy.
So one example, maybe not a big deal, maybe two,
not a big deal, but there were dozens
that the legal team was able
to outline in this particular case.
For example, teriflunomide is a generic drug used
to treat certain forms of multiple sclerosis.
The average acquisition cost for pharmacies
for this generic drug is 91 cents per 14-milligram tablet,
so a 90-day supply would cost $81.
This plan particularly paid though $10,239
for the same prescription, which is a 12,403% markup.
This particular lawsuit hasn't been granted class action
status yet it needs to be ruled on
to see if the case actually has merit
and it may be dismissed in this particular case.
But for those of us that are watching,
we think it's only a matter of time
before some employer has made an example of, so
what should employers do about this particular lawsuit?
Ultimately, what we're trying to do right
now is create awareness.
We don't think any particular employers are going to be sued
imminently, but we think it's really important
to understand the provisions
of the Pharmacy Benefit Manager contract that you have,
and be aware of how the pharmacy market
is changing dramatically.
You should be looking at terms like generic drug
or brand name drug and what the definitions are.
So take a look at your contract, dust off,
make sure you understand what the definitions are
and how it stacks up against an industry best practice.

metadata.title: Breaking: J&J ERISA Employee Benefit Lawsuit. Am I at Risk?
metadata.author: Frier Levitt
metadata.shortDescription:
This Changes Everything for Benefits Leaders with Fiduciary Duty

A Johnson & Johnson employee filed a class action lawsuit on February 5, 2024, sending shockwaves through the benefits community.  Alleging breach of fiduciary duty by the company, the lawsuit exposes alarming markups in prescription drug costs within the company’s health plan. Some of these markups are as high as 801% markup for an HIV drug, a 6,392% markup for a prostate cancer drug, a 9,592% markup for a leukemia drug, and a 12,403% markup for an MS drug. Despite hiring top benefit consultants and PBMs, serious mismanagement occurred, raising serious concerns about benefit management practices.

Together with Vivio, Frier Levitt co-founding partner Jonathan Levitt and CEO of Vivio Pramod John present a webinar, “Breaking: J&J ERISA Employee Benefit Lawsuit. Am I at Risk?”. During this webinar, the panelists delve into the class action, answering the following question:

(1) Is this lawsuit a big deal?
(2) Am I at personal risk?
(3) Could my company be sued?
(4) What should I do?

Who is this webinar for? Self-funded employers, benefits consultants and employee benefits professionals.

To learn more, visit: www.frierlevitt.com

metadata.title: ERISA Litigation 7: ERISA Pleading Requirements (6th Circuit)
metadata.author: Bentley Tolk
metadata.shortDescription: This video addresses ERISA breach of fiduciary duty pleading requirements in the Sixth Circuit.

segments.text: This is Bentley Tolk with the Orisa
litigation channel. I'm an attorney at
Par Brown Gill and Loveless in Salt Lake
City and uh welcome to another episode
of the Orisa litigation channel.
Today we're going to talk about a sixth
circuit case uh that addresses Orisa
breach of fiduciary duty pleading
requirements. This case is an older
case, but as uh we start up the Orisa
litigation channel again, I wanted to uh
address this case before we get back to
more current cases. This is the file
versus State Street Bank and Trust case.
The facts briefly are that GM had uh
various 401k plans for its employees.
One of the options for the plans was for
participants um to um participate in the
the GM common stock fund. Now
participants could choose which options
uh in which to invest their funds. They
could change the allocation for any
option on any business day. The
plaintiffs in this class action alleged
that the plans had invested well over a
billion dollars in the GM stock in GM
stock during the class period.
The plans allowed the GM common stock
fund uh to be invested in exclusively uh
in GM stock without regard to
diversification, market fluctuations,
risk profile, etc. However, the plans
also stated that if State Street is the
independent fiduciary determined in its
discretion from reliable public
information that there was a serious
concern about GM's short-term viability
or that there was no short-term chance
of recouping any substantial proceeds
from the sale of of stock and
bankruptcy, then State Street had to
devest the plan's holdings in the GM
common stock fund. According to the
complaint, during the relevant time
frame, GM's troubles were were well
documented. Uh, and according to the
complaint, there were uh discussions uh
commentators talking about bankruptcy.
The CEO was talking about restructuring.
The 10Q talked about doubts uh of the
ability of GM to survive as a going
concern. And uh according to the
complaint, State Street uh should have
recognized as of about July 2008 that
the GM stock was no longer prudent uh as
an investment for the plans. On November
21st, 2008, State Street told
participants that it was no longer
purchasing uh in in the fund due to
earnings and other concerns. However,
according to the to the plaintiffs,
State Street didn't devest at that time
and it waited until March 31st, 2009 to
decide to devest, which it did by April
Now, on June 1st, 2009, GM filed for
bankruptcy.
The plaintiffs filed this class action
against State Street, alleging breach of
fiduciary duty under section 409A,
alleging that there had been imprudent
management of plain assets under section
404. The district court granted State
Street's motion to dismiss, but the
sixth circuit reversed and remanded.
The holding was that the Cooper Munch
reasonleness presumption isn't an
additional pleading requirement and
doesn't apply at the motion to dismiss
stage. In other words, a plaintiff
doesn't have to plead enough facts to
overcome the presumption in order to
survive a motion to dismiss. The Cooper
Munch reasonableness presumption
according to the file case is an
evidentiary presumption and it isn't a
pleading requirement.
Now, according to the court, ESOP
fiduciaries wear two hats. They've both
follow the plan uh and ORISA as they
administer ESOP investments but the plan
is only followed to the extent it's
consistent with Orisa and there's an
abuse of discretion standard regarding
the ESOP fiduciary's decision to invest
in employer securities.
The Cooper Munch presumption um says
that a fiduciary's decision uh to remain
invested in employer securities is
presumed to be reasonleness, I'm sorry,
to be reasonable, but a pliff can rebut
that presumption by showing that a
prudent fiduciary acting under similar
circumstances would have made a
different investment decision. State
Street was entitled to the Cooper Munch
presumption, but the Sixth Circuit had
not addressed whether it applied at the
motion to dismiss stage. Now you'll see
on the slide that the sixth circuit
talked about what some of the other
circuits have have done and that some of
the other circuits had reached the
opposite holding and that they had held
that the Cooper presumption should be
considered at the pleading stage. But
the file case uh in the sixth circuit uh
distinguished those cases uh because
those circuits had adopted more narrowly
defined tests for rebutting the
presumption than the sixth circuit's
Cooper test. And you'll see on the slide
I I have here it talks about uh in the
second, third, fifth and ninth circuits
uh those circuits have adopted a
rebuttal standard in cases involving the
reasonableness presumption.
But the sixth circuit's rebuttal
standard is different. In the sixth
circuit, a plainif has to prove that a
prudent fiduciary acting under similar
circumstances would have made a
different investment decision. And
that's uh under Cooper. The Sixth
Circuit's rebuttal standard in Cooper
establishes an abuse of discretion
standard. Thus, the file case held in
the Sixth Circuit that while a complaint
has to plead facts to plausibly allege
that a fiduciary has breached its duty
to the plan, the pleadings don't need to
overcome the reasonleness presumption to
survive a motion to dismiss.
The file case disagreed with the
district court that because participants
could choose from a menu of investments
and could avoid GM stock altogether that
state street shouldn't be liable for
plaintiff's decision to stay invested in
the stock fund. It was enough for
plaintiffs to allege that state street
allowed the plans to still hold GM stock
well after it became imprudent to do so
and thus breached its duty to the plan.
This was sufficient pleading of
causation between State Street's breach
and the losses to the plans. The file
case held that as a fiduciary, State
Street needed to exercise prudence when
designating and monitoring the menu of
investment options that would be offered
to plan participants. State Street had
to select and maintain only prudent
investment options in the plan. The file
case also held that Orisa's safe harbor
provision in section 404 C and that
states that basically for any loss from
a breach resulting from the participants
exercise of control over the assets um
when the plan delegates asset control
directly to the participants. In other
words, there's a safe harbor uh that
that safe harbor provision is an
affirmative defense and it doesn't apply
on a motion to dismiss when a plainif
didn't raise it in the complaint.
Now, participant control under section
404C is determined under Department of
Labor regulations.
The district court ery on the section
404C safe harbor defense at this stage
in the pleadings according to the file
case because the complaint didn't raise
it.
404C according to the file case wouldn't
apply under these circumstances because
it doesn't relieve fiduciaries of the
responsibility to screen investments.
the safe harbor provision doesn't shield
a fiduciary for a decision that it did
control um such as the selection uh of
the menu of investment options that the
plan will will offer.
So that is a little bit about the uh the
file case. We will be discussing uh
current cases as they come down in
future episodes of the Orisa litigation
channel. Until then, this is Bentley
Talk.

metadata.title: Episode 172: ERISA Tobacco Surcharge Class Action Survives Motion To Dismiss In Ohio Federal Court
metadata.author: The Class Action Weekly Wire
metadata.shortDescription: This week’s episode features Duane Morris partner Jerry Maatman, special counsel Adam Brown, and associate Elizabeth Underwood with their analysis of an Ohio federal court decision partially denying an employer’s motion to dismiss an ERISA class action brought by former employees over its nicotine surcharge program.

segments.text: Hello everyone and thank you for joining
us for the next episode of the class
action weekly wire. I'm Jerry Maman, a
partner at Dwayne Morris and welcoming
my colleagues today, Adam Brown and
Elizabeth Underwood. Thank you both for
being on the podcast.
>> Good to be here, Jerry.
>> Thanks for having me, Jerry.
>> Today we're going to discuss a recent
ruling under ERISA that should catch the
attention of employers that use nicotine
or tobacco surcharges as part of their
employee health plans. The case is Kills
versus Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company
from the Northern District of Ohio.
On October 8, Judge Christopher Boyko
granted in part and denied in part
Goodyear's motion to dismiss a proposed
class action that challenged the
nicotine surcharge program.
The court allowed plaintiff's central
claim challenging the legality of the
surcharge to proceed
while dismissing their ERISA-based
fiduciary duty claims.
Adam, let's start with the basics. What
was Goodyear's program and what were
these employees challenging?
>> Well, Goodyear employees who wanted
health coverage were required to declare
during annual enrollment whether they
used nicotine products and employees who
identified themselves as nicotine users
paid an additional $100 per month
through 2025.
Uh beginning in 2026, that increased to
$150 a month or $1,800 a year.
Uh the plaintiffs are five former
Goodyear employees who paid that
surcharge and they alleged that
Goodyear's program violated ERISA
because its employee-facing materials
didn't provide all the required
information about alternatives that
employees could use to avoid the
surcharge.
>> I guess the important point here is that
ERISA doesn't simply prohibit every
difference in premiums associated with
nicotine use. Elizabeth, can you explain
the target of the plaintiffs here and
the wellness program and how fit into
the lawsuit.
>> Sure, Jerry. The statutory framework
permits different premiums associated
with participation and qualifying health
promotion and disease prevention
programs. For this type of health
contingent wellness program, however,
there are specific requirements,
including that the full reward be
available to similarly situated
individuals and that there be a
reasonable alternative standard for
certain individuals.
The regulations also require certain
plan materials describing an
outcome-based wellness program to
disclose the availability of a
reasonable alternative standard, provide
contact information, and state that
recommendations from an individual's
personal physician will be accommodated.
That last piece was particularly
important here.
>> Is that because Goodyear actually did
have a smoking cessation alternative
program here?
>> That's right, it did. The summary plan
descriptions identified the Quit for
Life program and explained how an
employee could have the surcharge
removed after completing the nicotine
cessation program with reimbursement
retroactive to the surcharges imposed
during that plan year.
But the plaintiffs alleged that Goodyear
didn't include the physician
accommodation statement in the SPD
and also didn't include all the required
information in every communication
discussing the nicotine surcharge
program.
And they pointed, for example, to
employee flyers that allegedly omitted
information about reimbursement and the
physician alternative.
Their theory was that those omissions
took the program outside the statutory
and regulatory requirements and
therefore made the surcharge itself
unlawful.
>> That, of course, leads to a standing
issue or, as courts frame it, injury in
fact because Goodyear argued that it
really was just an informational injury
rather than a pocketbook injury.
Elizabeth, why did the court reject that
argument?
>> Well, the court here made a key
distinction. The plaintiffs weren't
simply alleging that they were denied
information. They alleged that because
Goodyear failed to provide the required
disclosures, it couldn't lawfully impose
the surcharge in the first place. Each
of the plaintiffs had actually paid the
surcharge. So the court found direct
monetary harm sufficient for
constitutional standing. It rejected the
argument that the plaintiffs also had to
allege that they would have acted
differently if they had received the
missing information or that they
personally would have qualified for the
for the physician alternative.
>> That's a very important point for
employers. Notice problem that might
initially sound technical which became
much more significant in the lens of the
court in ruling on the motion to
dismiss.
There's also a very interesting argument
involving the Supreme Court's Loper
Bright decision.
Adam, walk us through that.
>> Sure. Goodyear argued that the
requirements to disclose the physician
alternative appeared in the regulation
rather than the statute itself.
And following the Supreme Court's 2024
decision in Loper Bright, Goodyear
argued
the regulation shouldn't receive the
type of agency deference that existed
previously under Chevron.
But the court wasn't persuaded. Judge
Boyko noted that Congress had authorized
the relevant federal agencies to
promulgate regulations necessary or
appropriate
to carry out ERISA.
And he concluded that the regulation
didn't conflict with the statute, but
instead permissibly filled in and
clarified the details of the statutory
notice requirements.
So the court held that the requirement
to disclose that position that physician
recommendations will be accommodated
remained valid even after Loper Bright.
And because the plaintiff plausibly
alleged that Goodyear's materials didn't
satisfy that requirement, the court
refused to dismiss their first claim.
>> But as I read the opinion, Goodyear was
partly victorious. What happened to the
fiduciary duty claim that was the
subject of the motion to dismiss?
>> The plaintiffs argued that Goodyear
breached its fiduciary duties by
collecting the surcharges and using
those funds to reduce its own financial
obligations to the plans.
They also alleged that this amounted to
improper self-dealing or a prohibited
transaction. The court dismissed those
theories.
The important distinction was between an
employer acting as an ERISA fiduciary
and an employer performing what we call
a settler function. The court relied on
authority holding that establishing,
funding, amending, and terminating a
plan are settler functions. And it
concluded that collection of this type
of surcharge was a feature of plan
design that did not implicate fiduciary
duties.
>> But there was also a second problem with
the fiduciary claims, wasn't there?
>> There was. The plaintiffs had
implausibly alleged that Goodyear's use
of the surcharge money actually caused
the plans themselves to suffer a loss.
The court noted that the plaintiffs
didn't identify a plan provision
requiring [clears throat] Goodyear to
contribute the surcharge amounts on top
of its own contributions, nor did they
allege facts showing that the plans were
underfunded or unable to pay employee
benefit claims because of what Goodyear
did. So although the challenge to the
legality of the surcharge survived, the
broader attempt to turn the collection
and use of those funds into fiduciary
duty and prohibited transaction claims
did not.
>> Let's rise up now at 100 thousand foot
level and talk about the practical
implications of this ruling
because I think this decision is
especially important for employers.
Adam, if you're advising a company that
has a tobacco or nicotine wellness
program, what do you think is the
central takeaway?
>> Employers should start by thinking about
communications. They shouldn't assume
that simply offering a smoking cessation
program resolves the issue.
What this decision shows is why
companies also need to examine the
materials that describe the program and
the surcharge. The regulation discussed
by the court
requires specified disclosures in plan
materials describing the terms of an
outcome-based wellness program, and that
includes notice of the reasonable
alternative standard, contact
information, and a statement that
recommendations from an individual's
personal position will be accommodated.
So employers should look at the SPD, but
they should also identify other
materials that describe the terms of the
program.
>> Elizabeth, I know you defend ERISA class
actions on a nationwide basis. What's
your take on the ruling and and would
you be advising employers in light of
it?
>> I would add that consistency is
important. One lesson from this case is
that an employer can have an alternative
program available and still face
litigation over whether it properly
communicated that alternative. And the
potential exposure can become
significant because these surcharges
recur month after month.
The complaint alleged, for example, that
Goodyear associates and beneficiary
spouses paid more than 17 million in

videos.full_text: Hello everyone and thank you for joining us for the next episode of the class action weekly wire. I'm Jerry Maman, a partner at Dwayne Morris and welcoming my colleagues today, Adam Brown and Elizabeth Underwood. Thank you both for being on the podcast. >> Good to be here, Jerry. >> Thanks for having me, Jerry. >> Today we're going to discuss a recent ruling under ERISA that should catch the attention of employers that use nicotine or tobacco surcharges as part of their employee health plans. The case is Kills versus Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company from the Northern District of Ohio. On October 8, Judge Christopher Boyko granted in part and denied in part Goodyear's motion to dismiss a proposed class action that challenged the nicotine surcharge program. The court allowed plaintiff's central claim challenging the legality of the surcharge to proceed while dismissing their ERISA-based fiduciary duty claims. Adam, let's start with the basics. What was Goodyear's program and what were these employees challenging? >> Well, Goodyear employees who wanted health coverage were required to declare during annual enrollment whether they used nicotine products and employees who identified themselves as nicotine users paid an additional $100 per month through 2025. Uh beginning in 2026, that increased to $150 a month or $1,800 a year. Uh the plaintiffs are five former Goodyear employees who paid that surcharge and they alleged that Goodyear's program violated ERISA because its employee-facing materials didn't provide all the required information about alternatives that employees could use to avoid the surcharge. >> I guess the important point here is that ERISA doesn't simply prohibit every difference in premiums associated with nicotine use. Elizabeth, can you explain the target of the plaintiffs here and the wellness program and how fit into the lawsuit. >> Sure, Jerry. The statutory framework permits different premiums associated with participation and qualifying health promotion and disease prevention programs. For this type of health contingent wellness program, however, there are specific requirements, including that the full reward be available to similarly situated individuals and that there be a reasonable alternative standard for certain individuals. The regulations also require certain plan materials describing an outcome-based wellness program to disclose the availability of a reasonable alternative standard, provide contact information, and state that recommendations from an individual's personal physician will be accommodated. That last piece was particularly important here. >> Is that because Goodyear actually did have a smoking cessation alternative program here? >> That's right, it did. The summary plan descriptions identified the Quit for Life program and explained how an employee could have the surcharge removed after completing the nicotine cessation program with reimbursement retroactive to the surcharges imposed during that plan year. But the plaintiffs alleged that Goodyear didn't include the physician accommodation statement in the SPD and also didn't include all the required information in every communication discussing the nicotine surcharge program. And they pointed, for example, to employee flyers that allegedly omitted information about reimbursement and the physician alternative. Their theory was that those omissions took the program outside the statutory and regulatory requirements and therefore made the surcharge itself unlawful. >> That, of course, leads to a standing issue or, as courts frame it, injury in fact because Goodyear argued that it really was just an informational injury rather than a pocketbook injury. Elizabeth, why did the court reject that argument? >> Well, the court here made a key distinction. The plaintiffs weren't simply alleging that they were denied information. They alleged that because Goodyear failed to provide the required disclosures, it couldn't lawfully impose the surcharge in the first place. Each of the plaintiffs had actually paid the surcharge. So the court found direct monetary harm sufficient for constitutional standing. It rejected the argument that the plaintiffs also had to allege that they would have acted differently if they had received the missing information or that they personally would have qualified for the for the physician alternative. >> That's a very important point for employers. Notice problem that might initially sound technical which became much more significant in the lens of the court in ruling on the motion to dismiss. There's also a very interesting argument involving the Supreme Court's Loper Bright decision. Adam, walk us through that. >> Sure. Goodyear argued that the requirements to disclose the physician alternative appeared in the regulation rather than the statute itself. And following the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright, Goodyear argued the regulation shouldn't receive the type of agency deference that existed previously under Chevron. But the court wasn't persuaded. Judge Boyko noted that Congress had authorized the relevant federal agencies to promulgate regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out ERISA. And he concluded that the regulation didn't conflict with the statute, but instead permissibly filled in and clarified the details of the statutory notice requirements. So the court held that the requirement to disclose that position that physician recommendations will be accommodated remained valid even after Loper Bright. And because the plaintiff plausibly alleged that Goodyear's materials didn't satisfy that requirement, the court refused to dismiss their first claim. >> But as I read the opinion, Goodyear was partly victorious. What happened to the fiduciary duty claim that was the subject of the motion to dismiss? >> The plaintiffs argued that Goodyear breached its fiduciary duties by collecting the surcharges and using those funds to reduce its own financial obligations to the plans. They also alleged that this amounted to improper self-dealing or a prohibited transaction. The court dismissed those theories. The important distinction was between an employer acting as an ERISA fiduciary and an employer performing what we call a settler function. The court relied on authority holding that establishing, funding, amending, and terminating a plan are settler functions. And it concluded that collection of this type of surcharge was a feature of plan design that did not implicate fiduciary duties. >> But there was also a second problem with the fiduciary claims, wasn't there? >> There was. The plaintiffs had implausibly alleged that Goodyear's use of the surcharge money actually caused the plans themselves to suffer a loss. The court noted that the plaintiffs didn't identify a plan provision requiring [clears throat] Goodyear to contribute the surcharge amounts on top of its own contributions, nor did they allege facts showing that the plans were underfunded or unable to pay employee benefit claims because of what Goodyear did. So although the challenge to the legality of the surcharge survived, the broader attempt to turn the collection and use of those funds into fiduciary duty and prohibited transaction claims did not. >> Let's rise up now at 100 thousand foot level and talk about the practical implications of this ruling because I think this decision is especially important for employers. Adam, if you're advising a company that has a tobacco or nicotine wellness program, what do you think is the central takeaway? >> Employers should start by thinking about communications. They shouldn't assume that simply offering a smoking cessation program resolves the issue. What this decision shows is why companies also need to examine the materials that describe the program and the surcharge. The regulation discussed by the court requires specified disclosures in plan materials describing the terms of an outcome-based wellness program, and that includes notice of the reasonable alternative standard, contact information, and a statement that recommendations from an individual's personal position will be accommodated. So employers should look at the SPD, but they should also identify other materials that describe the terms of the program. >> Elizabeth, I know you defend ERISA class actions on a nationwide basis. What's your take on the ruling and and would you be advising employers in light of it? >> I would add that consistency is important. One lesson from this case is that an employer can have an alternative program available and still face litigation over whether it properly communicated that alternative. And the potential exposure can become significant because these surcharges recur month after month. The complaint alleged, for example, that Goodyear associates and beneficiary spouses paid more than 17 million in nicotine surcharges from 2020 through 2025. That's an allegation at this stage, not a damages finding, but it illustrates why what looks like a relatively modest monthly surcharge can create substantial potential exposure when applied across a workforce over several years. >> And of course, we should emphasize this was simply a motion to dismiss, so the court had to assume the truth and validity of all the plaintiff's allegations. It made no finding that Goodyear violated ERISA, but it does set the stage for the remainder of the case in terms of the plaintiff's plausibly stating a viable claim, but now they have to prove it. And also the judge kicking out, severing the fiduciary duty part of the case. So it doesn't say you can't have these programs. It simply says there are caveats to doing so. >> Exactly. Employers should be looking not just at how their wellness programs are structured, but also at how they're communicated to employees. That distinction was central to the claim the court allowed to move forward in this case. >> Well, thank you both for your thought leadership and for your significant advice and takeaways for employers that they take from this particular decision. So thanks so much for joining us on this week's podcast. >> Thank you, Jerry. >> Thank you, Jerry, and thanks to the listeners.

This STUFF Is Complicated. Episode : Stop Loss is a Reimbursement.

https://medicalcaptive.com/
https://www.linkedin.com/company/medical-captive-underwriters/?viewAsMember=true

Background & Introductions

Don McCulley:

  - Began career as an accountant at a bank, moving into credit training where he read many contracts, and then into the insurance industry.

  - Has 20 years in the insurance industry, primarily focused on group captives.

  - Started working with employer stop-loss group captives in 2010.

  - Founded Medical Captor Underwriters in 2015.

  - Met Don McCulley in 2010, forming a significant professional and personal partnership.

Andrew Kuykendall:

  - Classically trained musician with conservatories and audio engineering background, which qualified him to work for his dad's insurance agency.

  - Spent 25 years as a consultant and 4 years running a TPA (Third Party Administrator).

  - Known as "Captive Man" in recent years.

  - Shared personal anecdotes about attending concerts with Andrew, including seeing Bob Weir and Wolf Brothers, highlighting their shared experiences and the importance of relationships in business.

 Main Discussion: Understanding Stop-Loss and Group Captives

Universal Truths in Stop-Loss

Stop-loss is a reimbursement contract:

  - This is the most important concept, as everything else flows from it. Stop-loss exists to reimburse claims, not to pay them directly.

  - Claims must first be paid, measured, and processed appropriately before reimbursement occurs.

Claims Lag:

  - There is an inherent delay ("claims lag") in the system between when a medical service is rendered (e.g., an X-ray for a sprained ankle) and when the claim is filed, adjudicated, and paid.

  - This lag can range from 30-45 days to several months, depending on the complexity of the claims.

Nature of Stop-Loss Contracts:

  - Stop-loss filings are actually property and casualty filings, not accident and health filings, and they come from property and casualty carriers.

  - This distinction is important for understanding coverage and regulatory requirements, and historically, 9 out of 10 Errors & Omissions (E&O) claims in the space came from stop-loss.

 Key Takeaways

1. **Read Your Contracts**: Consultants must thoroughly understand contract terms to protect their clients and understand what is going on within those terms.

2. **Read Your Reports**: Stay informed about when a claim is filed, when it has been filed, and understand the steps needed to get reimbursement for clients.

3. **Know Your People**: Build strong relationships, have confidence in those you work with, maintain great communication, and set realistic expectations.

-Final Thoughts:

  - The insurance process is complicated but manageable with experience and preparation, and it can even be fun.

  - Relationships often evolve from vendor-client to genuine friendships, reflecting the collaborative and relational nature of the industry.

metadata.title: Self-Funding’s Safety Net: Stop-Loss Explained
metadata.author: Roundstone Insurance
metadata.shortDescription: For many employers, the biggest barrier to self-funding is fear of the unknown, especially when it comes to catastrophic claims and financial risk. In this episode, Mike sits down with Lauren Gliha, Partner Solutions Manager at Roundstone, to unpack the truth behind those fears.

metadata.title: Video Series #9   Stop Loss - Who Pays the Million-Dollar Claim
metadata.author: The Benefits Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Stop-Loss Insurance: Your Employer’s Safety Net (and Why It Matters to You)

Ever wonder how employers protect themselves from unexpectedly large medical claims? That’s where stop-loss insurance comes in!

In this episode of our Benefits Education Series, we break down how stop-loss insurance works, how it protects employers from catastrophic medical expenses, and why that financial protection matters to employees, too.

Because understanding what happens behind the scenes of your health plan helps you better understand the benefits you rely on.

segments.text: Welcome back to our video series. I have
a question for you. Who do you think
pays that million dollar claim that hits
your employer's health plan? Do you get
a bill for it? No. It's stop loss. Your
stop loss carrier is probably the most
misunderstood or best hidden parts of
your health plan. You don't submit a
claim to it personally. You don't even
know who they are typically, but they
are the financial stability or the guard
rail that allows your employer to offer
a level funded or even a self-funded
plan.
Stop loss carriers take premium dollars
from the employer to back up the claims
account. They are the added layer of
risk protection.
For example, in our previous videos, we
explained how certain amount of premium
dollars goes into a claims fund or even
in the self-funded plan, your employer
may fund that claims account.
But once that claims account is drained
or experiences a big claim, who backs it
up? The stop loss carrier does. So if a
large claim comes through that claims
account, rather than draining it, think
of the stop loss carrier as the backup
for the financial stability to that
claims account. So here's our claims
account. We're paying the claims and
then a large claim comes through. Stop
loss will advance money to that claims
account. So there's two parts of the
stop loss payment. There's a lot more,
but we're going to stick with specific
and aggregate protection. Specific
deductible is like a deductible that you
have on your medical plan. Let's say you
have a $3,000 deductible plan. You are
assuming the first $3,000 of medical
risk. In that same way, a specific
deductible of $50,000 would protect the
claims account from any large claim over
50,000. So if you had a million dollar
claim, it doesn't wipe out our claims
account. The most that could be taken
out of that claims account is 50,000,
then the stop loss carrier would advance
the rest. In the same way, aggregate
protection protects the claims account
against large claimants across the whole
group. So you might say there's a
million dollars worth of aggregate
protection and total claims 1.2 million
for the group, then the stop loss
carrier would advance $200,000 to the
claims account effectively. So think of
stop losses that financial protection
that allows the smaller employer to
offer a level funded or even a
self-funded plan. It stabilizes the risk
and protects the claims account against
unexpected large claims. It's a policy

you remember from our previous video,
the pieces that make up your plan
design, you can check out other videos
if you didn't see it. I would suggest
that stop loss is one of the most
important because it provides the
financial stability and is actually the
risk management piece that keeps your
plan afloat and protects it against
large claimants. We'll see you again
next time. Thanks for joining.

metadata.author: Underwrite University

Stop Loss Reinsurance Introductory Course | Learn the Basics of Stop Loss Reinsurance in Simple Terms
Welcome to the "Stop Loss Reinsurance Introductory Course," where you'll learn the essential concepts and principles behind stop loss reinsurance. This course is designed for beginners, insurance professionals, and students who are new to reinsurance. It covers the fundamentals of stop loss reinsurance, its structure, benefits, and how it protects insurers from catastrophic losses. By the end of this course, you will have a strong understanding of how stop loss reinsurance works, its importance in risk management, and its role in the insurance and reinsurance industry. This video is perfect for anyone interested in gaining insight into stop loss reinsurance and enhancing their knowledge of reinsurance structures.

Learn how stop loss reinsurance can help insurers manage risk and protect against large losses by setting predefined limits. We will also discuss key topics such as aggregate stop loss, excess of loss, and proportional vs. non-proportional reinsurance. This course provides easy-to-understand examples to help clarify complex concepts, making it ideal for those looking to improve their understanding of reinsurance contracts and risk mitigation.

Make sure to subscribe to our channel for more in-depth courses and tutorials on reinsurance, risk management, and insurance topics. Share this course with your colleagues and friends to help them get a comprehensive introduction to stop loss reinsurance.

metadata.title: Can I Refuse My Workers Comp Audit?
metadata.author: Insurance Brokers of Arizona
metadata.shortDescription:
You received a notice from your insurance carrier that its time for your workers comp audit. You begin to panic a little and even consider not doing it. Ignoring the audit request can end up hurting you in the long run as it can potentially end up costing you more in premium and even make you ineligible for coverage with some work comp companies. 
Audits are designed to ensure that you didn't over-pay or under-pay your work comp premium for the prior policy term. The insurance company will look at your total annual payroll for each particular job classification. So if you're payroll was higher than what you anticipated, the audit would result in additional premium owed. Conversely, if your payroll was less than what you provided, you would most likely end up receiving a credit or refund from the insurance company. 
Working with an agent that can assist you during the audit process can be beneficial. Click the links below to get in touch with one of our agents!

metadata.title: Workers Comp Insurance Audit: What Actually Moves Your Premium
metadata.author: Nia Brooks
metadata.shortDescription:
A workers comp insurance audit is not a sign anybody suspects you. It is a scheduled term of your policy — and this is what actually moves the number when it happens.

The rulebook has a bookkeeper in it. It calls her Jane Doe. Her employer reported her under the clerical office code, the auditor found out she cleans the office, and her entire payroll moved. Nobody committed fraud. Nobody lied. In this episode Banks walks through exactly why, straight out of the manuals and statutes that decide it.

What you will know by the end:
• Why a form arrives after your policy year ends asking what you ACTUALLY paid people — and why the number on your policy in January was your own forecast, not a price somebody quoted you
• What a classification code really is (it is not a job title — the business gets the code), the exception list that contractors are standing in the middle of, and the Interchange of Labor rule that decides whether one person can be split across two codes
• Why a subcontractor who is definitely a subcontractor can still land on your payroll for rating — and why that is a completely different question from who pays an injured worker
• The one rule in here that pays you BACK: overtime extra pay is excluded from the payroll premium is calculated on, if your books show it separately

Correction from the last episode, made on air: I said the insurer sends somebody to look at your books. For a policy the size most small businesses have, they usually do not — it arrives as a form you fill in yourself.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 The bookkeeper in the rulebook
0:59 What you will know
1:26 The number on your policy was your own forecast
3:35 A classification code is not a job title
6:01 The Fine Print: Interchange of Labor
7:40 The ledger that pays you back: overtime
9:06 Your state: four things that vary
11:36 The subcontractor's certificate
14:26 Reality check, and when it is the professional's turn
15:34 Three things, with what they cost
16:37 A column in a ledger

📚 PRIMARY SOURCES
• North Carolina Rate Bureau — NC Basic Manual for Workers Compensation and Employers Liability, Rule 1 (rev. 7/1/2026) and Rule 2 (rev. 8/1/2023; Rule 2-H rev. 1/1/2024)
  https://www.ncrb.org/digitallibrary/basicmanual/Rule_2_-_Premium_and_Payroll.htm
• N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-19 — subcontractor liability and the certificate
  https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/PDF/ByChapter/Chapter_97.pdf
• North Carolina Industrial Commission — insurance requirements
  https://www.ic.nc.gov/wcinsrqmt.html
• Washington State Dept. of Labor & Industries — 2026 Rates per Hour Worked
  https://lni.wa.gov/insurance/_docs/2026RatesBusTypeClassCode.pdf
• Ohio Administrative Code 4123-17-14 (eff. 7/1/2024)
  https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-4123-17-14
• Texas Department of Insurance — workers' compensation for employers
  https://www.tdi.texas.gov/wc/employer/index.html
• Indiana Compensation Rating Bureau — independent bureaus and NCCI
  https://www.icrb.net/references/independent-bureaus-ncci-and-wcio/
• NCCI Insights — COVID-19, Premium Audits, and EBNR (Sept 2020)

Washington rates shown are 2026 COMPOSITE BASE rates per hour worked — before your own experience factor, and they include the portion withheld from the worker's paycheck. Read them as a comparison between codes, never as your bill.

▶ WATCH NEXT
Workers' Comp for Small Business — the threshold and the penalty: https://youtu.be/Ij4dF9QFRDU
1099 vs W-2 — the three tests that decide it: https://youtu.be/ekMWXi18-Yo
Insurance & Risk playlist: https://www.youtube.com/@The-Main-Street-MBA/playlists

⚠️ Education only. This is a workshop, not a law office — nothing here is legal, tax or insurance advice for your business. Rules vary by state and by rating bureau, and the figures quoted are North Carolina's and Washington's published values on the dates shown. When it is time to hire a professional, hire one: your broker or your state's rating bureau can give you your own current numbers.

metadata.title: Healthcare Direct Contracting Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Employers Can Enter Into Direct Contracts with Doctors, Hospitals and Other Healthcare Facilities for Medical Services for MemberS of Their Employee Health Plan.

Reimbursement Typically Takes the Form of a Bundled Payment or a Lower Rate of Fee-for-Service.

Employers with Greater Than 500 Employees Tend To Engage in Direct Contracting.  Mid-Market Employers with a High Concentration of Employees in One Geographic Area Tend to Engage in Direct Contracting as Well.

The Employer Frequently Uses an Independent TPA to Process the Claims for the Direct Contract.

Also, the Employer Health Plan Changes the 'Benefit Level' Such that Care at the Direct Contract Facility is Often at $0 Out-of-Pocket Cost for the Member.

Engaging the Plan Members with Navigation Services is Helpful to Make the Experience Integrated with the Overall Health Plan Offerings.

AHealthcareZ is 200+ Healthcare Finance Educational Videos.

💥 BOOK: Check out Dr. Bricker’s Book 16 Lessons in the Business of Healing here: https://www.ahealthcarez.com/healthcare-money-campfire-stories-book

AHealthcareZ Viewers Include: Employee Benefits Professionals, HR, CFOs, Insurance Brokers, Benefits Consultants, Doctors and Nurses in Leadership Roles, Hospital and Health System Administrators, Health Insurance Carrier and PBM Professionals, Pharma and Med Device Professionals, Academic Professors and Students in Healthcare Administration and Public Health.

90,000+ Views Per Month Across All Platforms.

Visit AHealthcareZ.com to Subscribe to the Healthcare Finance Video Newsletter.

metadata.title: Direct Contracting between Employers and Healthcare Providers: HSC's Two-Minute Warning
metadata.author: Healthcare Solutions Connection
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know that some innovative employers are cutting out the middle-man to contract directly with providers for the care of their employees?  It’s true. Large companies such as Boeing and Intel are leaving the insurance companies out of the picture altogether, and going directly to their local health systems and physician groups to negotiate contracts for employees’ healthcare. Sound appealing? Let me tell you a little bit about how it’s going from the perspective of one major employer.

About two years ago, the Boeing Company, based in Washington State with over 160,000 employees in the U.S., decided to try out a new model of care in Puget Sound, their home base. They approached two local Accountable Care Organizations, or ACOs, to develop a “preferred partnership” health plan option for their employees in the area. Employees could choose whether to join this preferred partnership option, or whether to stick with Boeing’s standard self-funded plan. Those who chose the preferred partnership plan received free direct primary care visits, free generic drugs, lower premiums, and higher contributions by Boeing to a Health Savings Account. 

Boeing tried this experiment because it believes that improving patient experience, improving quality, and increasing efficiency – tenets of the Triple Aim – are important to a healthy and productive workforce. 

So, how is this new approach going so far? Well, in the first year, 30% of employees chose the preferred partnership ACO option, with a satisfaction rating of 8.5 out of 10. Boeing has now expanded this approach to its employees in St. Louis and Charleston as well, with similar results. Cutting out the middleman payer has allowed Boeing to develop closer relationships directly with their providers, who now have a seat right at the table in negotiating their own contracts.

Look for more employers around the nation to move towards direct contracting with providers, and more providers looking to position themselves as good partners for these employers.
