metadata.title: Outfox Health - 3x3x3 Challenge With Beth Ann Lopez
metadata.author: BenefitsAlly | Home of the 3x3x3 Challenge
metadata.shortDescription:
Outfox Health uses AI to turn complex healthcare benefits into simple, real-time guidance, helping employees make better choices without adding vendors, changing networks, or long launch times.

Transcript:

What is Outfox Health?

So let's start with a situation we've all seen. An employee needs an MRI for back pain. Their 120-page benefits booklet says that it's covered at 80%, but what does that actually mean? At one hospital, the MRI costs $3,200. Three miles away, it's $680, one-fifth of the price. Yet the employee would never know the difference until the bill arrives. This complexity isn't just frustrating, it's expensive. Only 7% of Americans understand basic health insurance terms, and poor healthcare navigation leads to hundreds of billions of dollars in preventable losses every year, costing employers an average of $970 per employee. Outfox Health changes that. Our AI assistant turns complex healthcare benefits into simple real-time guidance, helping employees make better decisions about their care and costs.

How is Outfox Health different?

Outfox is a fully customizable operating system for healthcare navigation. Unlike traditional navigators, like Included Health or Accolade, we don't rely on large human advocate teams. Outfox uses AI to deliver real-time 24/7 support in multiple languages, tied directly to your existing benefits without adding new vendors or changing networks. And unlike general AI chatbot for employee benefits companies, our system is designed specifically for healthcare navigation, not generic benefits. We combine national price transparency data, provider quality metrics, and custom steerage algorithms. It also has the healthcare-specific safety guardrails in place. Employers can prioritize direct contracts, centers of excellence, or preferred providers and fine-tune navigation to their specific cost and quality goals.

Who is a good fit for Outfox Health?

Outfox is a strong fit for brokers working with self-funded employers who want better healthcare navigation without adding new complexity. We're especially valuable for employers with diverse and multilingual workforces, busy HR teams looking to reduce benefits questions, or clients that want to steer employees towards specific networks or contracts. Unlike most vendors that take months to implement, Outfox goes live in just 30 days with no complex integrations required. Brokers using Outfox will have faster launches, measurable cost savings, and a stronger client satisfaction, helping you grow and retain your book of business. 

Record Your 3x3x3 Challenge - https://links.benefitsally.com/3x3x3

metadata.title: How to Read Healthcare Reports: Analyze Employer Claims Data
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
This Video Describes a Way to Read an Employer Claims Cost Report to Find Actionable Information and to NOT Get Distracted by Less Important Data.

1)  Don't Look at the Report First... Rather Start with What Questions You Would Like to Answer and Then Find Those Answers Within the Report.

2) Review the High-Cost Claimants by Quarter or by Year.  Not Claims... Claimants.  Claimants with Greater Than $100K in Spend are Likely Too Embroiled in the Healthcare System and Their Doctors to be Intervenable, But Claimants with $20K - $100K in Spend Offer a Better Opportunity for Intervention.

3) For Each High-Cost Claimant (I.e. Each Individual Person), Review the Paid Amount by Diagnosis Code and Procedure Code Because the Spend by Diagnosis and Procedure Will Tell the Clinical Story of What is Going on with That Person.

4) Review the Paid Amount and Number of Claims by Facility (i.e. Hospital, Surgery Center, etc.) to Identify Facilities that Have Very High Spend with only a Very FEW Claims (e.g. Out-of-Network Dialysis Facility).

Reviewing Healthcare Claims Reports in This Manner Allows an Employer Group to Identify What Types of Plan Design Changes, Network Changes or Targeted Program Changes Will Be Helpful to Reduce Waste in the Future.

AHealthcareZ is 200+ Healthcare Finance Educational Videos.

metadata.title: Level-Funded Health Plans Explained Simply for Christian Employers
metadata.author: Imago Dei Insurance Advisors
metadata.shortDescription:
Level-funded health plans can be confusing, but they are worth understanding.

In this video, David explains level-funded health insurance in plain language for Christian businesses, churches, and nonprofits. You will learn how level-funded plans differ from traditional fully insured plans, why some employers consider them, and what cautions leaders should understand before making a decision.

Topics covered:

- What a level-funded health plan is
- How level-funded plans differ from fully insured plans
- Why fixed monthly payments can help with budgeting
- How claims funding, administration, and stop-loss protection work
- Why level-funded plans are not right for every organization
- Questions Christian employers should ask before considering this strategy

Imago Dei Insurance Advisors helps Christian businesses, churches, and nonprofits care for their teams with flexible employee benefits, health insurance strategy, and HR advisory support.

Schedule a Clarity Call: https://imagodeinsuranceadvisors.com/

Download The Christian Employer's Benefits Stewardship Guide: https://imagodeinsuranceadvisors.com/

segments.text: Hey, this is David with the Mago Day
Insurance Advisors. Today I want to
explain what are levelfunded health
plans. If you are a Christian business
owner, executive pastor, nonprofit
leader, CFO, or operations leader, you
may have heard the term levelfunded but
not had anyone explain what it actually
means. And that is a problem because for
some organizations, levelfunded plans
can be an important part of the benefits
strategy conversation. They are not
right for everyone. They are not
automatically cheaper. They are not a
magic solution. But they are worth
understanding. Let's start with a
traditional fully insured plan. In a
fully insured plan, your organization
pays a premium to the insurance carrier.
The carrier takes on the claims risk. If
your employees have a high claims year,
the carrier is responsible for paying
those claims. If your employees have a
low claims year, you typically do not
share directly in that upside. You pay
the premium, the carrier manages the
risk, and your renewal is usually based
on a mix of your group's experience,
broader market factors, plan design,
carrier pricing, and other underwriting
considerations.
A level funded plan works differently.
With a level-funded plan, your
organization pays a fixed monthly
amount. That amount usually includes
three parts. First, estimated claims
funding. This is money set aside to help
pay the expected medical claims for your
group. Second, administrative costs.
These are the costs to run the plan.
Third, stop-loss protection. This is
protection designed to limit the
organization's exposure if claims are
higher than expected or if a large claim
occurs. So, why do employers look at
levelfunded plans? There are a few good
reasons. One, predictability. The
monthly payment is designed to be level,
which can help with budgeting. Two,
potential upside depending on the
contract. If claims come in lower than
expected, the employer may be eligible
to receive some surplus back. Three,
better visibility. Level funded plans
may provide more insight into claims
experience, which can help leaders
understand what is driving cost and what
strategies may help over time. Four,
flexibility.
For some groups, level funded options
may open plan designs or strategies that
are not available in the same way
through traditional fully insured plans.
But there are also important cautions. A
level funded plan is usually
underwritten. That means the carrier or
administrator is looking at the health
and risk profile of the group before
deciding whether to offer coverage and
at what price. It may not be the right
fit for every organization. If the group
has higher expected claims, traditional
fully insured coverage may be the better
or more stable route. If the
organization does not want any added
complexity, level funded may feel like
too much. And even when a level funded
plan looks attractive in year 1, leaders
still need to understand how the renewal
works. A low firstear rate is not
helpful if the strategy is not
sustainable. At a Mago Day, we do not
believe in pushing one product or one
funding strategy. The better question
is, what structure helps this specific
organization care for its people,
steward its resources, and sustain the
benefits program over time? For some
Christian businesses, churches, and
nonprofits, that may be a fully insured
plan. For others, a level-funded option
may be worth considering. And for
others, the right answer may involve a
different strategy altogether, such as
an IC,
direct primary care, ancillary benefits,
or another customized approach. Here are
five questions to ask before considering
a level funded plan. First, how many
employees are likely to enroll? Level
funded options tend to become more
relevant when there is enough enrollment
to evaluate the group meaningfully.
Second, how stable is the organization?
If you are growing, hiring, or trying to
build a more intentional benefit
strategy, the funding structure matters.
Third, how much predictability does
leadership need? A level monthly payment
can help with budgeting, but leaders
should still understand what happens at
renewal. Fourth, how important is claims
visibility?
Some leaders want more insight into what
is driving cost so they can make better
long-term decisions.
Fifth, what kind of adviser do you have?
Level funded plans need to be explained
clearly. The trade-offs matter. The
renewal mechanics matter. The stop-loss
protection matters. The contract details
matter. This is not a place for a rushed
spreadsheet and a vague recommendation.
For Christian employers, benefits are
both a stewardship decision and a care
decision. You are trying to use
resources wisely while caring for real
people and families. Level funded plans
can be one useful tool in that
conversation, but the tool should never
drive the strategy. The mission, the
people, the budget, and the long-term
plan should drive the strategy. If your
organization has 10 or more employees
and you want to understand whether level
funded health insurance should be part
of your benefits conversation, schedule
a clarity call. We will help you
understand the options in plain language
and decide what questions to ask

metadata.title: Fully Insured vs Level-Funded: Which Is Better Long-Term for Small Businesses?
metadata.author: American Trust Administrators | Level Funding
metadata.shortDescription:
How long do you plan to be in business — three weeks, one year, or decades?
Your time horizon determines which health plan structure actually makes sense: Fully Insured, Level-Funded with shared surplus, or Level-Funded with 100% surplus return.

In this video, Tom Stein (CEO of American Trust Administrators) explains how planning for the future changes the rational choice for small and mid-sized employers. If you want simple short-term coverage, fully insured may fit. But if you are building something for the long term, the 100% surplus model becomes one of the most powerful tools available to small businesses.

⭐ WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

• Why fully insured plans benefit companies with short time horizons
If you’re unsure you’ll be operating 12 months from now, fully insured may be the best choice.

• Why level-funding becomes financially superior after Year 1
Pre-funded claims and transparent reporting let employers keep what they don’t use.

• The farm analogy that makes level-funding simple
If you owned the field, wouldn’t you want to keep the extra crop?

• Why 100% surplus matters for employers planning 2+ years ahead
Shared-surplus models are the “sharecropper” option. ATA’s 100% surplus lets Main Street keep its own yield.

• How business owners should answer the key question: “How long will you be in business?”
Their time horizon determines whether they should pick fully insured, partial-surplus level funded, or 100% surplus level funded.

⭐ WHY 100% SURPLUS MATTERS

For employers building a long-term business, keeping every dollar of unused claims compounds year after year — creating reserves, lowering real costs, and reducing dependency on large carriers.

ATA is one of the only administrators offering true 100% surplus return for level-funded plans.

⭐ FOR BROKERS: MASTER LEVEL FUNDING (LFU)

If you want to confidently explain funding structures and help clients plan for the next 1–10 years, join Level Funded University (LFU) — the only training program built to make brokers experts in level funding.

Inside LFU you’ll learn:

How to explain long-term vs short-term plan structures

How surplus works and why it matters

How to position 100% surplus as a differentiator

How to win 5–100 life groups with clear client guidance

👉 Enroll in Level Funded University: https://thomas-stein.mykajabi.com/offers/4vEU34b2/checkout?preview=true


⭐ ABOUT ATA

American Trust Administrators (ATA) has served Main Street employers for over 50 years with transparency, U.S.-based service, and a mission to keep employer dollars local instead of flowing to Wall Street.

ATA provides:

100% surplus return

Transparent accounting

Level-funded & self-funded expertise

Simple, stable plan options for employers from 5–250 lives

⭐ SEO KEYWORDS

level funded vs fully insured, level funded health plan explained, 100 percent surplus, ATA level funded plans, long-term health plan strategy, small business health insurance, stop-loss explained, health plan time horizon, level-funded surplus return, employee benefits planning, Level Funded University, LFU broker training

⭐ HASHTAGS

#LevelFunded #FullyInsured #HealthInsurance #ATA #AmericanTrustAdministrators #BrokerTraining #LFU #LevelFundedUniversity #SurplusReturn #SmallBusinessBenefits #MainStreetUSA #EmployeeBenefits #HealthPlanSavings #LongTermPlanning #InsuranceBroker #ATAPlans

metadata.title: How to Prepare Your First Level Funded Case
metadata.author: American Trust Administrators | Level Funding
metadata.shortDescription:
Your first few level funded cases are probably going to feel overwhelming.

That’s normal.

In this video, Tom Stein from American Trust Administrators walks independent brokers through the core pieces of the level funded quoting process — including how to set expectations, gather underwriting information, and avoid the mistakes that create bad renewals later.

If you’re new to:

level funded health plans
self-funded benefits
stop loss
or small group underwriting

this video will help you understand how experienced brokers structure the process upfront.

Topics covered:

Why level funded quoting takes longer than fully insured
The underwriting documents brokers need upfront
How to request employee applications correctly
Why quarterly wage & tax reports matter
How to set expectations with employers early
The importance of honest underwriting
Why rushed cases create long-term problems
How clean submissions improve renewals and retention

One of the biggest mistakes new brokers make is trying to force level funding into a fully insured timeline.

Level funded plans reward:

preparation
transparency
underwriting discipline
and accurate information.

At American Trust Administrators, we believe better underwriting leads to better long-term outcomes for brokers, employers, and employees alike.

If you’re building your level funded practice and want practical conversations around:

underwriting
retention
stop loss
small group strategy
and Main Street health plans

subscribe for weekly broker-focused content.

metadata.title: Fully Insured vs Level-Funded: Which Is Better Long-Term for Small Businesses?
metadata.author: American Trust Administrators | Level Funding
metadata.shortDescription:
Most brokers — and nearly all small business owners — only understand one type of health plan structure. But the U.S. health insurance market really runs on three major funding models, each with massive differences in transparency, cost, risk, and long-term value.

fully insured vs level funded long term, small business health plan strategy, level funded long term savings, health insurance planning horizon

In this video, Tom Stein, CEO of American Trust Administrators (ATA), breaks down the three primary health plan structures used by small and mid-sized employers:

Fully Insured (the “easy button” with a black box)

Level-Funded (transparent, stable monthly billing, and surplus return)

Self-Funded with Stop-Loss (long-term value but higher financial sophistication)

If you’re a broker or employer trying to understand how health plans really work, this is the clearest comparison on YouTube.

⭐ WHAT YOU’LL LEARN
1. Fully Insured Plans

Why they feel simple — but hide all claims data

Why carriers keep the surplus

Why small employers default to fully insured even though it’s the least transparent option

Why only ~25 million Americans are still in this model

2. Level-Funded Plans

Why level funding has grown 800% in the last decade

How claims, admin, and stop-loss are actually structured

Why level-funded plans give employers reporting and ownership of their unused claims dollars

Why level-funding is ideal for groups from 5–250 employees

How level-funding builds reserves and keeps Main Street money local

Why ATA returns 100% of unused claims dollars

3. Self-Funded with Stop-Loss

How claims are paid as they occur (no pre-funding)

Why CFO sophistication determines readiness

Why cash flow planning matters (aggregate deductibles & cash calls)

Why groups typically shift here around 125+ lives

PLUS: Which structure is best for which employer?

Tom breaks down the trade-offs so brokers and owners can choose the right path — not the easy one.

⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS FOR SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS

If you don’t understand the difference between fully insured, level-funded, and self-funded, your company is likely overpaying for health insurance.

This video gives you:

Clear insight into how your plan actually works

What you’re paying for

Where your money goes

And how to protect your team without wasting capital

ATA has been serving Main Street for over 50 years with transparent, U.S.-based level-funded and self-funded plans.

⭐ FOR BROKERS: MASTER LEVEL FUNDING (LFU)

If you’re a broker who wants to confidently explain these three plan types — and stop losing cases to competitors who understand level-funding — join Level Funded University (LFU).

In LFU, you’ll learn:

How to pitch level-funded plans

How surplus really works

Key differences brokers misunderstand

How to guide small businesses through plan structures

How to win 5–100 life cases with ATA’s 100% surplus return

👉 Enroll in Level Funded University: [Insert Link]
👉 Download free broker resources: [Insert Link]

⭐ ABOUT ATA


⚠️ Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal, tax, or insurance advice. Viewers should consult directly with a licensed insurance professional or benefits advisor for up-to-date and personalized guidance.      American Trust Administrators (ATA) operates as an MGU/TPA administering level-funded and self-funded health plans on behalf of licensed carriers. All information in this content is for educational purposes only. Nothing here constitutes legal, financial, medical, actuarial, underwriting, or insurance advice.

Plan designs, underwriting decisions, rates, surplus availability, and renewal outcomes vary by carrier, stop-loss policy, network, state regulations, and the unique factors of each employer group. Surplus return is not guaranteed and applies only to qualifying plans as defined in each group’s governing agreements.

All coverage determinations, claims adjudication, and benefits administration are subject to the terms of the applicable plan document, stop-loss contract, carrier guidelines, and state and federal regulatory requirements. Examples, case studies, and illustrations may not reflect actual client results.

Brokers must be properly licensed in applicable states and remain responsible for compliance with all federal and state marketing, solicitation, disclosure, and consumer protection regulations. Always review the plan document, SBC, carrier instructions, and compliance guidance before presenting options to employers.

Why leaving a level-funded plan early is a contract disaster

metadata.title: Unlocking Savings with Level Funded Health Insurance | Purchasing Strategies for HR, CFOs, and CEOs
metadata.author: BeneSmart - A Modern Approach to Benefits
metadata.shortDescription:
𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝟑 𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐈 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐩 𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝:

📆 Book a call to learn how our Benefit Cost Containment Blueprint can help you roll back your costs: https://benesmartservices.com/strategy-call/
🎥 See all 9 Steps of our Benefit Cost Containment Blueprint: https://youtu.be/0Qg-d4-Ylew
📝 Download our free Mid-Year Health Plan Review Checklist: https://adobe.ly/4mvZKr6

In this informative video, we explore how level funded health insurance can revolutionize your organization's approach to employee benefits. Designed specifically for HR professionals, CFOs, and CEOs, this video dives deep into innovative purchasing strategies that can significantly lower costs while maintaining comprehensive health coverage for your team.


Key Points Covered in the Video:

Introduction to Level Funded Health Insurance:
Understand the basics of level funded plans and how they differ from traditional insurance models.
Discover how these plans can provide cost predictability and potential savings.

Advantages of Level Funded Plans:
Learn about the financial benefits, including how level funded plans can help manage cash flow and reduce overall healthcare expenses.
Explore real-world examples of companies that have successfully implemented level funded insurance and realized substantial savings.

Strategic Implementation:
Gain insights into the step-by-step process of transitioning to a level funded health plan.
Tips on communicating the changes to employees and ensuring a smooth transition.

Purchasing Strategies for Lowering Costs:
Effective negotiation techniques with insurance providers to secure the best rates.
Innovative strategies to optimize the benefits package without compromising on quality.

Expert Insights and Recommendations:
Practical advice for HR, CFOs, and CEOs on making informed decisions for their organizations.
Whether you are aiming to reduce expenses, improve cash flow, or simply offer better health benefits to your employees, this video provides valuable insights and actionable strategies to help you achieve your goals.


Ready to take control of your health insurance costs? Watch the full video now and start implementing these proven strategies today!

The reference-based pricing contracts are written as a level funded or a self-funded contract, which actually is as good for the employer because if there's any unused claim funds those actually get refunded to the employer. So when you saw the savings for the reference-based pricing product, there could be additional savings on top that depending on what the claims are for that year. So utilization will matter. When you keep the claims low, the odds of the employer getting money back are pretty good. So keep that in mind, the plans are medically underwritten. So there are medical questions ask of the employees and the patients can be subject to balance billing. So let's run over what the balanced billing, what you need to know about balanced billing. Now, some carriers offer a billing assistance or balance billing assistance. So if an employee gets a bill in the mail, all they have to do is send it over to the agent and forwarded it up to the insurance company either and the insurance company will take that and start a negotiation process with the doctor or hospital or the provider and start seeing if they can negotiate that bill down to the Medicare benchmark rate that they're paying. So they do claims auditing as well. They can also help with scheduling assistance. So if you have a scheduled surgery and you need to go see a doctor for a knee replacement, they can tell you who's competitive in that market. So they do have scheduling assistance, provider location services. They can help you find doctors too, if you need one, just all you have to do is just call the number on the card and say, "Hey, I need help finding a doctor." And they can help you find somebody in your area. A lot of carriers offer legal services for billing resolutions. So when you get a bill in the mail the first thing you need to do is send it over to the insurance companies so they can negotiate the claim. What lot of these billing companies have done in the past is they would actually ding your credit for it right away. They would automatically send it to collections. Some of our the insurance companies we work with, what they do is they actually send a letter out to the provider or the billing service and say, "Hey, don't report this to our client. "We're going through a claims negotiation right now. "And so hold off on that." So they do send letters out for them. So keep in mind, education's important. Make sure that the employees know how to operate the plan. If you need help, of course, you can always call us here at the General Agency. And if you liked this video, remember to hit the like and subscribe button. And that being said, my name is Howard Deihl. I'm the owner of the General Agency and have a great day.

Most employers have never heard the truth about hospital billing — and most brokers don’t know how to explain it.
Today, Tom Stein breaks down exactly how Charge Masters, PPO Discounts, and Reference-Based Pricing (RBP) really work inside the American health system… and why understanding fair pricing is the key to protecting Main Street employers.

Whether you're a health insurance broker, GA, or business owner, this is the clearest explanation you’ll hear on:

🔍 CHARGE MASTERS: The Hidden “Menu Price” System

Why hospitals publish inflated “retail” prices

How a $96,000 bill becomes a $10,000 cash-pay offer overnight

Why Charge Masters distort the perceived value of care

How opacity benefits carriers and large systems — not employers

🔍 PPO DISCOUNTS: The Myth Behind the “Savings”

Why “40% off” is often meaningless

The difference between discounts and real costs

How PPO networks use inflated starting numbers to appear valuable

Why many brokers unintentionally reinforce the problem

🔍 RBP (REFERENCE-BASED PRICING): The Transparency Model

How RBP ties payment to actual reimbursement data

Why anchoring to Medicare + margin is more predictable and fair

How RBP protects small businesses from subsidizing government shortfalls

What RBP actually pays — and why hospitals still argue about fairness

🔍 THE MORAL QUESTION: What Is “Fair” in Healthcare?

Tom explains why pricing is not just a math issue — it’s a values issue:

Should small businesses pay 2–5× what the largest payer pays?

Why opacity disproportionately hurts honest, working-class families

How “discounts” hide predatory billing behavior

Why transparency is the foundation of truly fair pricing

🎙 How Surprise Billing Impacts Reference-Based Pricing 🎙
"With surprise billing reference-based pricing plans are freaked out, a lot of people are freaked out. They are thinking, 'is it the end of reference-based pricing?'. I look at it the opposite way, I think it is a huge opportunity..." 

In this excerpt of Episode 4, Vincent Lewis and Adam Russo of The Phia Group, LLC discuss the opportunity for reference-based pricing in the future, how Medicare pricing is not taken into account when finding a fair and reasonable price, and the problem with transparency in healthcare.  

➡️ Full Episode: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJgKtV47uQM

Partners saves millions by balancing the needs of employer groups with the needs of plan members. Our team is made up of nurses, underwriting experts and specialty vendors who collaborate to evaluate claims, find savings and give members the best possible care.

Small business owners in California need to know about the experience modification factors (EMOD) for Worker’s Compensation insurance. California is different from many other states in managing Workers’ Compensation, specifically because of the WCIRB. If your business qualifies for an experience rating, you must use it. Understanding this rating system is integral for your small business - our video also explains the effects of risk management, safety, compliance, and loss control on your EMOD.

The calculations used to determine your rate based on experience rating differ based on industry and your specific business operations. There is a lot of information to understand concerning how your business will be rated and how your premiums will be calculated using experience rating.

videos.full_text: workers compensation policies are experience rated policies now what that means is that your rates are going to be determined in part by the loss experience that your company has over time and the vehicle for accomplishing this is called your experience modification factor or your mod for short the calculation of your mod is done each year based on prior loss experience a mod of 1.0 has no effect on your final premium while a mod of 0.8 would provide you with a 20 premium reduction and a mod of 1.2 means that you have a 20 surcharge for past loss experience as you can imagine those who let their losses spiral out of control end up paying huge sums over time as a penalty after many years of no changes to the experience modification formula the ncci has announced a phase in change for the mod formula the formula itself is pretty complicated so i won't get into the details but it will help you to know that the formula has basically two components a loss frequency component and a loss severity component for many years every loss was capped at five thousand dollars on the frequency side of the equation the severity side of the equation includes the entire loss with no limit now under the old formula you would not be penalized anymore for a hundred thousand dollar loss than you would for a five thousand dollar loss beginning in 2012 that formula is changing to increase the cap gradients each year until the year 2015 when that cap will have risen to 17 000. after that the cap will be indexed for inflation so what does all this mean for you and your mod well first of all you have even more incentive to get your workers back to work sooner as they are now more and more of that loss is going to impact on the frequency side of the equation this makes it even more important that you carefully consider your workers compensation companies approach to claims now i prefer the dedicated work comp companies for my clients and this is because they are much more aggressive about getting injured workers back to work soon to keep the costs lower most of the dedicated comp companies have their own staff of nurses and case caseworkers to accomplish this and in the end what you pay for workers compensation insurance today may not be as important as what today's insurance company will cost you down the road if they don't actively manage your claims in an efficient manner at kleiner insurance group we work hard to help all of our clients become informed insurance consumers if we can help you with your workers compensation insurance needs please give us a call toll free at the number shown on the screen we look forward to putting our experience to work for you to save you big money on your workers compensation insurance now and in the future you

metadata.title: Fully Insured vs. Self-Funded vs. Level-Funded Explained
metadata.author: Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck
metadata.shortDescription:
Who actually pays your health insurance claims, your employer or the insurance company?

Most employees never think about how their health plan is funded. But for small business owners, understanding the difference between fully insured, self-funded, and level-funded health plans can make a big difference in how they approach employee benefits.

In Episode 8 of Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck, Brian Calvert breaks down the three main ways employers fund health insurance and explains how each structure works.

In this episode, we cover:

Fully insured plans: Why employers choose predictable monthly premiums.

Self-funded plans: How employers take on more financial risk in exchange for greater control and potential savings.

Level-funded plans: How fixed monthly payments, stop-loss protection, and potential year-end refunds work together.

What it means for employees: How funding decisions can affect coverage and benefits.

What small business owners should consider: How to approach choosing the right funding structure.

Whether you're a business owner reviewing employee benefits or an employee trying to understand your coverage, this episode will help make a complicated subject a little clearer.

Because health insurance doesn't have to suck. You just need to understand how it works.

Subscribe for more straightforward conversations about health insurance, and check out our companion newsletter, Clarity Notes.

#HealthInsurance #EmployeeBenefits #SmallBusinessHealthInsurance #SelfFundedInsurance #LevelFundedInsuranc

metadata.title: Is Level Funding Right for Your Company
metadata.author: JS Benefits Group

Is Level Funding Right for Your Company? | Jennifer Schaefer | JS Benefits Group

Is a level-funded health plan right for your company?

In this video, Jennifer Schaefer, MBA, ChFC, CLU, RHU, REBC, SHRM-SCP, Founder & CEO of JS Benefits Group, explains how level-funded health insurance works and what employers should consider before making a change.

A level-funded health plan can be an alternative to traditional fully insured group health insurance. Whether it makes sense depends on factors including company size, employee demographics, claims experience, plan design, healthcare costs, and risk tolerance.

What Is a Level-Funded Health Plan?

A level-funded health plan combines features of fully insured and self-funded health insurance. Employers generally pay a predictable monthly amount that can include expected claims, administrative costs, and stop-loss insurance. The exact structure varies by carrier and plan.

Is Level Funding Right for Every Company?

No. Employers should evaluate their current premiums, claims experience, workforce, plan design, financial goals, and risk tolerance before switching.

What Are the Potential Advantages?

Potential advantages may include:

• More predictable budgeting
• Greater visibility into healthcare spending
• Stop-loss protection
• Greater flexibility in plan design
• Potential opportunities for healthcare cost savings

Savings are not guaranteed and vary by employer and plan.

How Is Level Funding Different From Fully Insured Insurance?

With traditional fully insured coverage, the employer pays a premium and the insurance carrier assumes the insurance risk.

With level funding, the employer's monthly payment can include expected claims, administrative expenses, and stop-loss coverage.

How Many Employees Do You Need?

There is no universal employee-count requirement. Eligibility depends on the carrier, state, underwriting, plan design, and employee population.

Can Level Funding Save My Company Money?

It can, but savings are not guaranteed. Employers should compare their existing plan with alternative funding strategies using actual company data.

Should My Company Switch to Level Funding?

Not necessarily. The right decision should consider cost, risk, employee value, plan design, network requirements, stop-loss coverage, and long-term sustainability—not simply the lowest monthly premium.

Who Can Help?

An experienced employee benefits consultant can help employers compare fully insured, level-funded, and other health plan options.

At JS Benefits Group, we help employers evaluate funding strategies, optimize plan design, manage healthcare costs, and develop competitive employee benefits programs.

About Jennifer Schaefer

Jennifer Schaefer, MBA, ChFC, CLU, RHU, REBC, SHRM-SCP, is Founder & CEO of JS Benefits Group, an employee benefits and HR consulting firm based in Newtown, Pennsylvania.

Jennifer works with employers on employee benefits strategy, group health insurance, level-funded health plans, healthcare cost containment, plan design, HR consulting, corporate wellness, compliance, and benefits education.

JS Benefits Group serves employers throughout Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, New York, and beyond.

metadata.title: Mark Cuban and Cora Opsahl: The Truth About Pass-Through PBM Contracts and Generic Compliance Ratios
metadata.author: Relentless Health Value
metadata.shortDescription:
How Discount Theater and Generic Compliance Ratios Quietly Overcharge Patients and Employers. Episode 526.

Mark Cuban, co-founder of Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company, and Cora Opsahl, managing director of Peterson Health Analytics and former director of the 32BJ Health Fund, join Stacey Richter for an outtake from their conversation last fall (EP488) on the operational mechanics of the pharmacy supply chain.

They trace how a generic compliance ratio—typically requiring pharmacies to buy at least 92% of their generics from a single primary wholesaler—pushes independent pharmacies into paying a premium that gets passed straight to patients, and how so-called pass-through PBM contracts can pay pharmacies using one pricing formula while billing employers using an entirely different one.

Along the way, they walk through the classic generic imatinib example—a drug Cost Plus Drugs sells for $25 a month that a traditional PBM channel has billed at $9,000—to show why a discount off an inflated reference price is, as Cuban puts it, discount theater.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
✅ Why pharmacies get locked into overpaying: wholesalers set a Generic Compliance Ratio requiring pharmacies to buy at least 92% of their generics from them or face chargebacks and fees that wipe out their margin

✅ The classic generic imatinib example: Cost Plus Drugs sells it for $25 a month, while the same drug billed through a traditional PBM channel has run $9,000 a month—a “discount” off a $27,000 branded Gleevec price that Mark Cuban calls discount theater

✅ How specialty tiers compound the problem: because generic imatinib gets classified on a specialty tier, patients can owe 25% coinsurance calculated off the inflated WAC price rather than the drug’s real cost

✅ Why a “pass-through” PBM contract isn’t simple math: Cora Opsahl explains that PBMs often reimburse pharmacies on an acquisition-cost-plus formula while billing employers a completely different AWP-minus formula for the same claim

✅ Why claims audits keep finding money owed back to the plan—and why employers are often restricted to auditing only a pre-approved sample of 250 claims

✅ Mark Cuban’s advice for the next RFP: simply requiring that Cost Plus Drugs be included in the network is often enough on its own to get PBMs to offer better rebates and terms

WHY THIS MATTERS
As Stacey Richter puts it, where there’s mystery, there’s margin—and pharmacy pricing is thick with both. Generic compliance ratios, WAC-based specialty tiers, and pass-through contracts that pay pharmacies one number while billing employers another all point to the same underlying reality: so much of what gets called an expense in medicine is simply pricing failure. For plan sponsors and brokers heading into their next RFP, understanding these mechanics—rather than accepting a discount off an inflated reference price—is what it takes to move from passive price taker to informed decision maker.

Did you know that three massive Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) control over 80% of the market? If your business isn't using a transparent PBM, you could be overpaying by 30–50% on your pharmacy spend—and not even know it.

But this isn’t just a budget issue. When medications cost too much, employees may skip doses, ration their prescriptions, or avoid filling them altogether. That leads to worse health outcomes, higher long-term costs, and avoidable strain on your team.

In this video, we break down:
💊 How the PBM system really works (and who it’s working for)
📉 The hidden costs of non-transparent contracts
❤️‍🩹 Why pharmacy pricing is both a financial and human issue for your business
✅ What smart companies are doing to take back control

If you're serious about managing healthcare costs and protecting your people, this is a conversation worth having.

Visit https://www.BenefitsOnTheFly.com to book a call

Vernon Bonfield - Founder & CEO - Employee Benefits Broker
Washington Health Insurance Agency 
Benefits On The Fly

metadata.title: Modern PBM 101 with Alan Pannier, PharmD, MBA: Continuous Pricing Improvement
metadata.author: SmithRx
metadata.shortDescription:
Legacy pharmacy benefit management relies on rigid, fixed-pricing contracts that lock employers into static discount rates for years. While PBMs negotiate better drug prices across the supply chain over time, those savings are trapped behind fixed contract terms rather than reaching plan sponsors or their members.

SmithRx is taking a fundamentally different approach to pharmacy benefits. As a modern, transparent PBM, our platform-based pricing philosophy ensures that new cost savings negotiated across pharmacy networks and drug manufacturers are passed on to clients immediately.

Alan Pannier, Chief Strategy Officer at SmithRx, outlines how many benefit managers retain these savings for themselves and, conversely, how modern models can deliver a consistent reduction in per member per month (PMPM) spend.

Connect with Us:
Website: https://www.smithrx.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/smithrx

segments.text: My name is Alan Pannier, Chief Strategy Officer at SmithRx. And today we're going to talk about
continuous pricing improvement in pharmacy benefits. Historically, employer plan sponsors
contract with pharmacy benefit managers under a fixed pricing model, meaning that as they go
through the evaluation process and they select a pharmacy benefit manager to provide services for
them, they negotiate and agree upon fixed discount guarantees in their contract.
The challenge with this model, whether it's a traditional, spread-based pricing model or even
a pass-through model, is that in this contracting structure, the pharmacy benefit manager is then
incentivized to manage and set pricing towards these fixed rates. What this means for the plan
sponsor or the employer is that as time goes on underneath that contract, pricing is improving as
the PBM is consistently negotiating better pricing with the retail pharmacies and drug manufacturers.
There's also opportunities to optimize drug mix available in the market. As these opportunities
come about, the plan sponsor under their current arrangement with the PBM is not getting access
to this pricing because their pricing is set on this fixed agreement that they've come to
with the pharmacy benefit manager. At SmithRx, we take a fundamentally different approach. Our
platform-based pricing philosophy allows clients to continuously benefit from new pricing contracts
as we're negotiating across the supply chain. What this means for a plan sponsor is that as
we negotiate across the supply chain and receive better pricing improvements across our pharmacy
network and with drug manufacturers, this new updated pricing is applied immediately and plan
sponsors are able to see these benefits in real time as we apply the pricing across our book of
business using our platform based model. What this looks like in reality is consistent improvements
and a reduction in your per member per month spend over the course that you're with SmithRx.

Pharmacy benefit managers or PBMs are
companies that manage prescription drug
benefits on behalf of health insurers,
Medicare Part D drug plans, large
employers, and other payers.

and pharmacies to control drug spending,
PBMs have a significant
behind-the-scenes impact in determining
total drug costs for insurers, shaping
patients' access to medications, and
determining how much pharmacies are
paid.
PBMs have faced growing scrutiny about
their role in rising prescription drug
costs and spending.
What role do PBMs play in how much we
spend on prescription drugs? PBMs
operate in the middle of the
distribution chain for prescription
drugs. That's because they develop and
maintain lists or formularies of covered
medications on behalf of health
insurers, which influence which drugs
individuals use and determine
out-of-pocket costs. Use their
purchasing power to negotiate rebates
and discounts from drug manufacturers,
and contract directly with individual
pharmacies to reimburse for drugs
dispensed to beneficiaries.
The federal Centers for Medicare and
Medicaid Services found that PBMs'

manufacturers has helped lower drug
prices and slow the growth of drug
spending over the last 3 years. But PBMs
may also have an incentive to favor
high-priced drugs over drugs that are
more cost-effective.
Because they often receive rebates that
are calculated as a percentage of the
manufacturer's list price, PBMs receive
a larger rebate for expensive drugs than
they do for ones that may provide better
value at lower cost.
As a result, people who have a high
deductible plan or have copays based on
a drug's list price may incur higher
out-of-pocket costs.
What's the controversy over the rebates
PBMs receive from drug companies?
Drug manufacturers argue that the
growing rebates they pay PBMs are
forcing them to raise list prices for
their products. According to a recent
analysis, manufacturer rebates to PBMs
increased from $39.7 billion
to $89.5 billion in 2016,
partially offsetting list price
increases.
PBMs counter that they have been passing
along a larger share of the rebates to
insurers. There is a lot of debate over
whether PBMs should be able to keep the
rebates they receive from drug
manufacturers, which generally aren't
publicly disclosed. Some believe PBMs
should be compelled to pass through all
or a larger portion of these savings to
health insurers and other payers. If
PBMs were required to do this, insurers
could use the savings to further reduce
people's premiums and cost-sharing
payments.
A recent study found that the share of
rebates PBMs passed through to insurers
and payers increased from 78% in 2012 to
But many small insurers and employers
say they do not receive this share of
savings.
A separate controversy involves a PBM
practice known as spread pricing,
whereby PBMs are reimbursed by health
plans and employers a higher price for
generic drugs than what the PBMs
actually pay pharmacies for these drugs.
The PBMs then keep the difference.
Again, a lack of transparency allows
this to happen. The payment schedules
PBMs generate for pharmacies are kept
confidential from health plans.

regulate PBMs?

rebates.

need more data on the rebates PBMs
receive to gain a more complete
understanding of pharmaceutical spending
and where reforms may be needed. Two,
ban spread pricing. Policy makers could

through rebates to payers or to
patients.

According to a recent analysis, manufacturer rebates to PBMs increased from $39.7 billion in 2012 to $89.5 billion in 2016, partially offsetting list price increases. PBMs counter that they have been passing along a larger share of the rebates to insurers. There is a lot of debate over whether PBMs should be able to keep the rebates they receive from drug manufacturers, which generally aren't publicly disclosed. Some believe PBMs should be compelled to pass through all or a larger portion of these savings to health insurers and other payers. If PBMs were required to do this, insurers could use the savings to further reduce people's premiums and cost-sharing payments. A recent study found that the share of rebates PBMs passed through to insurers and payers increased from 78% in 2012 to 91% in 2016. But many small insurers and employers say they do not receive this share of savings. A separate controversy involves a PBM practice known as spread pricing, whereby PBMs are reimbursed by health plans and employers a higher price for generic drugs than what the PBMs actually pay pharmacies for these drugs. The PBMs then keep the difference. Again, a lack of transparency allows this to happen. The payment schedules PBMs generate for pharmacies are kept confidential from health plans. What reforms have been proposed to regulate PBMs? Policy makers have considered three principal reforms to regulate PBMs. One, require greater transparency around rebates. Federal and state policy makers likely need more data on the rebates PBMs receive to gain a more complete understanding of pharmaceutical spending and where reforms may be needed. Two, ban spread pricing. Policy makers could ban the practice to ensure that payers and employers are not overpaying PBMs for prescription drugs. A more limited proposal would mandate that PBMs update their cost schedules with pharmacies to reflect price increases for generic drugs. Three, require PBMs to pass through rebates to payers or to patients. To preserve some of their incentive to negotiate price reductions with drug makers, PBMs could be required to pass through 90% of their rebate savings to payers. Alternatively, PBMs could be required to pass through rebates to patients. The federal government has in fact proposed requiring PBMs contracted with Medicare Part D plans to pass through to patients at least 1/3 of the rebates and price concessions they receive. Thank you for listening. Please like and subscribe. I appreciate your time.

year. Health insurance costs are
increasing. [music] And one of the big
excuses for these never-ending increases
is that prescription drugs are getting
more expensive. [music] And while that
is true, the cost of produced drugs is
increasing, I would argue it's marginal
in comparison to what a middleman that
most have never heard of has done to the
cost of drugs. Because patients don't
get pills from them and they don't make
any drugs themselves, pharmacy benefit
managers were able to stay under the
radar historically until relatively
recently. But as some of the most
profitable middlemen in healthcare,
they're estimated to have generated just
under 600 billion last year in revenue.
They didn't hate that most people knew
nothing about them. That worked in their
favor. But we should know a lot more
about pharmacy benefit managers. They
control which drugs over 250 million
Americans are allowed to take, how much
those Americans are forced to pay for
those medications, and where they can
even go to buy them. So, let's get into
what PBMs do, how they make money, and
three of the big controversies
surrounding these guys. Let's dive in.
Now, I think I've actually watched every
single video on PBMs on YouTube, and
that's because I wanted to see how
others explained it. Admittedly, this is
a very complex topic. There's already a
lot of jargon in healthcare, and I think
there's maybe more jargon around PBMs
than 95 to 99% of other healthcare
topics. So, I'm going to do my best to
explain this in layman's terms and just
break down the basics of pharmacy
benefit managers. And I think the best
way to do that is to start with what
they do and who they do it for before
getting into all the money. So, PBM
primarily work for three groups. They
work for the government, insurance
companies, and American companies. Why
these three? Well, because these three
offer insurance plans to patients and to
their own employees. PBMs run the drug
part of the insurance plans for these
three groups. So, what does a PBM do
for, say, a decent-sized American
company that runs their insurance
inhouse? This is how a majority of
Americans get their insurance, by the
way. Well, so for that company, first
they need to figure out what drugs to
include on their insurance plan for
their employees. So, the first thing
that the PBM does is create something
that's called a formulary for this
company. A formulary is just an
insurance term that means a list of
approved drugs that the company will
offer to their employees. And to make
this list, the PBM will go out to all
the different drug companies, get
prices, and then decide which drugs will
be chosen. And for these formularies or
the list of approved drugs for these
employees, there's usually four
different tiers. Tier one is generic
drugs. This is the cheapest option.
These are the everyday medications with
the lowest co-pays for employees.
Usually go to the pharmacy, pay 5 to 10
bucks. Tier two is the preferred
brandame drugs. They cost more than
generics, but insurance still covers a
large portion of the cost. It's usually
20 to 40 bucks. Tier three is the
non-preferred brand name drugs. These
are the expensive brand names without
PBM discounts. Patients usually pay much
higher co-pays. Think $60 plus. You're
going to pay significantly more for this
tier than you would for tiers one or
two. And then tier four is specialty
drugs. So this is the most expensive
tier for complex chronic illnesses like
cancer. So instead of a flat copay,
patients usually pay a percentage of the
massive total cost. So, how does a
pharmacy benefit manager go about
choosing the drug or choosing which tier
it should go on? Well, that's heavily
dependent on something called rebates,
which we'll get into in a second. But
one thing I want to mention before is
that if a drug isn't on this list, then
the employee has to pay for it
completely out of pocket. So, what else
do PBMs do for this hypothetical
company? Well, second, they decide where
these employees can go buy their
medications. They'll build what's called
a pharmacy network. So, they'll contract
with mom and popies and more likely CVS
and Walgreens because some of these PBMs
are actually owned by the same people
who own CVS and Walgreens. And they'll
create an approved list ofarmacies that
these employees can go to. And if an
employee does decide to go to a pharmacy
that isn't on that list, the insurance
usually won't cover it. You'll have to
pay 100% out of pocket. And the third
thing that PBMs do is once the employee
goes to that approved pharmacy to pick
up the approved drug, the PBM will
process it. Meaning, when the pharmacist
scans their insurance card, that data
goes straight to the PBM. In a second or
two, their computer checks if the
insurance is active, looks up what tier
the drug is on, and decides exactly how
much the insurance company pays versus
how much cash that employee has to hand
over. So, to recap the basics of what
they do, they control what drugs
Americans can take, where they can go to
buy them, and then they run the tech
when they pay for them. So, now you know
the basics of the main things that PBMs
do. Now, let's take a look at how they
make their money and some of the
controversies.
So, why does this company even decide to
work with a PBM? Why not just negotiate
with the drug manufacturer or drug maker
and get the drugs that they need
themselves? Well, let's say this company
that we've been talking about only has
100 employees and they've got four
employees who have diabetes and need
insulin. Purely hypothetical, but this
big drug manufacturer is not going to be
offering any discounts for four
employees. PBMs, on the other hand, have
tons of companies that they negotiate
for, and that's millions of insulin
prescriptions. So, they get major
discounts, which is actually one of the
ways that PBMs make their money. It's
called a rebate. And before I explain
it, check out this breakdown of what a
rebate even is from KFF Health News. I
think they do a really good job of
explaining them.
>> Think of them like the coupons you send
in when you buy a new brand of soap or
an electronic gadget. Pop it in the mail
and a few months later you get a check
for $3. That happens with PBMs, but on a
much larger scale.
>> Now, PBMs get to share drug rebates with
the companies that they create that
approved drug list for or that
formulary. And since PBMs work for
hundreds of thousands of companies and
so they represent millions of patients,
they'll go to these four different drug
manufacturers or drug makers that make
insulin and then they'll say, "We'll put
your expensive brandame diabetes drug on
tier 2 of our formulary, meaning
millions of people will buy it, but only
if you give us a huge rebate." Then the
drug manufacturers will compete to give
the PBM the biggest rebate because they
want their drug on tier 2 for all of
those companies. Essentially, these drug
companies are having to buy their way on
to tier one or tier two of these
approved insurance lists. To reiterate,
if the drug isn't on tier 1 or tier two,
the drug company's losing out on a lot
of money because if one of those
employees want it, they'll have to pay
for it out of pocket versus the company
insurance plan covering most of it. So,
let's give a hypothetical. Let's say
those four drug companies give their
list price and then also the rebate
price that they're willing to pay that
PBM to get on a better tier. If you look
at this chart, the obvious choice is
option one. The PBM would get the
cheapest price for the company. But hold
up. Remember the PBM gets to share the
rebate. So that's not the one the PBM's
going to pick. The PBM's going to pick
Pharma Company 3. Why? Because even
though that drug has the highest sticker
price at $300, it also comes with the
biggest rebate. A $70 check that gets
split between the PBM and the company
after the drug is sold. And that's for
every single drug that's bought at the
pharmacy. Again, the bigger the rebate
check, the more money that they make.
And that actually means that they have a
financial incentive to choose the
highest pric drug if it has the biggest
rebate. So, the PBM takes Pharma Company
3, slaps it onto tier two of the
company's formulary, and ignores the
cheaper options. And the PBM can even
tell the company that they're making
this approved drug list for that it got
them the biggest discount out there.
They don't actually have to reveal the
cost of the other drugs. And I'll get
into why this is bad for patients in a
second, but how else do PBMs make money?
Well, another big way is through
something called spread pricing or a
spread, which in and of itself has
created a lot of controversy lately.
Now, remember I said that the PBM does
three big things, and that's related
here. They make those approved drug
lists for our company. They determine
what those employees pay for the meds
that they need. And third, they choose
where those employees can go to buy them
and basically do that whole drug
processing thing we mentioned at the
pharmacy. So think about that for a
second. They basically work with the
company in that interaction, but they
also work with the pharmacy as well. So
the PBM writes one contract with the
company and a completely separate
contract with the pharmacy. And the
crazy thing is neither side is allowed
to see what's in the other one's
paperwork. So let's continue that
previous example. Let's look at how this
plays out with the exact same company 3
insulin. The PBM goes to the company and
says, "Hey, for this insulin, the
sticker price is $300, but good news, we
negotiated a $50 rebate for you. So,
it's only going to cost you $250." So,
the company thinks that PBM did a great
job getting a discount. It pays $300,
but they're going to get a $50 rebate
later. Basically, $250. What that
company doesn't know is that that total
rebate check was actually $70, and the
PBM just quietly pocketed $20 of it for
themselves. But where it gets worse is
the spread part here. Then the PBM turns
around to the pharmacy that actually
handed the insulin to that company's
employee and says, "We're going to only
pay you $200 for that insulin. Take it
or leave it." The pharmacy has no choice
but to accept that $200 because if they
don't, the PBM will kick them out of the
approved network ofarmacies and then
they're going to lose out on thousands
of customers. And because the PBM
actually runs the billing software at
the register, their system automatically
charges the employer the $250, pays the
pharmacy $200, and then they pocket that
$50 difference. That $50 is the spread.
So, on the single prescription, the PBM
made a secret $20 off the rebate and a
secret $50 off the spread. It's a
completely hidden markup on millions of
drugs every single day. And PBMs also
make money through administration fees
with those companies and different
things, but that's for another video.
Let's get into three of the big
controversies surrounding PBMs.
Now, you might be thinking, if a big
drug company has to hand over massive
rebates to get on these approved
insurance lists or these formularies,
aren't they losing a lot of money? Well,
no, because they're not stupid. They
already know that they're going to have
to pay these big rebates to PBMs to play
the game, to make it onto the formulary.
So, what do they do? Here's what the
former CEO of a major drug company
speaking before Congress said.
>> If you bring a product to the market
with a low list price in this system,
you get punished financially and you get
no uptake because everyone in the supply
chain makes money as a result of a
higher list price. Basically, it creates
this vicious cycle where the list price
of medications keeps going up and up and
up every single year just so that PBMs
can negotiate bigger discounts even
though the actual cost to make the
medication maybe hasn't changed that
much. And besides the company, this
brings us to another person who pays
this inflated price, the patient.
Remember, if you're prescribed an
expensive tier three or tier 4 specialty
drug, you usually aren't paying a flat
$10 co-pay. You're going to be paying a
percentage of the total cost, like 30%
co insurance, or you're paying
completely out of pocket until you hit
your high deductible. Well, the problem
is here. Your bill at the pharmacy
register is based off that inflated
initial list price that the drug company
sets. It's not based off the secret
rebate that the PBM made because that's
secret. Now, you'd think that companies
that are using these PBMs are at least
saving money. But it's hard to say
because PBM contracts are basically a
giant black box. Many employers are
flying totally blind. When a company
suspects that they're being overcharged
and asks to see the receipts, like,
"Hey, what did you actually pay the
pharmacy versus what you charged us?"
The PBM can just say no. They actually
write clauses into their contracts
calling the real drug cost confidential
trade secrets. So even though some
employers believe that they're getting
these incredible deals from PBM because
they see these rebate checks, they might
actually be paying more than they needed
to. And when the company's overall
healthcare costs go up as a result, they
either need to eat that or ask the
employees to pay a larger share. Now,
this is just a basic breakdown of how
PBMs work. We're just scratching the
surface here. I'll be dropping a future
video going much deeper into the system,
but you can check out my video on how
pharmaceutical companies play a part in
exorbitant drug prices here. This is
Tyler Dutchover.

What that company doesn't know is that that total rebate check was actually $70, and the PBM just quietly pocketed $20 of it for themselves. But where it gets worse is the spread part here. Then the PBM turns around to the pharmacy that actually handed the insulin to that company's employee and says, "We're going to only pay you $200 for that insulin. Take it or leave it." The pharmacy has no choice but to accept that $200 because if they don't, the PBM will kick them out of the approved network ofarmacies and then they're going to lose out on thousands of customers. And because the PBM actually runs the billing software at the register, their system automatically charges the employer the $250, pays the pharmacy $200, and then they pocket that $50 difference. That $50 is the spread. So, on the single prescription, the PBM made a secret $20 off the rebate and a secret $50 off the spread. It's a completely hidden markup on millions of drugs every single day. And PBMs also make money through administration fees with those companies and different things, but that's for another video. Let's get into three of the big controversies surrounding PBMs. Now, you might be thinking, if a big drug company has to hand over massive rebates to get on these approved insurance lists or these formularies, aren't they losing a lot of money? Well, no, because they're not stupid. They already know that they're going to have to pay these big rebates to PBMs to play the game, to make it onto the formulary. So, what do they do? Here's what the former CEO of a major drug company speaking before Congress said. >> If you bring a product to the market with a low list price in this system, you get punished financially and you get no uptake because everyone in the supply chain makes money as a result of a higher list price. Basically, it creates this vicious cycle where the list price of medications keeps going up and up and up every single year just so that PBMs can negotiate bigger discounts even though the actual cost to make the medication maybe hasn't changed that much. And besides the company, this brings us to another person who pays this inflated price, the patient. Remember, if you're prescribed an expensive tier three or tier 4 specialty drug, you usually aren't paying a flat $10 co-pay. You're going to be paying a percentage of the total cost, like 30% co insurance, or you're paying completely out of pocket until you hit your high deductible. Well, the problem is here. Your bill at the pharmacy register is based off that inflated initial list price that the drug company sets. It's not based off the secret rebate that the PBM made because that's secret. Now, you'd think that companies that are using these PBMs are at least saving money. But it's hard to say because PBM contracts are basically a giant black box. Many employers are flying totally blind. When a company suspects that they're being overcharged and asks to see the receipts, like, "Hey, what did you actually pay the pharmacy versus what you charged us?" The PBM can just say no. They actually write clauses into their contracts calling the real drug cost confidential trade secrets. So even though some employers believe that they're getting these incredible deals from PBM because they see these rebate checks, they might actually be paying more than they needed to. And when the company's overall healthcare costs go up as a result, they either need to eat that or ask the employees to pay a larger share. Now, this is just a basic breakdown of how PBMs work. We're just scratching the surface here. I'll be dropping a future video going much deeper into the system, but you can check out my video on how pharmaceutical companies play a part in exorbitant drug prices here. This is Tyler Dutchover.

metadata.title: Healthcare’s New Frontier | The Future of Employee Benefits
metadata.author: Maxwell Health
metadata.shortDescription:
Healthcare's New Frontier — A Pathway from Reactive to Preventive Care
What if benefits advisors could help employers reduce healthcare costs, improve employee access to care, and create new opportunities to grow their own practices?
For decades, our healthcare system has focused primarily on treating conditions after they develop. Meanwhile, chronic medical conditions and healthcare costs have continued to place increasing pressure on American employers and families.
But advances in technology, healthcare connectivity, and artificial intelligence are creating new opportunities to change that equation.
Introducing Maxwell Health.
Maxwell is a healthcare optimization platform designed to help benefits advisors and employers move beyond traditional annual insurance renewals toward a more continuous, data-driven approach to managing healthcare costs, employee engagement, and health outcomes.
In this executive briefing, we explore:
• The Problem: Why rising chronic conditions and healthcare costs are creating an increasingly unsustainable burden.
• The Solution: How preventive care, connected healthcare data, and emerging technology can create opportunities for better healthcare decisions.
• The Maxwell Platform: How Strategy Optimization, Implementation Optimization, and Performance Optimization work together to help employers improve their healthcare programs.
• The Broker Opportunity: How benefits advisors can differentiate their practices, develop new revenue opportunities, strengthen client relationships, and acquire new employers.
A New Opportunity for Benefits Advisors
Maxwell is designed to empower independent health insurance brokers and employee benefits advisors with tools to compare traditional group health insurance, ICHRA, and self-funded alternatives, simplify implementation, and support continuous healthcare optimization.
Our mission is to help transform healthcare from a predominantly reactive system into one that is increasingly preventive, accessible, and cost-effective.
Ready to explore Maxwell Health?
Visit https://www.maxwellhealth.io to learn more about the platform or request a demonstration.
Maxwell Health
Healthcare Optimization

metadata.title: Can Your Small Business Afford Employee Benefits? 4 Options | Benefit Experts
metadata.author: Benefit Experts
metadata.shortDescription:
"We can't afford benefits" usually means the wrong plan was priced. This video covers what going without really costs (longer hiring, turnover, wage pressure) and four ways small businesses offer coverage: a small-group plan where you set the employer share, a level-funded plan (refunds are possible, not promised), an HRA with a fixed allowance, and voluntary benefits employees pay for through payroll deduction.

Read more: https://benefit-experts.com/blog/group-benefits-guide/
Talk with Benefit Experts: (206) 556-2993

0:41 Option 2: level-funded
0:52 Option 3: an HRA
1:01 Voluntary benefits
1:13 How we start
1:24 Find out what it could cost

What is reference-based pricing, how does it work, and what does it cost employers? This video covers how self-funded plans pay hospitals a set multiple of Medicare instead of network rates, how employers set it up, what the research shows about prices, and the two catches to know: balance billing and hospitals that won't take part.

metadata.title: Gag Clauses and Fiduciary Attestations
metadata.author: Clear Value Benefit Compliance
metadata.shortDescription:
Join our LinkedIn Group: https://www.linkedin.com/groups/14209570/

The No Surprises Act bans “Gag clauses” that prevent disclosure of price or Quality information in agreements between health plans and certain service providers. Plan Sponsors are now required to attest annually that they comply with this requirement.

So, what is a Gag Clause? A Gag clause is a contractual term used to describe a provision of a contract between parties that restricts the amount of information a provider may share with a fiduciary or that limits the circumstances under which a provider may recommend a specific treatment option. 

To put this another way, the Act itself prohibits Health Plans and Insurance issuers from entering into contracts with health care providers, provider networks, TPAs or other services providers that would restrict the plan from providing, sharing or accessing certain information.

Specifically, contracts cannot restrict a plan from:

Electronically accessing De-identified claims information or data from a participant, enrollee or beneficiary upon request. 

They cannot restrict a plan from disclosing provider specific quality of care information to plan sponsors, beneficiaries, participants or referring providers.

And They cannot restrict a plan from sharing the information just mentioned previously or directing such information to be shared with a Business Associate.

The first gag clause attestation is due to be submitted by December 31, 2023. This covers the period of time beginning December 27th, 2020 through the date of the attestation. Ongoing these attestations will be due by December 31st of each year.

Plan Sponsors should work to ensure that any contracts with TPAs or other network service providers do not contain gag clauses. In addition plan sponsors need to complete the attestation by December 31st. 

Plan Sponsors, otherwise known as fiduciaries that do not comply may face a penalty for as much as 100 dollars per affected individual per day, for a violation. 

For help with preparing these attestations, self-funded groups can reach out to HealthCareReporting.com, where a service member can walk you through the process of submission.
